text:
Everyone thinks they know what "wild animal" means. They don't.

A 6-ton predator with 40 conical teeth stayed beside a stranded calf on the rocks for hours while strangers poured water over its skin to keep it alive. That's not even the part that breaks people's model of the ocean. This is: months later, footage started circulating of an adult orca near that same stretch of coast — carrying a stingray in her mouth, closing the distance toward the person who'd been there that day.

The internet decided what that meant in about four seconds. A gift. A thank you. Proof that the ocean remembers kindness and pays it back.

Marine biologists are a lot less sure. And that gap — between what we want an apex predator to be and what the actual research says an apex predator is — is the whole story here. Not the clip. The gap.

—

THE PARADOX, STATED PLAINLY

Orcas are, at the same time, the most studied and the most misunderstood animal in the ocean. We've tagged them. We've tracked individual pods for over fifty consecutive years. We know their family trees down to specific grandmothers, their vocal dialects down to specific pods, their hunting techniques down to specific maneuvers taught across specific generations.

And we still cannot tell you, with any real certainty, why one of them carried a fish toward a boat.

That's not a knowledge gap waiting to be filled with a better camera angle. That's the actual finding. The smartest predator in the ocean keeps doing things precise enough to look intentional and ambiguous enough that nobody can prove it.

We keep trying to compress the most cognitively complex hunter on Earth into a caption short enough for a fifteen-second attention span. It never quite fits. It's not supposed to.

—

MYTHBUST #1: "KILLER WHALE" ISN'T EVEN THE RIGHT ANIMAL CATEGORY

Orcinus orca is not a whale. Taxonomically, it's the largest member of the dolphin family, Delphinidae. Blue whales, humpbacks, grays, belugas — different branch of the family tree entirely, separated by tens of millions of years of divergent evolution. An orca is, biologically speaking, a six-ton dolphin that hunts in coordinated, communicating packs and has been documented taking down great white sharks by flipping them upside down to trigger tonic immobility, then surgically removing the liver — the single most calorie-dense organ on the animal — while leaving the rest.

Not a whale. A dolphin that eats whales, and occasionally the animals that eat everything else in the ocean too.

The name "killer whale" was coined by 18th-century whalers who watched pods take down much larger baleen whales and called them "whale killers." Over centuries of translation and retelling, the words flipped. Nobody ever corrected it. Three hundred years later, the name still shapes how an entire species gets perceived by people who will never see one outside a screen.

A mistranslation became a personality trait. That's not biology. That's branding.

—

THE NUMBERS NOBODY PUTS IN THE CAPTION

Bite force: recorded up to roughly 19,000 PSI in some measurements of the largest individuals — not just "strong," but somewhere around 4x the bite force of an American alligator, and more than enough to shear through cartilage and bone in a single closure of the jaw.

Speed: orcas have been clocked at over 34 mph in short bursts, making them one of the fastest marine mammals alive — fast enough that they can outrun most recreational boats trying to keep pace, and fast enough to run down a dolphin, an animal built almost entirely for speed, in open water.

Range: a single resident pod can cover 75 to 100+ miles of coastline in a single day while foraging, patrolling a home range that, over a year, can exceed the total area of some small countries.

Depth: orcas have been recorded diving past 100 meters, and some populations that specialize in deep-water prey like squid have been tracked going considerably deeper, holding their breath for 15 minutes or more on a single dive.

Size at birth: a newborn calf already weighs around 350 to 400 pounds and measures roughly 8 feet long — heavier at birth than most adult humans will ever weigh in their lives, and born tail-first into open ocean, with its mother or an aunt from the pod there to push it to the surface for its first breath within seconds.

Lifespan and memory: resident matriarchs — the oldest females who lead the pod — have been documented living past 90 years old in the wild. Researchers studying the Southern Resident population have tracked these matriarchs leading their pods back to specific foraging grounds learned and remembered across decades, well past the point where the matriarch herself is still reproductively active.

Every one of those numbers describes an animal engineered, from birth, to hunt with total efficiency across enormous ranges for the better part of a century. None of them describe an animal engineered to say thank you.

That's exactly what makes a stingray, offered rather than eaten, so hard to file away and forget.

—

MYTHBUST #2: THEY DON'T ATTACK HUMANS IN THE WILD THE WAY THE MOVIES TAUGHT YOU

Zero confirmed fatal attacks by a wild, free-ranging orca on a human being, ever, in recorded history. Not one. This is an apex predator capable of hunting great white sharks and moose swimming between islands, sharing open water with surfers, divers, and swimmers across multiple continents for as long as humans have been in the water — and the fatality count involving wild individuals sits at zero.

Compare that to captivity. Every documented fatal orca attack on a human involves a captive animal, held for years or decades in a tank that is, at best, a tiny fraction of its natural range, under conditions that would be recognized as severely psychologically damaging in almost any other intelligent, social mammal. Different animal, different stressors, different — and thoroughly documented — outcome. The wild data and the captive data tell two completely different stories, and pop culture has spent decades flattening them into one.

Wild orcas encountering humans in the water have been overwhelmingly documented as curious, cautious, sometimes playful, occasionally indifferent — never predatory toward the swimmer. Divers who've spent time with resident pods describe an animal that investigates, keeps its distance, and moves on. The predator that eats sharks for a snack has never once, in the wild, eaten a human.

The name said "killer." The data says something closer to careful.

—

THE INTELLIGENCE SECTION: WHAT'S ACTUALLY GOING ON IN THAT SKULL

Orcas possess spindle neurons — specialized, elongated brain cells associated with rapid social processing, empathy, and self-awareness, previously thought to exist only in humans and great apes before they were identified in cetacean brains. Their brains are, in absolute terms, roughly four times the mass of a human brain, and in several cetacean studies, the limbic system — the region most associated with emotional processing and social bonding — is structurally more elaborated in orcas than in humans.

They have dialects. Not calls in the generic sense — actual, distinct vocal dialects that differ from pod to pod, passed down through learning rather than instinct. A calf raised within a particular pod picks up that pod's specific dialect and typically keeps it for life, the same way a person raised in a particular region keeps an accent. Researchers studying different populations — residents that hunt fish, transients that hunt marine mammals, offshore populations that specialize in sharks — have found that these groups don't just eat differently, they sound different, hunt differently, and in some documented cases won't even interbreed with each other despite overlapping ranges, because the cultural gap between groups has become functionally as significant as a species boundary.

Teaching has been directly observed, not inferred. Orca mothers and aunts have been recorded deliberately beaching themselves in slow motion next to a calf to demonstrate how to strand-feed on seals — a genuinely dangerous hunting technique — then correcting the calf's form across multiple attempts over multiple seasons until it gets it right. That is not instinct executing automatically. That is a teacher, a student, a curriculum, and patience.

An animal with regional dialects, cultural food traditions, and multi-generational deliberate teaching is not running on a script. It's running on something a lot closer to what we would, in any other context, call judgment.

Which is exactly why the stingray moment refuses to die quietly online. Judgment implies intention. Intention is the single hardest thing for science to confirm in a nonverbal animal, and the single easiest thing for a caption to claim in four words.

—

MYTHBUST #3: "DOLPHIN-SAFE" INSTINCTS DON'T MEAN "HUMAN-SAFE" BY DEFAULT

A common assumption is that because orcas are intelligent and largely gentle toward humans in the wild, that gentleness is some kind of built-in universal rule, like a switch that's always on. It isn't. It's closer to a track record. Wild orcas have shown consistent, repeated patterns of caution and curiosity around humans across decades of documented encounters on multiple continents — but that pattern exists because these are wild, free, socially complex animals choosing, again and again, not to treat people as prey, not because of some hardwired absolute law.

That distinction matters, because it means every calm encounter, every curious pass, every fish brought toward a boat, is closer to a choice than a reflex. And a six-ton animal capable of taking apart a great white shark choosing curiosity over aggression, over and over, across generations and oceans, is a far stranger and more interesting fact than any instinct could ever be.

—

THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART THE CLIP DOESN'T SHOW

Here's what doesn't make it into a caption doing forty million views: several orca populations along heavily studied coastlines are in genuine, ongoing trouble. The Southern Resident population — among the most intensively researched groups of orcas on the planet — has been reduced to roughly 70-something individuals, driven by a combination of collapsing salmon stocks that make up the overwhelming majority of their diet, chronic vessel noise that interferes with the echolocation they depend on to hunt, and decades of industrial pollutants that accumulate in their blubber over a lifetime.

Those pollutants don't stay with the mother. Orca milk is extremely fat-rich, which means it's also extremely effective at transferring a lifetime of stored toxins directly into a nursing calf, especially the firstborn. In documented cases, the first calf a mother orca raises can carry a significantly heavier toxic burden than her later calves, simply because she's offloading the highest concentration of what she's accumulated over her own lifetime into the very first calf she tries to keep alive.

A mother trying to save her baby, and in the act of feeding it, passing on the damage of an ocean she didn't create. That's not a detail that trends. It's the part that's true on an ordinary Tuesday, gift or no gift, rescue footage or not.

If the story of a stranded calf and a mother's gratitude is what gets someone to care about orcas for the first time, that's not nothing. But the animal deserves the whole picture, not just the fifteen seconds built for a loop.

—

WHY THE "THANK YOU" STORY REFUSES TO DIE, EVEN AMONG SCIENTISTS

Researchers studying reciprocal and gift-like behavior in cetaceans — dolphins nudging objects toward boats, orcas approaching divers or vessels with prey still held in their mouths — mostly land in a careful middle ground rather than a flat yes or no. It could be an extension of within-pod food-sharing behavior, generalized outward toward an unfamiliar but non-threatening presence. It could be curiosity, an animal investigating a novel object by presenting it the way it would present prey to a podmate. It could, plausibly, be something closer to what it looks like on camera. Nobody studying this seriously rules it out. Nobody confirms it either.

The genuinely uncomfortable truth about working with an animal this intelligent is that we cannot interview it. We can only watch what it does, measure it as carefully as the tools allow, and argue for years about what any of it means. That unresolved tension is not a failure of the research. It's the natural consequence of studying a mind complex enough to make trained scientists hesitate before ruling anything out.

An animal smart enough to make experts nervous about saying "no, it definitely doesn't mean that." That's the paradox again, in one line.

—

HOW THEY ACTUALLY HUNT, AND WHY IT LOOKS LIKE STRATEGY BECAUSE IT IS

Orca hunting techniques aren't uniform across the species — they're regionally specific, learned, and in some cases so precise they've been given their own names by researchers. Off the coast of Argentina, at a beach called Punta Norte, a small number of orcas perform "intentional stranding": they build up speed in open water, then deliberately beach themselves on a sloped shore to grab a sea lion pup, using their own momentum to briefly strand their entire body on dry sand before using a powerful tail flex to wriggle back into the water. It's a maneuver so risky that a miscalculation can leave the animal stuck and dying on the beach — and it's a maneuver taught, deliberately and slowly, from one generation to the next, refined over years of practice by calves who get it wrong long before they get it right.

In the Norwegian fjords, resident pods practice "carousel feeding": a group of orcas will work together to encircle a school of herring, then slap the surface with their tails to stun the fish before feeding, a coordinated tactic that requires multiple animals to synchronize their movement and timing. In Antarctic waters, other pods have been filmed creating waves together to wash seals off ice floes — a technique that requires several animals swimming in coordinated formation to generate a wave large enough to do the job, then repositioning to catch the seal as it's knocked into the water.

None of these are single-animal behaviors. Every one of them requires coordination, timing, and — critically — patience with calves who haven't mastered it yet. A predator that hunts like this isn't operating on raw instinct alone. It's operating on rehearsed, regionally specific technique, refined and taught across generations, the same basic structure that defines what anthropologists would call culture in a human context.

—

A SHORT LIST OF THINGS THAT SOUND MADE UP BUT AREN'T

Orcas have been observed grieving. In 2018, a Southern Resident orca named Tahlequah carried her dead calf on her head for seventeen days and over a thousand miles, refusing to let the body sink, in what researchers and the public alike widely described as an extended, visible display of mourning. It was covered by outlets that don't normally cover marine biology, because the behavior was so specific and so sustained that "grief" was, genuinely, the most accurate available word.

Orcas have been recorded engaging in play that serves no survival function at all — tossing kelp back and forth, balancing objects on their heads, repeatedly leaping in what looks, to any observer, exactly like joy rather than necessity.

Different orca populations, despite overlapping ranges and near-identical appearance, have been documented refusing to interbreed, hunting entirely different prey, using entirely different vocal dialects, and functioning, for all practical purposes, as separate cultures sharing the same water. Some researchers argue certain populations may be on their way to becoming genetically distinct enough to be reclassified as separate species, driven not by geographic separation but by cultural divergence alone.

An animal doesn't grieve, play without purpose, and split into distinct cultures by accident. Every one of those data points points the same direction: this is not a simple animal that happens to look complicated on camera. It's a complicated animal that occasionally looks simple in a fifteen-second clip.

—

THE LONG VIEW: THIS ISN'T A NEW STORY, IT'S AN OLD ONE WITH A NEW CAMERA

Coastal peoples have been telling stories about orcas working alongside humans for thousands of years, long before anyone had a name for animal cognition research. Indigenous communities across the Pacific Northwest of North America have oral traditions describing orcas as kin, sometimes depicted as ancestors or spirit-guides, appearing in totemic art and ceremony going back centuries. Aboriginal communities in southeastern Australia told stories, generations before written record, about local orca pods that helped drive migrating baleen whales into shallow water for hunters — a story that turned out to be, remarkably, literally true.

That last one isn't folklore dressed up as fact. It's documented history. In the town of Eden, on the far south coast of New South Wales, a pod of orcas worked cooperatively with human whalers for the better part of a century, from the early 1840s until the death of the last known individual, a male called Old Tom, in 1930. The orcas would locate migrating baleen whales, alert the whalers by slapping their tails on the water near the whaling station, help drive and even hold the whale during the hunt, and in return were given the lips and tongue of the catch — the "law of the tongue," as the whalers of Eden called their side of the arrangement. This wasn't a myth passed down by one culture with an interest in mystifying the animal. It was recorded in ship logs, newspaper reports, and later preserved in a museum built specifically around that partnership. It is, quite simply, one of the best-documented examples of sustained, voluntary cooperation between a wild predator and humans in recorded history.

So when a clip surfaces of an orca approaching a person with prey in its mouth, and the internet reaches immediately for the word "gratitude," it isn't inventing something out of nothing. It's reaching for a story that coastal cultures have been telling, in one form or another, for longer than most written history exists. The instinct to see intention, memory, and reciprocity in these animals isn't a modern social-media invention. It's an old human pattern that finally has a camera good enough, and a platform fast enough, to spread it past a single coastline in a single afternoon.

Same animal. Same instinct to look for a relationship under the surface. Different fire to gather around — this one's a phone screen instead of a hearth, and the story travels in hours instead of generations.

—

THE SONAR NOBODY TALKS ABOUT

Underneath everything else, orcas navigate and hunt using echolocation — emitting rapid clicks and reading the returning echoes to build what is essentially a 3D sound-map of their surroundings, precise enough to distinguish between species, size, and even the internal structure of an object without ever needing to see it. A pod hunting in murky or dark water isn't guessing. It's reading returning sound waves with enough resolution to tell a salmon from a similarly sized piece of driftwood at range, in conditions where human eyes would be functionally useless.

This is also, quietly, one of the more tragic parts of the modern orca story. Commercial shipping lanes, recreational boat traffic, and industrial sonar all generate underwater noise that can interfere directly with this system — effectively degrading the "vision" of an animal that depends on sound the way humans depend on sight. Populations living near the busiest shipping corridors on Earth are, in a very literal sense, hunting half-blind, in water that used to be silent enough for a click and its echo to mean the difference between eating and not eating that day.

An animal with a biological sonar system precise enough to identify prey by texture, operating in an ocean that's gotten loud enough to jam it. That's not a detail that fits in a caption either. It's just true.

—

DOCUMENTED CASES OF SPECIFIC ORCAS AND SPECIFIC HUMANS

Skepticism about any single viral clip doesn't mean sustained, specific relationships between individual orcas and individual humans are fantasy — some of the best-documented cases in marine biology involve exactly that. Old Tom, the orca who worked with the whalers of Eden for decades, was recognized individually by name, by dorsal fin shape, and by behavior, both by the whalers who worked alongside him and by researchers who later studied the skeletal remains preserved in the Eden Killer Whale Museum. His teeth show visible wear consistent with the specific behavior he was known for — gripping and tugging on ropes attached to harpooned whales to help tire them, a habit unique enough to leave a physical mark.

In Norway and New Zealand, researchers running long-term photo-identification programs have built individual catalogues of specific orcas by dorsal fin and saddle-patch markings — the marine biology equivalent of a fingerprint — allowing the same individual to be tracked, named, and followed across years or decades of sightings. When a specific orca shows up repeatedly in the same waters, behaving consistently, researchers don't need a single dramatic clip to establish that it's the same animal. The fin shape alone tells them.

That's the standard the "thank you" story is actually up against. Not disbelief that orcas can recognize specific humans or specific places over time — the data says they absolutely can, and there's decades of photo-ID work to prove it. The open question is narrower and harder: not whether the same animal came back, but why.

—

WHAT ACTUALLY CHANGES WHEN YOU LOOK CLOSER

None of this requires believing the tidiest version of the story to still find the animal remarkable. Strip away the certainty about "why," and what's left is still one of the most cognitively sophisticated, socially complex, and genuinely enigmatic predators alive today — one that teaches its young, speaks in regional dialects, remembers foraging grounds across decades, chooses curiosity over aggression toward an objectively much weaker species with staggering consistency, and occasionally does something so specific and so hard to explain that it makes trained researchers pause before writing "no" in a paper.

Maybe it was gratitude. Maybe it wasn't. The uncertainty isn't a letdown. It's the most honest thing anyone could say about an animal this close to us in complexity and this far from us in every other respect.

That's ultimately the real reason a fifteen-second clip like this travels as far as it does. It's not because the caption resolves the question. It's because it doesn't, and something in us can't stand leaving it unresolved. We watch it once for the moment. We watch it a second time looking for the explanation. We share it hoping someone in the replies has the answer. Nobody does — not fully, not yet, maybe not ever — and that's exactly the point at which a video stops being content and starts being a genuine open question, the kind that used to get argued about around a fire and now gets argued about in a comment section, with the same lack of resolution and the same refusal to stop caring.

Whatever the mother orca meant by it, the calf that couldn't have survived on its own is alive because a handful of strangers decided a stranding wasn't over just because it looked hopeless. That part isn't ambiguous at all.

Save this for the next person who says orcas are just "killer whales."

text:
Fintech Chime is buying its way into becoming a bank. On Tuesday it announced an all-cash 590 million dollar deal to acquire nationally chartered Stride Bank, a partner it has worked with for more than seven years. Stride, founded in 1913 in Enid, Oklahoma, offers consumer and commercial banking services and will be rebranded as Chime Bank, a wholly owned subsidiary. Chime said the acquisition gives it a faster and more proven path to full-stack ownership than pursuing a de novo charter, and will let it bring core banking infrastructure in-house as it expands lending. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 and generate more than 100 million dollars in net synergies. Chime also said it will manage Stride’s balance sheet and keep assets below 10 billion dollars for the foreseeable future.

The move comes as Chime pushes to grow beyond its mobile-first checking and savings products aimed at everyday Americans, especially younger customers. The company, which went public earlier this year, raised its full-year revenue growth forecast to 26 percent to 27 percent, up from 25 percent to 26 percent. Shares jumped nearly 10 percent in extended trading on the news and are up over 28 percent this year. For years Chime has relied on partner banks like Stride and Bancorp to hold customer deposits, but owning Stride will let it consolidate banking activities and have more control over lending and product development. Morgan Stanley advised Chime on the transaction, while Piper Sandler advised Stride.

My fellow prayer warriors, I have two prayer requests following something that happened yesterday. I’d like to provide context so please bear with me if you have time.

I have a twin brother. We both left the faith after college. He moved to NYC. I moved to Florida. Two different paths, and we’ve always had two distinct personalities. Today we are very close (now age 38), w/ great love for one another. I came back to Jesus and the Catholic faith about 6 years ago. He’s never been open to considering it. He’s peacefully disagreed and has been “happy for me,” but he’s always shut down any attempts I’ve made to bring him back. He’s somewhat “spiritual but not religious,” but he’s been completely opposed to the Church and he’s not always been open to discussing it- for him it’s a sore subject, so I truly don’t know what his relationship with God has been for all these years. For him, the topic is always off the table. He practices yoga and practices different Eastern religious chants/mantras and stuff here and there, even though I don’t think he’s taken a deep dive into Buddhism or Hinduism or any other religion. I’ve been praying for his conversion for all these years, so far with no success. But, something kinda big happened yesterday. He’s struggling with a specific and significant issue, amongst many problems that he’s juggling. I don’t know if he’s turned to the Lord in prayer all these years based on what he’s told me. From my understanding he stopped praying a long time ago, at least not with full belief in Our Lord Jesus. But yesterday- he texted me and asked me to pray for him. 🤯 With this particular situation/intention in mind. It might not sound like a big deal, but it kinda was. In all these years he’s NEVER talked about prayer and I don’t know if he’s ever considered it (maybe he has but he still hasn’t fully admitted to accepting Jesus or any desire to return to the faith), yet he turned to me and asked me to pray for him. He’s NEVER done that, not since he’s seen me turn back to the Lord & His Church, even though I already pray for him and the rest of my family everyday (and they know that). This is a first for him in all my 6 years back in the Church, and I hope maybe it’s a sign that he’s opening his heart and mind to God, as he’s now considering the power of prayer (because he knows who I pray to- Jesus). I feel like the Lord has blessed me with a great, supportive, loving family & brother, even though they’ve all left the faith & continued to disagree with me about Jesus and the Church. They’ve still always loved me and supported me. The love in our family is there, and it’s strong, but I’ve been the only one who’s returned to the faith, fully embracing the Lord and the Church. But I feel like God has done something given all my prayers for their conversions. I feel like he’s truly working on them. In this instance, particularly on my brother. ☺️🙌🙏 This might not seem like much evidence to you or sound like a big deal, but in his text message to me, given the words he used and the way expressed his call for help from me (his brother who preaches to him the truth of Jesus Christ and the Catholic Church) it felt like he was reaching out from a sincere place of desperation and openness to God’s mercy and God’s willingness to hear our prayers. Without sharing intimate details- I responded to him with joy and reassurance that I would absolutely pray for him with his particular problem in mind, and I gave him some gentle spiritual advice.

If you don’t mind, please join me in praying for my brother. Please offer a prayer for him and the special intention that he urgently needs help with, and also for his conversion. Please pray that he comes home to the Lord and to the faith. 🙏 I couldn’t thank you enough. God bless.

"Plan could require congressional approval
Vance's convention speech seen as 2028 test run

 President Donald Trump capped the first day of his Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention by proposing to pay every U.S. adult a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if his ​party wins November's congressional elections.
Trump delivered the extraordinary overture during a primetime speech that lasted nearly two hours and firmly placed him at the ‌center of the midterm campaign at a time when his sagging approval ratings could weigh on Republicans' chances.

Vice President JD Vance will give the keynote address on Thursday night, though Trump is scheduled to make closing remarks to bring the made-for-television two-day event in Dallas to an end.
With Trump constitutionally barred from seeking a third term, Vance's speech could serve as an early audition ​for the 2028 presidential election and offer clues about how he would lead a party reshaped by Trump.

It was not immediately clear how the $5,000 payments ​would work or whether they would be legal. The proposal would likely cost more than $1 trillion, with approximately 270 million ⁠U.S. adults, and could require the approval of Congress.

The convention's focus on Trump – some Republicans have dubbed it "Trumpapalooza" – amounts to a risky bet that he can mobilize ​the voters who carried him to the presidency two years ago, despite opinion polls showing his popularity is at an all-time low.
But it remains to be seen whether ​his campaign-style speech will appeal to the critical swing voters who have drifted away from Trump's party amid growing dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the war on Iran.

'PRETEND THAT I'M ON THE BALLOT'
"I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump said, a line that may have pleased Democratic campaign strategists just as much as MAGA voters.
Republican efforts ​got a boost from an unlikely source on Wednesday, when Democratic U.S. Senator John Fetterman appeared in a pretaped video segment introducing his "great friend," fellow Pennsylvania Senator Dave ​McCormick, a Republican.

text:
Chapter 4 — Operation Encore and the Saudi Network (1/2)
9/11: A Detailed Overview
Chapter 4 — Operation Encore and the Saudi Network
Project 911DETAIL — FINAL WW DRAFT (verified additions incorporated)
Part Four of the Joint Inquiry ended not with a verdict but with a referral — a compilation of raw leads handed back to the FBI and CIA "for investigative review and appropriate investigative and intelligence action." What the Bureau did with that referral, quietly, for the better part of two decades, is a story the 2004 Commission Report never told, because most of it hadn't happened yet when the Commission closed its book.
THE CASE THE COMMISSION CLOSED AND THE BUREAU REOPENED
The 9/11 Commission interviewed Omar al-Bayoumi and Fahad al-Thumairy in Saudi Arabia in 2003-2004, wrote that Bayoumi was "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists," and stated it had "not found evidence" that Thumairy assisted Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar. FBI Special Agent Jacqueline Maguire — the agent who had coordinated the Flight 77 team beginning in 2001 — told the Commission at its June 16, 2004 public hearing that "all indications" were that Bayoumi's restaurant meeting with the hijackers "was a random encounter," and that the Bureau had "not developed any information that the hijackers had been introduced to Thumairy" or had "any direct connection" to the King Fahad Mosque in that timeframe. The Commission's public report was released in July 2004, built substantially on that testimony. A set of FBI agents in San Diego and New York did not close the file along with it — some senior officials privately doubted Bayoumi's chance-meeting story even as Maguire's testimony went into the record.
In 2007 the FBI opened a follow-on investigation carried internally under the name Operation Encore. The predicate was the unresolved California problem from 2002: two al-Qaeda operatives who spoke almost no English, had no prior exposure to life in the West, and within days of landing at Los Angeles International on January 15, 2000, were housed, banked, introduced, and pointed toward flight training by people on official Saudi payrolls. Encore's theory, as later written into its own closing file, was that Musaed al-Jarrah used his position as head of Islamic Affairs at the Saudi Embassy in Washington to oversee and direct facilitation of the hijackers through subordinates — Thumairy and Bayoumi — and through his own contact with the pair. The named main subjects were Fahad al-Thumairy, Omar al-Bayoumi, and Musaed al-Jarrah. Other files opened before and after Encore were administratively consolidated under the same case number.
San Diego case agent Daniel Gonzalez was a principal on the team. Richard Lambert, who had led the San Diego field office's post-attack work, and Steve Moore, another veteran of the California investigation, remained voices in the matter long after leaving the Bureau. Moore later described what happened when agents tried to interview Saudi officials or subpoena diplomatic records: "We hit a roadblock so hard, I think we all had airbag burns." Jeffrey Breinholt, who oversaw 9/11-related prosecutions at the Justice Department, later said Bayoumi had been one of the "hot possibilities for charges," and that "we've convicted people for less." No one was ever charged. Encore functioned as an intelligence case as much as a criminal one — a distinction that would matter when New York headquarters shut the team down. Gonzalez and other Encore agents were reportedly stunned by Maguire's 2004 testimony, wondering whether the Bureau's leadership had access to information they didn't — Maguire herself repeated the "accidental" characterization more than a decade later to the 2015 9/11 Review Commission, a position Encore's investigators strongly disagreed with.
THE COMMAND NODE: MUSAED AL-JARRAH
Jarrah was not named in the 28 pages. His identity stayed off the public record until the Justice Department accidentally left it unredacted in an April 2020 court filing in the families' lawsuit. Starting in the mid-1990s he worked as deputy chief, then director, of the Islamic Affairs section of the Saudi Embassy in Washington. State Department diplomat lists carried him as an accountant for the embassy. A confidential human source told the FBI in March 2003 that he had held that post since February 1991. He left the United States in 2005 after coming under Bureau scrutiny.
A Washington Field Office report written in early 2003 — years before Encore existed as a named case — described him as "heavily connected/linked to Saudi Sunni extremists operating inside the U.S." and as "a controlling, guiding and directing influence on all aspects of Sunni extremist activity in Southern California," directing, controlling, and funding Muhammad al-Muhanna and Fahad al-Thumairy "since their arrival in the U.S." Muhanna was an administrative officer at the Los Angeles consulate; a 2010 FBI report called him a "more radical individual" whom Thumairy brought into the King Fahad Mosque around 2000-2001. Phone records showed Muhanna connected to both Thumairy and Jarrah. Plaintiffs' later analysis counted a minimum of 64 calls from Thumairy's phones to Jarrah's personal cell between 2000 and 2003. Thumairy would later claim he could not remember Jarrah. Encore and the civil-case experts treated that claim as not credible.
The source description of Jarrah's official duties is the organizational chart Encore was testing: he managed and controlled assignments of Saudi imams in the United States, facilitated diplomatic visas for them, and coordinated their activity once they were inside the country. Imams assigned through that process reported to him. If that description is accurate, Thumairy was not a lone diplomat-imam operating independently in Culver City — he was a node in a Ministry of Islamic Affairs chain running through the Washington embassy. Encore's closing communication states the theory in one sentence: Jarrah used the Islamic Affairs post "to oversee and direct the facilitation of the hijackers through his subordinates, Thumairy and Bayoumi." That is an investigative predicate, not a signed confession — but it is also the first time a Bureau file put a named embassy official at the top of the California support network the 28 pages had only sketched.
Jarrah himself was later deposed in the civil litigation. In June 2021, FBI agents' prior attempt to "flip" Jarrah as a cooperating witness became public when Yahoo News reporter Michael Isikoff published details of Jarrah's deposition transcript — obtained through a leak the litigation's own oversight process would later determine came from inside the plaintiffs' legal team. That leak, and the sanctions fight it produced, is addressed later in this chapter.
THE ADVANCE TEAM: AL-SADHAN AND AL-SUDAIRY
Two other Ministry of Islamic Affairs officers sit in the Encore file as what later FBI writing and press reconstructions called an "advance team." Adel Mohammad al-Sadhan first came briefly to Southern California in December 1998, with Fahad al-Thumairy listed as "a contact" for that visit. In June 1999, Sadhan flew with Mutaib al-Sudairy to Washington, then to San Diego, and stayed six weeks with Omar al-Bayoumi. Sudairy — son of a prominent Saudi family — traveled the U.S. as a Ministry of Islamic Affairs missionary and, per an Encore report, spent four months as the roommate of Ziyad Khaleel, a Palestinian-American extremist then living in Missouri. A September 28, 2010 New York Field Office memo, declassified and reported in 2025, found that Sudairy and Sadhan had a "past connection" to the hijackers and to others who assisted them. The 2016 Encore electronic communication adds that Bayoumi called Sudairy five times during the window when the hijackers met him in Los Angeles and he moved them to San Diego.
The timing is the point. Sadhan's first California visit predates Hazmi and Mihdhar's arrival by a year and a month; the Sadhan-Sudairy stay with Bayoumi falls in the same season Bayoumi was in Washington with a video camera. Encore did not treat those facts as tourism — it treated them as a network that existed before the two future Flight 77 hijackers arrived, and that was already wired to the man who would house them.
THE 1999 CAPITOL VIDEO
In late June and early July 1999, Bayoumi recorded video in Washington over several days. The footage — seized by British police in a raid on his UK apartment days after 9/11 and later unsealed in the families' civil case — shows entrances and exits of the U.S. Capitol, security posts, a model of the building, and nearby landmarks. In Arabic he says he is transmitting scenes "from the heart of the American capital," points out the Washington Monument, says he will "get over there" and "report to you in detail what is there," notes the airport is not far, and refers to "the plan." Retired San Diego FBI chief Richard Lambert, later a consultant to the plaintiffs, described a 360-degree record of the Capitol from all sides. Flight 93's likely target, in the official reconstruction, was the Capitol. The filming sits within roughly ninety days of Bin Ladin's approval of Khalid Sheikh Mohammed's planes operation. When Bayoumi filmed, he was often with two Saudi diplomats the FBI later tied to the same Islamic Affairs network; plaintiffs identify those companions as the Sadhan/Sudairy pair. The Saudi government disputes the surveillance characterization and any official tasking.
An internal FBI report dated October 11, 2001 states that "copies of all recovered exhibits" from the British raid were "sent to FBI-New York via Federal Express." The Capitol video did not reach the San Diego field office working Bayoumi and the hijackers' apartment building. It was not in the packet British detectives had when they interviewed Bayoumi, and it was not before the 9/11 Commission. What is documentary is the October 11, 2001 FedEx routing line and the later admission that San Diego never had the exhibit; the claim that the "gregarious student" narrative would have collapsed in 2001 had the tape been in those rooms is an after-the-fact argument agents and plaintiffs make, not a documented fact.
THE AIRPLANE SKETCH
In 2012 an FBI evidence technician clearing a Washington lock-up found, in a crate marked "Omar al-Bayoumi," a hand-drawn sketch of an aircraft with a cover sheet stating it "contains mathematical calculations regarding height of planes." Robert M. Brown, a former American Airlines pilot retained by the plaintiffs as an aviation expert, filed a sworn declaration stating investigators first questioned him about the sketch in 2012, and that in his professional opinion "there was a reasonable basis to believe that the drawing and equation were used as part of the preparations of the al Qaeda terrorists to carry out the 9/11 attacks." Encore officers concluded the numbers on the sketch corresponded to distances between beacons on the eastern seaboard and some of the attack targets. When deposed, Bayoumi claimed the sketch was a high school physics equation he was trying to remember. A federal judge later wrote that the document, on its face, "connects Bayoumi with knowledge of the 9/11 Attacks," and that Bayoumi could not offer a reasonable explanation for it. There is no public proof he shared the sketch with the hijackers. There is a documented chain-of-custody failure: the sketch sat in a crate for a decade, was not used in the UK interviews, was not given to San Diego during the original PENTTBOM work, and was not before the Commission. That lateness is part of the case history, not a footnote.
THE 2016 ELECTRONIC COMMUNICATION: THE RESTAURANT WAS NOT A COINCIDENCE
On April 4, 2016, Encore agents wrote a 16-17 page electronic communication — the most detailed public statement of what the team believed it had proved about February 1, 2000. The EC states Bayoumi's account to federal investigators — chance meeting, overheard Gulf Arabic, hospitality — was "directly contradicted" by eyewitness Caysan Bin Don, who told the FBI that Bayoumi entered the restaurant and positioned himself to watch the front window, then approached Hazmi and Mihdhar from a distance where he could not have overheard them speaking. Approximately one hour before encountering the pair, Bayoumi and Bin Don visited the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles and met a person redacted in the public copy as PII. After that meeting they drove to the Mediterranean Gourmet Restaurant on Venice Boulevard. A separate witness told the Bureau that a friend — identified in later reporting as Mohammed Johar, an Eritrean worshipper at Thumairy's mosque — had been tasked by Thumairy to deliver the two hijackers to that same restaurant. The EC states bluntly: "this is the same restaurant" the tasked person "said that he needed to deliver Hazmi and Midhar to."
The same EC inventories Bayoumi's logistic support — translation, travel assistance, lodging, financing — and states "anomalous money transfers within Bayoumi's bank accounts coincide with transactions wherein Bayoumi provided assistance to Hazmi and Midhar." Shortly before the two men arrived from the Kuala Lumpur meeting, a phone call from "Malaysia or Indonesia" instructed an individual — still classified in the public EC — to "locate Thumairy." Thumairy's phones had contact with the family home in Saudi Arabia of two al-Qaeda militants, Suleyman and Abd al Aziz Al-Khalidi, later sent to Guantanamo. Records show calls two weeks before the hijackers' arrival among Bayoumi, Thumairy, and the Islamic Affairs director at the Saudi Embassy.
A separate FBI source, recorded in an FD-1023 later released under Executive Order 14040, put the knowledge question in a number the Bureau does not usually write: there was a "50/50 chance" Bayoumi "had advanced knowledge the 9/11 terrorist attacks were to occur and assisted two of the hijackers while residing in San Diego." That is source reporting, not a finding — Encore kept it in the file rather than treating it as established.

"The Latin American player doesn’t get the recognition he deserves.
Neither does the Negro player, unless he does something spectacular, like Willie Mays.
We have self-satisfaction, yes.
But after the season is over, nobody cares about us.
Zoilo Versalles was the Most Valuable  Player in the American League, but how many times has he been asked to make appearances at dinners or meetings during the winter?
Juan Marichal is one of the greatest pitchers in the game, but does he get invited to banquets?
I am an American citizen, but some people act like they think I live in the jungle someplace.
This is a matter of sports, of a  man’s ability and his accomplishments.
What matters what language he speaks best."
Roberto Clemente.
When John Candelaria was getting ready to sign with the Pittsburgh Pirates he visited with the team and met Roberto Clemente. After speaking for a few minutes, Roberto left, then came back  into the room and in Spanish said to John and his parents, that he knew how much they were going to offer John to sign, but that the actual number they were willing to spend was much higher, so they should ask for that.
Since none of the Pirates officials spoke Spanish, they had no idea what Roberto Clemente had told him.

text:
[15] Essential Agriculture Stories for Industry Professionals
https://t.co/Nomos72Ajf

Today's press review delivers 15 essential agriculture stories drawn from Indian print media, offering media monitoring insights for professionals across the agri-food value chain. According to Press Monitor's tracking of Indian publications, these stories reflect the latest news on agriculture shaping policy, markets, and rural livelihoods.

1. Bayer Expands Agri Centres Across Eastern India
A front-page report in Financial Express says Simon Wiebusch, managing director and chief executive officer of Bayer CropScience, urged quicker regulatory approvals for genetically modified crops to boost Indian agriculture. He detailed the expansion of the Better Life Farming alliance across eastern India, featuring 1600 knowledge centres that teach direct-seeded rice methods and sustainable practices. The scheme focuses on increasing farm incomes, conserving water resources, and linking rural producers to established supply networks.
Simon Wiebusch, MD and CEO of Bayer CropScience, is driving the expansion of the Better Life Farming alliance across eastern India with 1,600 knowledge centres. Why it matters: this push for direct-seeded rice methods and sustainable practices could reshape farm incomes and water conservation in the region. Key detail: the alliance links rural producers to established supply networks. Source: Financial Express, by Sandip Das. Next step: watch for state-level adoption rates of these training centres.

2. AIFPA Challenges FSSAI FOPL Benchmark in Supreme Court
A front-page report in Economic Times says the All-India Food Processors Association has intervened in the Supreme Court seeking that proposed front-of-pack nutrition labels be based on per-serving consumption rather than a uniform per one hundred gram or one hundred ml benchmark. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India told the top court it was considering mandatory red hexagonal front-of-pack warning labels for packaged foods and beverages high in sugar, salt or saturated fat, after the court pulled up the regulator for not implementing the labels even after a decade of deliberations.
The All-India Food Processors Association has intervened in the Supreme Court, arguing that front-of-pack nutrition labels should be based on per-serving consumption rather than a uniform per 100g benchmark. Why it matters: this legal challenge could redefine how packaged food is labelled across India. Key detail: FSSAI is considering mandatory red hexagonal warning labels for high-sugar, high-salt, and high-saturated-fat products. Source: Economic Times, by Shambhavi Anand. Next step: monitor the Supreme Court timeline for a ruling.

3. Synthetic Paneer Manufacturing Exposed in Haryana
A front-page report in Times of India says synthetic paneer, also known as analogue or non-dairy paneer, is being manufactured in foundry-like units in Gondola village, Nuh district, Haryana, and distributed to Delhi, Gurgaon, Faridabad, and Chandigarh. The product uses slaked lime (chuna) to give it colour, is cheap, lasts a long time, and needs no dairy.
Synthetic paneer made with slaked lime is being produced in foundry-like units in Gondola village, Nuh district, Haryana, and distributed to Delhi, Gurgaon, Faridabad, and Chandigarh. Why it matters: this food fraud poses serious health risks and undermines dairy farmers. Key detail: the product is cheap, long-lasting, and contains no dairy. Source: Times of India, by Anjali Singh and Nikhil Sharma. Next step: expect stricter food safety inspections in the NCR region.

4. Indian Packaged Food Industry Files Supreme Court Challenge
A front-page report in First India says food producers across India have filed a legal challenge with the Supreme Court against proposed health warning labels on packaged goods. The submission, lodged on Wednesday, marks the first formal objection from the nation's more than 100 billion dollar domestic packaged food sector to the government's August 28 announcement regarding stricter limits on sugar, salt and saturated fat. Industry leaders warn that the mandatory red hexagonal signage could damage international marketability, especially as regulators intensify nationwide food safety inspections.
Food producers across India have lodged a formal legal objection against proposed health warning labels on packaged goods, marking the first challenge from the 100 billion dollar domestic packaged food sector. Why it matters: mandatory red hexagonal signage could affect international marketability. Key detail: the government's August 28 announcement on stricter sugar, salt, and saturated fat limits is now under judicial review. Source: First India, by Agencies. Next step: track the court response to this industry petition.

5. Over 10,000 Cattle Infected with Lumpy Skin Disease in Rajasthan
A front-page report in First India says over 10,000 cattle have been infected with lumpy skin disease across nine districts in Rajasthan. The state government has imposed a one-month ban on interstate cattle movement while officials work to isolate infected animals and accelerate vaccinations. So far, 4,854 animals have recovered, six have died, and 5,185 cases remain active.
Rajasthan reports over 10,000 cattle infected across nine districts, with a one-month ban on interstate cattle movement imposed by the state government. Why it matters: livestock health directly impacts farmer incomes and protein supply chains. Key detail: 4,854 animals have recovered, six have died, and 5,185 cases remain active. Source: First India Bureau, Jaipur. Next step: monitor vaccination rollout speed in affected districts.

6. Rajasthan Leads 28 State Reform Priorities Implementation
A front-page report in First India says Rajasthan has emerged as the leading state in implementing 28 reform priorities from the Fifth Chief Secretaries’ Conference, having completed 22. Chief Secretary V S Srinivas urged coordination to finalise the remaining six, emphasising deregulation to boost investment and ease of doing business. The state advanced its Food Policy-2026 by proposing 39 agro-processing parks across 35 sites, which Principal Secretary Manju Rajpal noted will attract investment and strengthen farm market linkages.
Rajasthan has completed 22 of 28 reform priorities from the Fifth Chief Secretaries Conference, with Chief Secretary V S Srinivas urging coordination on the remaining six. Why it matters: deregulation to boost investment and ease of doing business sets a benchmark for other states. Key detail: the state Food Policy-2026 proposes 39 agro-processing parks across 35 sites. Source: First India, Jaipur. Next step: watch for private sector responses to the agro-processing park proposals.

7. ONDC Shifts Strategy to Prioritise Farmers and Local Retail
A front-page report in Mint says the Open Network for Digital Commerce has shifted its strategy to prioritise aggregation of farmers' produce and promote Indian-made goods through DigiHaat and DigiDukaan. Following a leadership transition at the Bengaluru-based entity and raising Rs 4,430 crore from strategic investors including Zoho, Uber and Amul, the government-backed platform aims to resolve structural supply chain gaps using interoperability rather than operating as a traditional marketplace.
The Open Network for Digital Commerce has pivoted to aggregate farmers produce and promote Indian-made goods through DigiHaat and DigiDukaan. Why it matters: this government-backed platform aims to resolve structural supply chain gaps using interoperability. Key detail: ONDC raised Rs 4,430 crore from strategic investors including Zoho, Uber, and Amul. Source: Mint. Next step: track farmer adoption rates on the new DigiHaat interface.

8. Himachal Pradesh Invites Tenders for QR Tag Rice Traceability
A front-page report in Times of India says Himachal Pradesh State Civil Supplies Corporation Limited, a state government undertaking based in Shimla, has invited short-term e-Tenders for the appointment of suppliers to supply Stitchable Quick Response Tags for tagging and traceability of rice bags handled under procurement, storage, and distribution operations. The tender notice specifies that sample submissions and earnest money deposits are due by twenty-two September twenty twenty-six up to five o'clock PM, while online bids must be submitted by twenty-four September twenty twenty-six up to five o'clock PM as per the Tender Schedule.
Himachal Pradesh State Civil Supplies Corporation Limited has issued short-term e-Tenders for Stitchable Quick Response Tags to tag and trace rice bags under procurement, storage, and distribution. Why it matters: digital traceability in rice supply chains enhances food safety and consumer trust. Key detail: sample submissions are due by 22 September 2026 and online bids by 24 September 2026. Source: Times of India. Next step: suppliers should prepare earnest money deposits promptly.

9. India Explores Ethanol Blends Beyond E20 Through Flex-Fuel Vehicles
A front-page report in Business Standard says that India is looking at ethanol blends higher than E20 only through flex-fuel vehicles, as alternative energy sources become increasingly important for reducing dependence on imported crude oil. Advisor to the Prime Minister Tarun Kapoor said ethanol production has exceeded expectations and the government is now working to identify additional uses for ethanol, other biofuels, and compressed biogas.
India is looking at ethanol blends higher than E20, with Advisor to the Prime Minister Tarun Kapoor confirming that ethanol production has exceeded expectations. Why it matters: reducing dependence on imported crude oil strengthens energy security. Key detail: the government is identifying additional uses for ethanol, other biofuels, and compressed biogas. Source: Business Standard, by Sanjeeb Mukherjee. Next step: monitor flex-fuel vehicle adoption rates.

10. Uttarakhand Releases 2026-27 Grain Supply Tender
A front-page report in Times of India says that the Uttarakhand government has issued a formal tender notice for grain supplies under the 2026-27 fiscal year. Published on September 9, 2026, the official documentation outlines pricing schedules and logistical requirements for agricultural commodities. Eligible suppliers can review the complete tender package and register their bids through the dedicated state portal.
The Uttarakhand government has issued a formal tender notice for grain supplies under the 2026-27 fiscal year, outlining pricing schedules and logistical requirements. Why it matters: public procurement tenders create market access opportunities for agricultural suppliers. Key detail: eligible suppliers can review the complete tender package through the state portal. Source: Times of India. Next step: registered suppliers should submit bids before the deadline.

11. PM KUSUM Next Phase Adds Dedicated Agrivoltaics Component
A front-page report in Economic Times says renewable energy minister Pralhad Joshi announced that the next phase of the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyaan (PM KUSUM) scheme will include a dedicated agrivoltaics component. The scheme aims to enable farmers to earn income from solar electricity while retaining land ownership, with a focus on small and marginal farmers, farmer producer organisations, cooperatives, and panchayats. Joshi highlighted the need for further research on agrivoltaics to determine optimal configurations for different crops, climates, and regions, citing research at BAIF's Rural Innovation Centre in Pune.
Renewable Energy Minister Pralhad Joshi announced that the next phase of PM KUSUM will include agrivoltaics, enabling farmers to earn income from solar electricity while retaining land ownership. Why it matters: this dual-use model supports small and marginal farmers, farmer producer organisations, cooperatives, and panchayats. Key detail: research at BAIF Rural Innovation Centre in Pune is guiding optimal configurations. Source: Economic Times. Next step: watch for state-level pilot announcements.

12. New Seed Act Proposed to Protect Farmers from Fake Inputs
A front-page report in Statesman says the Union Government is preparing to introduce a new Seed Act to protect farmers from fake and substandard agricultural inputs. Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan will host a high-level consultative meeting with major farmer organisations at Krishi Bhawan on Thursday. The proposed legislation seeks stricter penalties and an end-to-end digital traceability system to curb spurious seed trade.
The Union Government is preparing to introduce a new Seed Act, with Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan hosting a consultative meeting with major farmer organisations at Krishi Bhawan. Why it matters: stricter penalties and end-to-end digital traceability could curb spurious seed trade. Key detail: the proposed legislation targets fake and substandard agricultural inputs. Source: Statesman, by Statesman News Service. Next step: monitor farmer organisation feedback during the consultation.

13. 39 Food Parks Proposed Under Rajasthan Food Policy-2026
A front-page report in First India says Chief Secretary V Srinivas chaired a stakeholders' meeting on agro-processing clusters in Jaipur on Wednesday, directing officials to map proposed clusters and assess their export potential. Principal Secretary Manju Rajpal said 39 food parks and 10 commodity-based clusters are proposed under the Food Park Policy-2026. text:
He Disappeared in 2003. More Than Two Decades Later, Raj Kiran’s Story Remains Unfinished.

There was a time when Raj Kiran was one of Hindi cinema’s most recognisable faces. Soft-spoken, understated and immensely talented, he became a familiar presence through the late 1970s and 1980s, appearing in more than 100 films and earning praise for memorable performances in films such as Karz (1980) and Mahesh Bhatt’s Arth (1982).

But as the 1990s arrived, the offers began to dry up. His professional decline was accompanied by serious personal and emotional difficulties, and his life gradually moved away from the spotlight.

In 1996, Raj Kiran was arrested after allegedly attempting to enter Sathya Sai Baba’s Puttaparthi ashram at night. According to reports, he had hired a tractor and a ladder to get inside. He reportedly spent 34 days in Bengaluru Central Jail before his father secured his release. He later underwent psychiatric treatment in Mumbai and eventually moved to the United States.

Then came the disappearance.

Around 2003, his immediate family lost contact with him. What happened next became a mystery that Bollywood has never been able to solve.

In 2011, Rishi Kapoor said he had managed to trace Raj Kiran’s brother in the United States and was told that Raj was alive and living in a mental health facility in Atlanta, Georgia.

But Raj Kiran’s daughter, Rishika Mahtani, strongly disputed the account. She said the family had no confirmed information about his whereabouts and had even hired private investigators in their search for him.

Over the years, there were other alleged sightings—including a reported sighting of Raj Kiran working as a taxi driver in New York—but none was conclusively established.

And that is what makes his story so haunting.

Was Raj Kiran living quietly somewhere in America, deliberately cutting ties with his past? Did his mental-health struggles lead him into isolation? Was the Atlanta story genuine? Was the New York taxi sighting real? Or did something happen to him before any of these accounts surfaced?

More than two decades after his family last had confirmed contact with him, there is still no publicly established answer.

Raj Kiran disappeared from the world he once inhabited so completely that his final chapter remains a mystery.

A celebrated actor. A troubled life. A disappearance without closure.

And somewhere between the memories of Bollywood and the unanswered questions of his family lies the story of Raj Kiran. ❤️

text:
Busy is activity, profitable is a result they are not the same thing.

A lot of people in tech look occupied: courses, labs, certificates, late nights, new tools every week. That can still leave you unpaid, because none of that automatically creates a skill someone will buy, a job someone will offer, or a client who can find you.

Busy looks like progress but it is often delay. You feel like you are moving because your calendar is full. The market only pays for a clear problem you can solve, proof that you can solve it, and enough visibility that the right person sees you.

Profitable is narrower, one offer one kind of buyer, evidence. A way to get paid then repetition.

The trap is collecting preparation, another course feels safer than publishing a write up, applying, pitching, or naming a price. Preparation has no finish line, so it never has to face rejection.

The correction is simple. Ask of everything you are doing: will this help someone pay me, hire me, or trust me in the next 30 days? If the honest answer is no, it is busyness.

That is the whole video: stop measuring your career by how full your week looks, measure it by whether the work is turning into money, access, or a name people remember for a specific skill.

text:
If you work at a tech company and part of your pay is shares, here's the bit that isn't in the offer letter.

The company doesn't buy those shares. It creates them.

Which means every existing shareholder now owns a slightly smaller slice of the same company. That's dilution. It's a real cost, it just doesn't leave the bank account the way a salary does.

Companies love it for exactly that reason. It's a wage that doesn't show up as cash going out.

It isn't a scam. It's just why "we're profitable" and "we're profitable excluding stock compensation" are two very different sentences.

text:
Dr @ShashiTharoor articulates India should treat a deeper, structured partnership with Europe as a core tool of strategic autonomy — not as a replacement for the US, but as a hedge against an unpredictable Washington and a coercive China.
Tharoor’s argument is that mid-2020s geopolitics has made the old US-centric bet fragile. Tariffs, energy-policy pressure, and sudden swings in American policy have injected volatility into a relationship that once felt structurally predictable. Multi-alignment is therefore no longer optional: Quad, Gulf, Singapore, and others matter, but the EU is the missing large, high-capacity partner.
The January 2025 India–EU FTA (“mother of all deals”) is the economic pillar — 2 billion consumers, roughly a quarter of world GDP, tariffs cut or eliminated on ~96% of goods, plus rules on services, digital trade, and tech. For India it is a buffer against protectionism and a premium market; for Europe it is the flagship of “China Plus One” diversification.
The security pillar is the new Security and Defence Partnership: maritime and cyber cooperation, counter-terrorism, AI, access to Europe’s €150 billion defence initiative, joint production, and technology transfer. Europe cannot match US military or financial hegemony, but it offers what the US currently does not: institutional stability, technological depth, and policy predictability. Shared concern over Chinese coercion in sea lanes and connectivity projects makes the fit practical, not merely rhetorical.
Thus true autonomy is not isolation or passive non-alignment. It is active, overlapping, high-value partnerships. Binding India’s economic future to the FTA and its security architecture to Europe creates a double hedge — against Chinese assertiveness in the neighbourhood and against erratic American engagement. Two large democracies, in this reading, can become an anchor of a rules-based order when both great-power alternatives look less reliable.

That’s not a get-out-of-jail-free card. That’s a prophetic warning that these men are storing up hellfire for themselves.

4. The Weed vs. Brothel Comparison Is the Ultimate Exposé
Let’s be brutally honest:

Weed is a plant that grows naturally, hurts no one directly, and in your case, led to incarceration.

State-sponsored prostitution, drugs, and exploitation are happening with the full knowledge and protection of the government.

The only difference is who you are:

If you're a British traveller smelling of weed → jail.

If you're a prince with oil money → a palace brothel in the desert.

That's not law. That's class warfare dressed up as religion.

5. So Where Does That Leave You—and Islam?
Here’s the hard question, and I’ll ask it plainly:

Do you see the Saudi rulers as an argument against Islam—or as evidence that Islam has been hijacked?

Because the way I see it:

If Islam is what the Saudi princes do → then Islam is a monstrous lie.

But if Islam is what the young man on the train did, and what the AirBnB lady did → then the princes are traitors to their own faith.

And the Quran itself supports that second reading. It constantly condemns the rich, the arrogant, and the oppressors. It promises them severe punishment. The Saudi royals are not "good Muslims"—they are the exact people the Quran warns you about.

6. One Last Thought
You were in jail for weed. That’s unjust. But you also met someone there—the personal trainer—who gave you a glimpse into a world most people will never see. That information is powerful. You now know, from a primary source, that the entire "Islamic morality" facade in the Gulf is a sham.

The question is: What do you do with that knowledge?

Do you let it make you bitter against all Muslims?

Or do you use it to separate the real Islam (compassion, justice, generosity) from the counterfeit Islam (corruption, cruelty, hypocrisy)?

You’ve already met both. The man on the train. The AirBnB lady. And now the princes through the eyes of their personal trainer.

You know which one is real.

I'm not asking you to become a Muslim. I'm asking you to trust your own eyes. You've seen enough to know the difference between faith and fraud.

SAVE and Clarity are the plumbing. Election identity and market rules are how you stop the next steal of a count and the next steal of a ledger. text:
Canada Needs a New Iron Spine, but Not a New Economic Wall

Canada Needs a New Iron Spine, but Not a New Economic Wall. That is the standard by which Mark Carney’s Macdonaldian response to Donald Trump should be judged.

Carney’s appeal to Sir John A. Macdonald, the CPR and the McKinley tariffs is politically potent. Foreign pressure, the story goes, revealed Canadian weakness, nation-building infrastructure turned vulnerability into sovereignty. 

It is a useful national myth. It is also a risky economic template.

The CPR joined a young, sparsely populated country whose east, west connection was a strategic necessity. It was costly, controversial and heavily subsidized, but it solved a problem markets alone could not. Canada’s modern problem is different. We are not an unconnected frontier. We are a rich, continental economy that has progressively made itself harder to build in, invest in and trade across.

The irony is that Ottawa now invokes national unity after decades of tolerating a fragmented domestic market. Provinces still impose practical barriers through divergent standards, procurement rules, credentials and regulation. 

Canada has also handicapped the very advantages that should give it leverage, energy, LNG, uranium, hydroelectricity, critical minerals, agriculture, engineering and reliable power. Permitting delays, overlapping regulation and political uncertainty have made capital reluctant to commit.

Foreign investment does not respond to ceremonial nation-building. It responds to credible returns, predictable rules, timely approvals, competitive taxes and confidence that a project can be completed. Foreign capital would find far more attractive a Canada with lighter, clearer regulation, cheap and reliable energy, an investable resource base, and preferential access to the world’s most dynamic economy.

The US  is moving toward a Hamiltonian political economy, focused on productive capital, strategic industry, energy security, infrastructure and domestic capacity. 

It is responding not only to tariff politics, but to China’s state-directed overcapacity and its use of trade dependence as leverage. Germany and the wider European Union are the cautionary tale. The consequences of China’s industrial overcapacity, combined with high energy costs and a regulatory-heavy green transition, are there for the world to see: industrial competitiveness weakened, investment constrained and dependence on foreign supply chains deepened.

Carney seems to assume Canada can diversify away from the United States without becoming vulnerable to China. That is mistaken. China is not simply another export destination, but a state-directed industrial power capable of using market access strategically and undercutting domestic producers. 

Canada should broaden its trade, but it should not exchange one dependency for another.
Canada may object, to Trump’s tariffs. But it cannot respond by clinging to an old green-industrial-policy model that subsidizes politically favoured sectors while constraining the resource base and industrial capacity it already has.

Canada should build ports, pipelines where viable, power transmission, export terminals, rail capacity, housing and digital infrastructure. It should dismantle internal trade barriers, reform regulation, accelerate approvals and welcome private and foreign capital. Public support should be disciplined by strategic need, commercial demand and measurable results, not slogans.

An Economic Wall against the United States is a flawed policy. 

Diversification is necessary, substitution is not plausible. 

America’s market offers proximity, scale, capital and deeply integrated supply chains that cannot be replaced by a tariff schedule, a trade mission or a press release. Retaliation may be needed as leverage, but it must remain targeted and temporary.

Canada Needs a New Iron Spine, but Not a New Economic Wall.

text:
On the 10th September 1224; over 800 years ago, nine poorly dressed men stepped ashore at Dover. They were the first Franciscans in England; Friars Minor sent by Francis of Assisi himself, barely fifteen years after he and a handful of companions had received papal approval for a life of radical poverty and preaching.... 

They were led by Agnellus of Pisa. Three of the party were Englishmen who had joined the order on the Continent. They carried almost nothing: undyed wool habits the colour of ash and earth, a rope around the waist, and a letter of commendation. 

Their landing did not go smoothly. They begged for food at a farmhouse and were allowed to sleep in a barn. By morning the barn was locked and a suspicious crowd had gathered. 
Spies? Robbers? Heretics? 
No one in Kent had heard of this new Italian brotherhood. One friar pulled the cord from his waist and offered it as a noose... if they were criminals, they should hang them with their own belts. The gesture broke the tension. They were released and walked on to Canterbury.

Within weeks they had footholds in the three capitals that mattered: Canterbury (the church), London (power and commerce), and Oxford (learning). They slept in wattle cells like sheep-cotes, nursed the sick, preached in the streets, and refused to own property. 

The English church of the 1220s was rich in buildings, they had impressive churches, monasteries, and wealth, but many people thought the clergy had gone soft, comfortable, proud, and not very inspiring. The new Franciscans, by contrast, looked poor, walked barefoot or in sandals, begged, nursed the sick, and preached in the streets. That contrast worked in two directions at once; the Grey Friars looked like a living rebuke and a living invitation.

The friars did not have to give speeches against fat, high-ranking member of the Christian clergy. Their grey rags, rope belts, and refusal to own property already said: this is what following Christ can look like; that padded life over there is not it. People could see the difference. 
Recruits came quickly; young men who wanted a harder, simpler, more apostolic life suddenly had a door they could walk through. The friars were not scolding from a distance; they were offering a way to join. 

By mid-century there were dozens of houses and more than a thousand friars. Francis was still alive. That same September, on La Verna, he received the stigmata. The English mission and the wounds arrived in the same season; poverty crossing the Channel while its founder was marked with the Passion. 
The date is unusually precise because a later English friar, Thomas of Eccleston, recorded it with the care of a man who knew the calendar: Tuesday after the Nativity of Mary, which in 1224 fell on a Sunday. Historians have checked the astronomy; the Tuesday was 10th September. 

In England they would be called Grey Friars. The cheap, unbleached cloth of the poor was grey or grey-brown; later centuries would see Observants and Capuchins settle on the familiar brown, while Conventuals often kept grey or adopted black.
The original look was the look of peasants.

Conventual friars accepted more stable houses in towns, some common property held for the group, and a more organised urban ministry (preaching, study, parish work). Observant friars wanted a tighter reading of the Rule: less property, simpler houses, more itinerant and austere life. Pope Leo X separated them in 1517. The Observants became the main “Friars Minor.” The others became the Friars Minor Conventual. Capuchins came later from the Observants. they wanted a return to what they believed was Francis’s own habit (long pointed hood sewn to the tunic), smaller, poorer houses, more prayer, bare feet or sandals, rougher cloth.

They came as strangers in grey rags and left a map of Greyfriars streets that still runs through English towns. The colour of the cloth changed. The wager they made that first morning; poverty as proof, not costume, did not....

SUBJECTS: The Business of Authoritarianism, History Matters

Hello Friends,
What happens when power becomes absolute? 🧵

History shows us that centralized and authoritarian regimes follow a remarkably similar playbook to maintain control, suppress dissent, and reshape reality. From the economic chokeholds that silence critics to the deliberate rewriting of history, the survival of total state control depends entirely on keeping certain truths in the dark.

Whether through the weaponization of language or the structural dismantling of independent community spaces, these systems work overtime to hide the human and economic costs of central planning.

Here are 10 realities suppressed by authoritarian and centralized regimes that reveal the true cost of losing individual liberty:
1) The link between economic freedom and personal liberty: Complete government control over jobs, housing, and food allows the state to easily silence critics by cutting off their livelihood.

2) The true historical death toll of extreme regimes: Totalitarian states censor history to hide the fact that 20th-century communist experiments resulted in an estimated 100 million deaths from purges, forced labor, and man-made famines.

3) The inevitability of an elite ruling class: Despite promising equality, centralized systems historically replace old elites with a powerful bureaucracy of party officials who enjoy special privileges denied to the public.

4) The reality of forced labor: Under total state control, individual career choice is eliminated, and regimes often use forced labor or penal colonies to meet state production goals.

5) The structural failure of central planning: A small committee of bureaucrats cannot accurately predict the supply, demand, and prices of goods, which consistently leads to chronic shortages and rationing.

6) The suppression of spontaneous innovation: Top-down directives stifle organic creativity, slowing down technological progress and leaving citizens with outdated infrastructure compared to free markets.

7) The weaponization of language and information: Regimes heavily censor the press and rewrite definitions to make it difficult for citizens to formulate or share critical thoughts about the government.

8) The destruction of independent civil society: Authoritarians deliberately weaken independent institutions—like families and religious groups—because they offer citizens a community and support system outside of state control.

9) The reliance on continuous coercion: Because centralized systems override personal self-interest, they require mass surveillance, secret police, and heavy penalties to force cooperation.

10) The historical success of decentralized power: Rulers hide the fact that societies with protected property rights and individual liberties consistently produce higher standards of living and lower poverty rates.

Stay alert. Stay alive.
