text:
BORN RUNNING: THE STORY OF A WILDEBEEST CALF ARRIVING IN THE HERD

The footage is not dramatic in the way a chase or a violent kill scene is dramatic. There is no lunging predator, no cloud of dust kicked up by galloping hooves, no screaming alarm calls rippling through the herd. Instead there is something quieter and, in its own way, far stranger: a female wildebeest standing calmly in short green grass, surrounded by half a dozen herd-mates who barely glance up from grazing, while behind her a glistening, membrane-wrapped shape emerges very slowly from her body, front hooves and muzzle first, until a newborn calf is hanging half-delivered beneath her body, already stretching its head down toward the ground as though it cannot wait to stand. This is a wildebeest calving, one of the more extraordinary and least appreciated events in the entire natural world, and the fact that it is happening in the open, in full daylight, with the rest of the herd continuing to eat grass just a few feet away, is itself one of the most important facts about the species.

The animal at the center of the clip is almost certainly a blue wildebeest, scientific name Connochaetes taurinus, sometimes called the common wildebeest or brindled gnu, the more numerous and more widely distributed of the two wildebeest species found across the African continent today, the other being the considerably rarer black wildebeest confined mostly to parts of South Africa. Fact: blue wildebeest are found across a broad swathe of eastern and southern Africa today, but the vast majority of the roughly one and a half million individuals alive at present belong to a single enormous population that migrates in a continuous, roughly circular route between the Serengeti National Park in Tanzania and the Maasai Mara National Reserve in Kenya, a population so large and so tightly bound together in its movements that it is often simply referred to as "the migration," as though no other population of the species mattered, which in terms of sheer scale is more or less true.

Calving itself is precisely where the wildebeest's biology becomes genuinely remarkable, and it is the one single detail that separates this species from almost every other large hoofed mammal in Africa. Fact: unlike most African antelope and buffalo, which give birth more or less continuously throughout the year or across an extended breeding season, the vast majority of wildebeest cows in the great migratory population synchronize their calving into an astonishingly narrow window, with the overwhelming bulk of births, often described as eighty to ninety percent of the entire annual calf crop, occurring within just a two to three week period each year, typically in late January through February, on the short-grass plains of the southern Serengeti. The result is one of the most concentrated birthing events of any large mammal anywhere on the planet: several hundred thousand calves born within a matter of days of one another, spread across an open plain that predators can only patrol in limited numbers at any one time.

That synchronization is not a coincidence or a side effect; it is widely understood by biologists as a direct evolutionary strategy against predation, and it works through simple, brutal arithmetic. Fact: researchers studying the Serengeti migration have documented that when several hundred thousand calves are born within roughly the same two-week window, the population of resident predators, lions, hyenas, leopards, cheetahs, and African wild dogs, cannot possibly consume more than a small fraction of the available calves before the survivors have had time to grow stronger, faster, and harder to catch, a phenomenon ecologists call predator satiation. A cow calving in near-total isolation outside that window, or a species that spreads its births evenly across twelve months, offers predators a small, steady, endlessly renewable supply of vulnerable young; a herd that floods the plain with newborns all at once, by contrast, temporarily overwhelms every predator in the area, so that even though individual calves are picked off constantly during the peak of calving season, the herd as a whole loses a smaller overall percentage of its young than it would if births were spread out.

The apparent calm of the herd in the video, animals grazing peacefully within arm's reach of a birth in progress, reflects the fact that this scene, however unusual it might look to a human observer, is simply routine for a wildebeest herd in calving season. Fact: female wildebeest generally do not withdraw from the herd to give birth in seclusion the way many other large mammals do; most cows calve directly within the herd, sometimes in open view of dozens of other animals, a behavior consistent with the species' broader strategy of relying on the safety of numbers rather than concealment at almost every stage of life. Newborn wildebeest calves have essentially no camouflage to speak of, being born a warm sandy-brown color quite different from the darker, greyish-blue coat of the adults, and no real means of hiding on the open, short-grass plains where the majority of births occur, so the herd's primary defense strategy is not stealth but sheer overwhelming density, dozens or hundreds of adult bodies surrounding every vulnerable newborn at the critical early moments of its life.

What follows birth is, by the standards of the mammal world, an almost unbelievably fast developmental sprint, and it is the detail most frequently cited whenever the species comes up in conversation. Fact: a healthy wildebeest calf is typically able to stand on its own within about six minutes of being born, and can be running alongside its mother at speeds sufficient to keep pace with the herd within as little as thirty minutes to a few hours, one of the fastest recorded times to full mobility of any large land mammal on Earth, an adaptation directly tied to the fact that lions, hyenas, and cheetahs are actively hunting on the very same plains where calving takes place and a calf that takes a full day to find its legs, the way many other ungulate species do, would simply not survive long enough to grow up. The calf visible in the video, already pushing its head down toward the ground while still only half delivered, is not behaving oddly; it is displaying, from literally its first moments outside the womb, the urgent physical instinct that has kept the species numerous across a landscape thick with large predators for hundreds of thousands of years.

Even that speed is not quite enough on its own, and wildebeest calves rely on a second critical adaptation layered on top of rapid mobility: near-instant recognition of their own mothers in an enormous, visually and audibly chaotic crowd. Fact: within minutes of birth, a wildebeest calf and its mother establish a strong mutual bond based on a combination of scent, vocal calls, and visual imprinting, allowing the calf to reliably pick its own mother out of a herd that may contain thousands of nearly identical-looking adults moving, calling, and jostling simultaneously, a feat of rapid sensory learning that researchers studying ungulate behavior consider one of the most impressive examples of precocial bonding in the animal kingdom, precisely because the margin for error is so small; a calf that becomes separated from its mother for even a short period on the open plains during calving season faces a dramatically elevated risk of predation, since without her guidance and protection it has essentially no ability to defend itself.

The physical process visible in the footage, the pale, glistening amniotic membrane still partially wrapped around the calf's head and shoulders as it emerges, is a completely normal part of ungulate birth and is not itself unusual to the species. Fact: like most large hoofed mammals, wildebeest give birth with the calf still enclosed inside the thin, translucent amniotic sac, which typically ruptures naturally during delivery or is broken and licked away by the mother within the first minutes after birth, an important behavior that also happens to remove birth fluids that would otherwise carry a strong scent capable of attracting predators from a considerable distance; that maternal cleaning process, alongside the swift disposal or consumption of the placenta itself in many recorded cases, functions as an additional layer of scent-based protection at exactly the moment when both mother and calf are at their most vulnerable and least mobile.

Stepping back from this single birth, the broader picture of the wildebeest's reproductive biology reveals just how tightly the entire migration's annual rhythm is built around this narrow calving window. Fact: the timing of the mass calving season on the southern Serengeti plains is itself closely tied to seasonal rainfall patterns, since cows time their births to coincide with the brief period each year when the short-grass plains are flush with new, highly nutritious growth following the short rains, providing lactating mothers with the calorie-dense forage needed to produce enough milk for a rapidly growing calf during exactly the weeks when milk demand is highest, a level of ecological synchronization between rainfall, grass growth, hormonal timing, and birth that took researchers decades of long-term field study to document and confirm in full.

The scale of the resulting migration, of which this calving event is really only the opening act, remains genuinely difficult to grasp even for people who have seen it described many times. Fact: the annual Serengeti-Mara migration involves the coordinated, roughly clockwise movement of more than one million blue wildebeest, accompanied by several hundred thousand plains zebra and gazelle that travel alongside them for mutual protection and complementary grazing habits, covering a round-trip distance of several hundred miles each year as the combined herds follow the rains north into Kenya's Maasai Mara during the dry months and back south into the Serengeti's short-grass plains in time for the next calving season, an annual cycle so large and so consistent that it is visible in satellite imagery and remains one of the very few land migrations of its kind and scale left anywhere on the planet.

That migration is punctuated by the most famous and most frequently filmed moment in the entire wildebeest calendar: the crossing of major rivers, above all the Mara and Grumeti Rivers, both of which host large populations of Nile crocodiles that gather specifically to intercept crossing herds. Fact: river crossings during the migration can involve tens of thousands of wildebeest attempting to cross a single stretch of water within a matter of hours, often triggered by the herd's collective decision-making rather than any single obvious leader, a process that frequently results in chaotic pile-ups, drownings, and heavy predation by waiting crocodiles, but that nonetheless allows the vast majority of the herd to reach the other side successfully, the sheer number of crossing animals functioning as the same kind of predator-satiation strategy that protects newborn calves during the earlier calving season, just applied to a very different and far more visually dramatic threat.

Physically, adult wildebeest are considerably larger and more heavily built than most casual viewers expect from an animal so often filmed running in vast, seemingly delicate herds across open grassland. Fact: adult blue wildebeest typically stand between about forty-five and fifty-eight inches at the shoulder and weigh between roughly three hundred and six hundred pounds depending on sex and region, with males running noticeably larger and heavier than females, and both sexes possess sturdy, curved horns capable of inflicting serious injury on a predator, giving the species a genuine defensive option in addition to raw speed once individuals reach adulthood, even though newborn calves like the one in the video are entirely dependent on flight, herd density, and their mother's protection during their first vulnerable weeks of life.

The wildebeest's unusual, somewhat ungainly appearance, an oddly proportioned combination of a heavy, buffalo-like front end, a sloped back, spindly hindquarters, and a long, horse-like tail, has earned it a reputation across popular culture as one of the more comically awkward-looking large mammals in Africa, a reputation the species has done little to shake given its habit of galloping, bucking, and kicking apparently at random even when no predator is nearby. Fact: field researchers have documented what they describe as apparently spontaneous, predator-free bursts of galloping and pronking behavior within wildebeest herds, sometimes called "sunbathing frenzies" or simply unexplained stampedes, that appear to spread rapidly through a herd for no immediately obvious external trigger, a behavior still not fully explained but generally thought to serve some combination of social bonding, stress release, and general herd-level communication rather than genuine alarm.

None of that comic reputation, though, changes the fact that the wildebeest occupies an outsized and genuinely critical role in the ecosystems it inhabits, one considerably larger than its slightly ungainly silhouette might suggest to a casual observer. Fact: as the single most numerous large grazing mammal across much of East Africa's savanna ecosystems, wildebeest grazing pressure actively shapes the height, composition, and nutrient cycling of entire grassland landscapes, and their sheer biomass supports an enormous proportion of the region's large carnivore populations; multiple long-term ecological studies of the Serengeti ecosystem have concluded that the health of the wildebeest population functions as a reliable indicator of the broader health of the entire savanna system, since so many other species, from the grass itself to the lions at the top of the food chain, depend directly or indirectly on the migration's annual rhythm of grazing, calving, and movement.

The calf glimpsed emerging in the video, then, is not simply an individual animal beginning its own life; it is one small, immediate data point in a reproductive event repeated on a scale of hundreds of thousands of near-simultaneous births, itself only the opening stage of an annual migratory cycle that shapes the ecology of an area larger than some entire countries, and a life that, within the space of about six minutes, will go from complete helplessness inside an amniotic sac to standing on its own four legs on the open plain. Fact: despite the extraordinary predation pressure faced during calving season, when studies estimate that a substantial share of the annual calf mortality across the whole migratory population occurs, enough calves survive the critical first weeks that the overall migratory wildebeest population has remained remarkably stable at roughly one to one and a half million animals for decades, a level of ecological balance between predator and prey achieved not through the survival of any individual calf but through the sheer, overwhelming statistical weight of hundreds of thousands of births compressed into a single, brief, chaotic, closely watched season on the plains.

The name itself carries a small history worth pausing on. Fact: "wildebeest" comes directly from Afrikaans, roughly translating to "wild beast" or "wild cattle," a name given by early Dutch-descended settlers in southern Africa who were struck by the animal's fierce, bull-like appearance and its untamed, skittish temperament, while the alternative name "gnu" is generally believed to derive from the Khoikhoi word for the animal, an onomatopoeic rendering of the loud, distinctive, grunting "ge-nu" call that both wildebeest species make almost constantly, a sound so central to the species' identity on the plains that field guides and safari drivers often identify a distant, unseen herd purely by the low, continuous chorus of grunts carrying across open grassland long before any actual animals come into view.

That call is not simply background noise; it plays an active and fairly specific social role, particularly during the mating season that precedes the calving event captured in the video by roughly eight and a half months. Fact: wildebeest gestation lasts approximately two hundred fifty to two hundred sixty days, meaning the rut, the concentrated breeding period during which males compete intensely for mating access, occurs in the preceding May or June, timed with remarkable precision so that calves arrive en masse the following February when the short-grass plains are at their most productive. During the rut, adult males establish small, temporary breeding territories within the herd, sometimes only a few dozen meters across, and defend them vigorously against rival males through a combination of loud, continuous grunting, ritualized sparring with their curved horns, and vigorous scent-marking, with the most successful males mating with dozens of females passing through their territory over the course of just a few frantic weeks, a breeding strategy that concentrates conception into a narrow window just as tightly as birth is later concentrated into its own narrow window eight and a half months afterward.

Perhaps the single most dramatic chapter in the wildebeest's modern history has nothing to do with predators at all, and instead involves a virus most people have never heard of. Fact: in the late nineteenth century, a catastrophic outbreak of rinderpest, a highly contagious viral cattle disease accidentally introduced to the Horn of Africa through imported livestock, swept across the continent and devastated wildebeest populations along with buffalo, giraffe, and numerous other hoofed species, in some regions killing off more than ninety percent of local wildebeest herds within just a few years and fundamentally reshaping the ecology of the Serengeti for decades afterward, since the resulting collapse in grazing pressure allowed woodland and scrub to encroach heavily onto what had previously been open grassland. It was not until large-scale cattle vaccination campaigns finally brought rinderpest under control in East Africa during the 1950s and 1960s that wildebeest numbers began a dramatic, well-documented recovery, rebounding from an estimated low of a few hundred thousand animals to well over a million within roughly two decades, a rebound so rapid and so thoroughly studied that it remains one of the most frequently cited case studies in all of wildlife ecology for demonstrating how a single disease event, and its later removal, can reshape an entire ecosystem's population dynamics and vegetation structure.

The close, near-constant association between wildebeest and plains zebra during the migration is itself worth a closer look, since it is not simply a matter of two species happening to move in the same direction at the same time. Fact: zebras and wildebeest form what ecologists call a facilitative grazing relationship, in which zebras, equipped with a digestive system adapted to process tougher, more fibrous plant material, feed first on the taller, coarser upper grass stems of a given patch of savanna, physically clearing the way and exposing the shorter, more tender, higher-protein grass shoots beneath that wildebeest strongly prefer and are better equipped to digest efficiently. Zebras also possess notably strong long-term spatial memory of watering holes and migration routes built up across individual lifetimes, and several field studies have suggested that mixed herds benefit from the zebra's route knowledge in years when rainfall patterns shift unpredictably, while wildebeest, present in vastly greater numbers, provide the zebra herds with a substantially larger buffer of potential prey for patrolling predators, a mutually reinforcing partnership that helps explain why the two species are so consistently photographed and filmed moving together across the same stretches of plain throughout the migratory cycle.

Predator pressure on wildebeest is not limited only to the dramatic set-piece events of calving season and river crossings; it is a constant, year-round feature of the species' existence, and the specific predators involved shift depending on age, location, and time of year. Fact: lions are considered the single most significant predator of adult wildebeest across most of their range, capable of bringing down even large, healthy bulls through coordinated pride hunting, while spotted hyenas, hunting both individually and in coordinated clans, account for a substantial share of predation on calves and weakened or injured adults, and cheetahs and African wild dogs, though generally too small to tackle a healthy adult wildebeest safely, are capable of taking down calves and yearlings with enough speed and coordination. Wildebeest are not entirely passive in the face of this pressure, either; adult wildebeest, and particularly adult males, have been documented mobbing and aggressively confronting hyenas and even lions in defense of calves, using their horns, weight, and numbers to drive off a predator that might otherwise have made a successful kill, a level of collective anti-predator behavior that is considerably more assertive than the skittish, purely flight-based reputation the species often carries in popular imagination.

Tourism built around this narrow window of the calving season has become a significant part of the region's conservation economy. Fact: the short window of mass calving on the southern Serengeti plains each February now draws a substantial, reliably predictable seasonal influx of safari visitors hoping to witness births and newborn calves finding their legs for the very first time, a level of interest that conservation economists say has made protecting the migratory corridor and calving grounds financially valuable to local economies and national governments alike, an incentive layered on top of the purely ecological arguments for conservation.

Watching the calf in the footage stretch its head toward the grass while still only half born, surrounded by herd-mates who show no particular alarm at the sight, it is worth remembering exactly how much evolutionary history is compressed into that single ordinary moment: a species whose entire reproductive strategy has been shaped, generation after generation, around the brutal, practical arithmetic of predator satiation, around calves that must find their legs in minutes rather than days, around mothers that must recognize their own offspring instantly in a crowd of thousands, and around a herd that has learned, over an immense stretch of evolutionary time, that the safest place to give birth is not somewhere hidden and alone but directly in the open, surrounded by exactly the same kind of company now grazing quietly a few feet away. The calf does not know any of that history. It only knows, from the very first seconds of its existence, that it needs to get its legs underneath it, find its mother's scent, and be ready to run, because on the plains where it was born, running is not a skill to be learned gradually over the course of a childhood but a condition of survival owed within minutes of taking a first breath.

Umbilical endometriosis: can cryoablation offer a minimally invasive alternative? 🧊 🎀

Umbilical endometriosis is rare, but it can cause significant cyclical pain, bleeding, cosmetic concerns, and reduced quality of life.

De Rycke et al. evaluated percutaneous image-guided cryoablation for symptomatic umbilical endometriosis in 17 women, cryoablation achieved complete pain relief in 82% of patients, significant reduction in peak pain scores, median MRI nodule volume reduction of 73%, and high cosmetic satisfaction. Most procedures were performed as outpatient treatment 🩻🧊

The umbilical location brings unique technical challenges, including skin involvement and proximity to the peritoneum, making careful image guidance, protective maneuvers, and ice-ball monitoring especially important 🎯

text:
🚨When Raman Lamba’s tragic passing forced the cricketing world to make helmets mandatory for close-in fielders🚨

In February 1998, Raman Lamba was fielding in a club match for Abahani Krira Chakra in Dhaka, Bangladesh.

The captain asked him to stand at forward short leg—just yards from the batsman.

Someone offered him a helmet.

Lamba waved it off with a smile.

There were only three balls left in the over, and he believed putting on the gear would only waste time.

On the very next ball, batsman Mehrab Hossain pulled a vicious, full-blooded shot off the middle of the bat.

The leather ball struck Lamba flush on the temple with devastating force.

It rebounded so hard that the wicketkeeper caught the deflection.

Lamba collapsed to the turf.

He slipped into a coma shortly after and passed away three days later at just 38 years of age.

His tragic passing forced cricket worldwide to make helmets mandatory for close-in fielders.

He lost his life to a split-second casual decision…

and changed the safety rules of modern cricket forever.

text:
Case For Christ Bible
Duration: 365 days
What Physical Torture Would the Messiah Endure?
Isaiah 50:4–9

Even before Jesus was crucified, he underwent a merciless beating and public mocking that were meant not only to inflict maximum pain but also to humiliate him. Isaiah prophesies this torture and abuse that the Messiah would have to endure.

Isaiah 50:6 foretells that the Savior would offer his back to those who beat him, which prophesies the vicious flogging that Jesus endured. In ancient Roman times, flogging was often administered before crucifixion and was done with a whip made of strips of leather embedded with lead balls and shards of bone to inflict gaping wounds that caused the victim unbelievable agony. The church historian Eusebius described a later Roman flogging by saying, “[The victim’s] veins were laid bare, and the inner muscles and sinews, and even the bowels, were exposed.” The New Testament confirms that Jesus received the prophesied flogging (see Matthew 27:26; John 19:1).

Isaiah also predicts that the Messiah would endure mocking and spitting. Jesus experienced the cruel taunts of the temple guards (see Luke 22:63–65), of the Roman guards (see Matthew 27:27–31), of the onlookers, of the religious leaders and even of the robbers crucified with him (see Matthew 27:39–44).

Despite his innocence, Jesus did not fight the intense physical and verbal abuse heaped upon him. Instead, he accepted the pain, fulfilling the Messianic prophecies of Isaiah and proving, “Surely he was the Son of God!” (Matthew 27:54).

Tomorrow is Bhādrapada Amāvasyā, the sacred new moon day in the Hindu month of Bhādrapada, dedicated to honoring Kula Devīs, invoking maternal Śakti, and seeking divine grace and protection for the family.

🌺 The Sacred Legacy of Bhādī Amāvasyā: Śakti, Sacrifice & the Kuldevīs 🌺

Bhādī Amāvasyā, the new moon of Bhādrapada, holds deep spiritual weight for the Mārwāṛī community worldwide. While millions turn toward great pilgrimage sites of Rajasthan, this day is, at its heart, about family heritage, lineage, and maternal Śakti. 

In Mārwaṛī culture, each clan (gotra) and lineage traces its spiritual protection to a specific Satī, a divine mother figure who watches over the prosperity, health, and continuation of the family tree. It is to her that every Mārwāṛī household turns on this sacred day.

Rāṇī Satī Dādījī, From the Mahābhārata to Jhunjhunū

When Abhimanyu fell in battle, his wife Uttarā wished to join him through Satī. Kṛṣṇa stayed her, for she carried his child, but promised fulfillment in a future life.

Uttarā was reborn as Nārāyaṇī Bāī, Abhimanyu as a merchant, Tandhan Dās. Devoted and at peace, their fate turned on a coveted white mare. When Tandhan refused to yield her, a duel followed, and he was later ambushed and killed by the enraged King of Hisār.

Nārāyaṇī Bāī did not flee, she rose, faced the king's forces alone, and avenged her husband. Her purpose fulfilled, she asked Rāṇā, their loyal caretaker, to build her pyre, blessing him so his name would forever precede hers. She became Rāṇī Satī. Their ashes were carried on the white horse, and where it stopped, in Jhunjhunū, her temple now stands, Dādījī worshipped not as an idol, but as a Triśūl, radiant with cosmic and maternal energy.

Dhandhan Satī Dādī, A Bond Beyond Battle

For families whose Kuldevī is Śrī Dhandhan Satī Dādīji, this day carries a gentler story, not of battle, but of sibling devotion and sat.

In the village of Sīsvāl, Haryāṇā, sisters Tīḍā and Gelā  were born to Balcand Jī and Pūrṇī Devī, and loved their younger brother Bholānāth Jī beyond life itself. When he was fatally bitten by a snake while grazing cattle, the sisters could not bear existence without him. Bound by love and spiritual virtue, they sat upon his funeral pyre together, merging their lives with his, immortalized as Dhandhan Satī Dādīji.

Generations later, around Samvat 1766, descendants with families, migrating toward Rājasthān, carried six sacred bricks from the Sīsvāl shrine. Resting beneath a Pīpal tree in the dunes of Dhandhan village, they set the bricks down, and could not lift them again. An Ākāśvāṇī, a celestial voice, commanded a temple be built there. Thus rose *Śrī Dhandhan Śakti Mandir, where Tīḍā-Gelā Mā still blesses her devotees.

Bhādī Amāvasyā: A Shared Devotion

Whether at Jhunjhunū, Dhandhan, or the family altar, the day unfolds the same way:

🔱 Maṅgal Pāṭh: verses of the Devī's life and glory recited.

🔱 Offerings of Faith: a Svastik drawn; rolī, cāval, mehandī, bindī, and red cunarīs offered.

🔱 Community & Sevā: prasād shared, families gathered, blessings sought for health, prosperity, and harmony.

The Meaning Behind

At the heart of every Satī story lies "sat", a rare, inner spiritual power born of pure, selfless love. In sacred stories, the actions of Rāṇī Satī Dādījī or Dhandhan Satī Dādīji were driven by an unyielding Śakti. It was a devotion so absolute that physical life separated from their loved ones lost all meaning. Recognizing that deep bond and honoring the glory of their loyalty is fundamental to Mārwāṛī faith.

We revere extraordinary women acting out of spiritual agency, fierce love, and eternal dedication, celebrating the ultimate strength of the feminine spirit. 

The immortal glory of Dhandhan Satī Dādīji and Rāṇī Satī Dādījī lives on, not in the fires of the past, but in the enduring Śakti, maternal shelter, and protective grace they grant to every household today.

Jai Dādī Kī! 🙏

text:
To be fair, my column of yesterday could easily be viewed as a real downer . . . I mean, seriously, I was talking about my descent into the agony of depression that took me to the very brink of ending it all. I ended my narrative by describing how my older sister had taken care of me, listened and prayed, and (in essence) forced me to rest and gave me food for nourishment. When I headed home very late that night, that bitter thought was gone through the grace of God.

“So, what happened next?”

I guess I did leave a bit of a cliffhanger (no pun intended) . . . sorry about that. Before putting my head on the pillow that night, I called out for Thursday and Friday; I thought I might, maybe be okay to return to the post office by Monday. And sleep came quickly – I’d crawled into bed without even cleaning off my makeup, and was praying when my eyes closed and I fell into a deep slumber. A Facebook post, made when I arrived home, was short and ended by saying, “Thank you to my sister for immediately changing her plans this afternoon, and for distracting me all evening with a 750-piece puzzle. She was a life saver.”

I woke sometime in the morning, the brightness of the sunshine spilling through the windows forcing my eyes open, and became aware that my little cat was curled up on my hip. Before my morning devotion, I checked Facebook and found that a friend had invited me to attend church with she and her husband that Sunday. I’d never heard of the church, and honestly was scared to even darken the door of another house of worship, so I went to their website and found that their statement of beliefs aligned perfectly with what I’d known my entire life . . . I wrote back to say yes, and we arranged a time and a place to meet at church.

Rejection didn’t scare me – it terrified me. Yet, I reasoned, perhaps I’d get one good service in before being told to leave – perhaps garnering enough spiritual nourishment to give me strength for the coming week. Instead, I immediately felt the Spirit of God surrounding the entire building, and as I met my friends and we found our seats, I sat, full of anticipation.

I also had only one tissue.

By the time praise and worship was over, the sleeve of my sweater was quite damp . . . during that short segment after the song service when handshakes are exchanged, I had someone I’d met at the post office approach me and it was so good to reconnect and be told I was loved and welcomed . . . and then the sermon began, and I sat, entranced, listening and learning and relaxing. Although there was special prayer down front, I held back – and my friends instead prayed for me where we sat. Now, unbeknownst to me, one of the pastors had seen me in the foyer after the service, and that afternoon (thanks to a welcome card I filled out) both sent me a text message and a friend request on Facebook. And then, on Monday or Tuesday, his secretary contacted me, asking if I could meet with Pastor Matthew the following Sunday morning before the start of church. At first, I froze . . . the last two times I’d met with senior pastoral staff, it had ended very badly for me . . . but something (someOne) prompted me to say yes, and not to worry.

Back at work, I muddled through. Since I’d have been taken off the clock for the foreseeable future had I confessed what really happened, I kept it bottled up . . . now, reading back through my journal, the week was only just okay. Understand that I prayed constantly, morning, night, even over meals, but careful to keep the tears from spilling over my face and giving away the depth of emotion that a blessing for a lunchtime chicken salad cracker kit evoked.

I was at church early that Sunday, and was met by a staff member who took me back to Pastor Matthew’s office . . . I was tense and guarded, but sat at his invitation and listened as he began by saying that he loved to tell stories, but was often guilty of giving away the ending during the beginning. And then he said that this was one of those times, and spoke words that still prompt tears and still warm my heart, “You are welcome here.” We talked for over an hour with me telling my story and he asking questions and interjecting words of wisdom now and again . . . I made it to my seat about forty-five minutes into the service, and so stayed for the second service. More tears. More sodden Kleenex. And something deep within that I’d forgotten – hope for the future.

My days, and especially the nights, were tough. What I felt was a combination of anticipation, fear of rejection, hope for healing, and disappointment as every little thing seemed like a personal attack on me. The depression hadn’t eased, and the suicidal ideation continued – but it was easier to ask Jesus to cradle me in His arms and easier to fall asleep without the hurt I’d felt. I prayed multiple times a day for deliverance, for healing from a depression that pills couldn’t touch, and began to pray specifically for complete deliverance.

At the end of service the third week, I went forward for prayer, and found a couple who looked past who Teresa was and had been, and instead simply lifted me up in prayer . . . goodness something was waiting for me, and it was so close. Yet, the week ahead was fraught, and the satan was actively putting doubt in my mind, throwing obstacles at me, and there were a couple days when I felt at my lowest. The satan is cunning, and he wanted to succeed in his destruction of my life and knew he almost had me. Still, I prayed. I prayed and I worshipped and I sang songs of praise, because I knew, I KNEW that God could heal me, and I thanked Him for that deliverance. That Saturday, I posted a few words on Facebook, anticipating church the next day . . .

“I want to worship until the chains fall off”

I arrived quite early, was given a cup of coffee, found two empty seats in the foyer and sat in one of them, praying, anticipating, and then talking to another woman who later told me she had seen a vision of those two seats and who knew she supposed to sit there – although she didn’t know why. The sanctuary doors opened, and I again sat with my friends, in the very back, right on the aisle, and when the service began, I couldn’t keep from weeping before the Lord as I gave thanks while singing and praying. I don’t remember a single word of the sermon (I’ve gone back and watched it again, and still, now knowing what was to come, I still can’t remember a word) but our pastor was talking about the Spirit, and I sat, with eager anticipation, hoping and praying for special prayer to be offered. It was.

As I started down the aisle, tears already clouded my eyes – in front of me I saw no one else other than two women standing there with the kindest looks on their faces. All I could say before I began crying was that I needed relief from a deep depression, and both women began to pray, both in the Spirit and in English – and they were praying with such specificity, knowing nothing else about me, that it was clear that God was there with us. As we stood, both holding of them with an arm on me and the other in the air, I felt a warm hand on the top of my head, and heat seeping through my brain.

There was no one standing in front of us.

We prayed for several more minutes before stopping, and as I mopped my face dry, we were joined by the woman who I’d met just before the service began – she had been praying with us while sitting behind on the front row . . . and I couldn’t stop smiling. I KNEW that I’d been touched by God, and that the healing promised by the stripes on the back of our Lord Jesus Christ was at work within.

I just noticed the word count . . . I’m sorry for the length of this and will try to close the narrative soon.

As we stood talking, praising God, and just relaxing in the Spirit, we collectively noticed that the worship team was on the stage and as we turned to leave, they began to play for the second service. I don’t know what my face looked like or if I’d even bothered with makeup that morning, but I just couldn’t stop smiling. The weight of the world had fallen off my shoulders, and as I found my Jeep and crawled inside, I continued to praise Him for His mercy and healing. On Monday, customers and coworkers alike could tell something was different; Wednesday came, and my counselor pooh poohed the thought that I’d been healed, but she was glad I was having a couple of good days.

And I started expressing things like the pure joy I was experiencing, happiness I felt, and the joyous song that spilled from my lips during every conversation, be it a customer, coworker, or even just a fast-food worker. I had been set free, and I thanked Jesus over and over and over.

A few months or so had passed, and as I talked to God one night, I told Him that if we were supposed to forgive seventy times seven, then I’d thank Him seventy times seven. Then I stopped for a moment, and said, “You’ll get tired of hearing me say thank you.”

God laughed!

Psalm 18:1-6
1 I love you, Lord, my strength.
2 The Lord is my rock, my fortress and my deliverer;
my God is my rock, in whom I take refuge,
my shield and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold.
3 I called to the Lord, who is worthy of praise,
and I have been saved from my enemies.
4 The cords of death entangled me;
the torrents of destruction overwhelmed me.
5 The cords of the grave coiled around me;
the snares of death confronted me.
6 In my distress I called to the Lord;
I cried to my God for help.
From his temple he heard my voice;
my cry came before him, into his ears.

text:
🇯🇵 To everyone visiting Japan.

Japan’s shrines and temples are beautiful, but first and foremost, they are sacred places where people still come to pray.

Shrines and temples also have different customs.

⛩️ SHRINE AND TEMPLE ETIQUETTE IN JAPAN

【SHINTO SHRINES ⛩️】

① Bow before entering the torii

A torii marks the entrance to sacred ground. Give a slight bow before entering.

② Avoid the center of the path

The center, called seichu, is traditionally considered the path of the kami. Walk along the side when possible.

③ Purify your hands and mouth

If there is a temizuya, cleanse your hands and mouth before praying. Never put the ladle directly to your mouth.

④ Offer money respectfully

Do not throw your offering aggressively. The amount does not matter. Offer it respectfully.

⑤ Ring the bell if there is one

Some shrines have bells and others do not. Follow the customs of that shrine.

⑥ Two bows, two claps, one bow

This is the basic custom at many shrines, although some have different traditions.

⑦ Bow when leaving

It is polite to turn toward the shrine and bow again when leaving through the torii.

【BUDDHIST TEMPLES 🛕】

⑧ Bow at the temple gate

Give a slight bow before entering.

⑨ Avoid stepping on the threshold

It is polite to step over thresholds rather than on them.

⑩ Do not clap

This is a major difference from Shinto shrines. At temples, quietly put your hands together and pray.

⑪ Follow the temple’s rules for incense

The number of sticks and customs vary by temple and Buddhist sect.

⑫ Incense smoke is not required

Some people draw incense smoke toward their bodies, but this is not required at every temple.

⑬ Do not ring bells without permission

Some temples allow it, while others restrict it. Check the signs first.

【BOTH SHRINES AND TEMPLES】

⑭ Be quiet near places of worship

People are praying. Avoid loud conversations and unnecessary noise.

⑮ Remove hats and sunglasses when appropriate

Removing them during worship is more respectful.

⑯ Stay out of restricted areas

Never cross fences or ropes for a photo.

⑰ Do not touch statues or sacred objects

They are cultural treasures and objects of worship.

⑱ Respect sacred trees

Do not touch or climb them unless permitted.

⑲ Check photography rules

Photos may be prohibited inside or around sacred objects.

⑳ Do not photograph people praying without permission

Respect their privacy and worship.

㉑ Do not block paths with tripods or selfie sticks

Do not occupy entrances or approaches for photos.

㉒ Do not climb torii, buildings, statues, or stone monuments

Sacred and historic structures are not photo props.

㉓ No graffiti or stickers

Never carve names into buildings or torii or put stickers on them.

㉔ Tie omikuji only where permitted

Do not tie them to random trees or buildings. Taking them home is often fine.

㉕ Respect ema prayer plaques

Do not touch other people’s wishes or photograph and share them without permission.

㉖ Treat goshuin with respect

They are traditionally connected with visiting and worshipping at shrines and temples. Do not rush staff or cause a disturbance.

㉗ Treat omamori and ofuda respectfully

They are more than ordinary tourist souvenirs.

㉘ Eat and drink only where appropriate

Eat and drink only in permitted areas.

㉙ Take your trash with you

Many shrines and temples have no trash cans.

㉚ Follow local rules

Customs and restrictions vary. When unsure, follow the signs and instructions.

The most important thing is not memorizing all 30 rules.

These places are not theme parks.

They are not studios for social media videos.

For hundreds, sometimes more than a thousand years, people have prayed here and protected these sacred places.

Be a little quieter.

Pay attention to those around you.

And respect the place you are visiting.

That is enough.

We sincerely welcome everyone who visits Japan. 🇯🇵⛩️

text:
NTT (TSE: 9432) wrote the dates down before it had the products.

In November 2022 it published a timetable for IOWN 1.0 through 4.0, with years and performance multiples attached to each step.

Three years later, one of those numbers held up against actual hardware.

Start with IOWN 1.0.

It launched in March 2023 as a 100 Gbps dedicated line, initially offered within a single prefecture by NTT East and NTT West.

Latency reached 1/200 of conventional networks.

Capacity barely moved: 1.2 times, because the service still used existing optical transceivers.

It was a commercial launch that NTT's own explanation made look closer to a proof of concept.

The 2022 roadmap then ran forward.

IOWN 2.0 in fiscal 2025, targeting 13 times the network power efficiency and 8 times the server power efficiency.

IOWN 3.0 in fiscal 2029.

IOWN 4.0 from fiscal 2030, targeting 100 times.

At the Osaka Expo in 2025, NTT demonstrated an optical computer consuming 1/8 the power of a conventional system.

The 2022 server target was 8 times.

1/8 is the same number.

But it was a system demonstration, not a commercial product. NTT says the result came from combining advanced devices, computer architecture and software.

The efficiency target held. The product timetable became more complicated.

The current device roadmap shows PEC-2 connecting boards across CY2025 and CY2026, PEC-3 connecting packages in CY2028, and PEC-4 connecting dies in CY2032.

Commercial PEC-2 switch samples are now scheduled for Q4 2026. PEC-3 samples are scheduled for Q4 2028.

The old and new roadmaps do not map cleanly onto each other, because one step was split into multiple products. Calling every change a delay would confuse a change in taxonomy with a change in execution.

What can be said is narrower.

The fiscal 2025 target appeared as a working demonstration in 2025. The commercial switch sample follows in late 2026.

Here is the physical reason it saves power.

A conventional optical switch carries roughly 30 centimetres of electrical wiring between the optical module and the switch IC.

NTT's photonic-electronic convergence switch reduces that electrical path to about 30 millimetres.

Electrical transmission consumes more power as the path gets longer. Optical transmission is far less sensitive to distance.

At 102.4 Tbps, NTT says that architecture cuts the power consumption of the switch itself by about 50%.

Its stated device target is 3.9 pJ/bit, picojoules per bit.

I would not place that number directly beside figures published by NVIDIA.

NVIDIA describes its photonics switch in different units: electrical loss falling from as much as 22 dB to about 4 dB, and interface power falling from roughly 30 W to as low as 9 W.

Same engineering problem. Different measurement boundary.

The IOWN Global Forum published a paper in January 2026 explaining why that matters: energy-efficiency metrics across components, networks and systems stop at different points and are not directly comparable as published.

The organisation putting out the performance target also put out the warning.

Now the part that matters for who gets paid.

NTT Innovative Devices designs the CPO switch module and coordinates the partners.

Broadcom ($AVGO) supplies the 102.4 Tbps switch LSI.

Accton (TWSE: 2345) designs and manufactures the switch box.

Two subsidiaries of NTT Innovative Devices supply the photonic and the electronic integrated circuits.

Both of them sit in the United States: one in Beaverton, Oregon, one in Middletown, New Jersey.

Shinko Electric manufactures the substrate and assembles the CPO switch module.

Shinko was delisted from the Tokyo Prime Market in June 2025.

The company making the substrate and assembling this module is no longer something public-market investors can buy.

On 9 September I wrote that the layers Broadcom described as locked in are the layers Japan sells. This sits one level under that sentence.

Then came two documents.

On 29 August, Nikkei reported that Japan's Ministry of Defense plans to introduce the core of IOWN into the network connecting Self-Defense Force units and bases nationwide.

The named technology was the All-Photonics Network.

Related spending would enter the fiscal 2027 budget, with full-scale operation targeted from fiscal 2028, according to the report.

Two days later, the Ministry published its fiscal 2027 budget-request summary.

IOWN does not appear in it.

Neither does APN.

What does appear is this: 47.8 billion yen, plus an amount to be determined, for strengthening the Defense Information Infrastructure.

The stated function is to build a high-speed, high-capacity and resilient multilayer communications base that can remain available during jamming or disasters.

That is close to the function IOWN is being sold to perform.

But the technology is not named, and 47.8 billion yen is the broader Defense Information Infrastructure request, not an IOWN contract value.

This does not establish that the reporting is wrong.

The document is a summary rather than the full budget estimate, and the next Defense Buildup Program has not yet been revised. Projects affected by that revision remain subject to decisions during budget compilation.

It establishes something narrower.

The reporting names the technology.

The budget names the function.

Those are two different kinds of evidence.

At this point IOWN has produced a working demonstration, a dated commercial-sample plan and a named component supply chain.

It has not yet produced a publicly named defense contract or a disclosed revenue bridge.

I would not trade the word IOWN in a headline.

The signal comes when the function gets a vendor name, and when the budget line becomes an order.

Sources: NTT's November 2022 results briefing as reported by Nikkei; NTT Innovative Devices, 6 October 2025; Nikkei xTECH, 7 October 2025; IOWN Global Forum, January 2026; Nikkei, 29 August 2026; Japan Ministry of Defense FY2027 budget-request summary, 31 August 2026.

According to Press Monitor's tracking of Indian publications, this press review delivers media monitoring, media intelligence, and print media monitoring insights on news on retail and consumer goods across 16 stories from today's print editions.

1. Fuel Price Crisis Deepens as Brent Crude Crosses $100
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says state-owned fuel retailers are losing ₹5 per litre on petrol and ₹23 per litre on diesel as international oil prices crossed $100 per barrel, the highest since July. Fresh hostilities in West Asia, including tit-for-tat exchanges between the US and Iran, pushed Brent crude above $100. India, which imports over 88% of its crude, faces pressure on its trade balance and the rupee.

Retail fuel pricing directly impacts consumer spending and logistics costs across the retail supply chain. State-owned retailers are losing ₹5 per litre on petrol and ₹23 per litre on diesel as Brent crude exceeds $100 per barrel, the highest since July. India imports over 88% of its crude, facing pressure on trade balance and the rupee.

Key detail: Retail pump rates unchanged for over three months while India's crude oil import bill surged over 56% during April-July to USD 63.4 billion.

Source: Free Press Journal

Next step: Watch for potential retail fuel price adjustments if crude sustains above $110 per barrel.

2. CaratLane Expands Across Eastern India with 40-50 New Outlets Planned
A front-page report in Financial Express says CaratLane plans to open five to seven new stores across Eastern India over the coming months and add 40 to 50 outlets nationally in FY27 to bolster retail presence. The same report notes Petroñas Lubricants India signed an initial pact with Tata Motors for a pilot project for a structured and scalable used automotive lubricant recycling model simultaneously across Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu.

The Tata Group-owned jeweller's multi-channel growth signals confidence in regional retail demand. CaratLane plans to open five to seven new stores across Eastern India over the coming months, alongside adding 40 to 50 outlets nationwide in FY27, building on more than 388 existing stores.

Key detail: 69 stores already in the eastern region, with strategic investments in retail network, product portfolio, and omnichannel capabilities.

Source: Financial Express, The Pioneer

Next step: Track store openings in the eastern region over the coming months.

3. Rentomojo IPO Oversubscribed 1.42 Times on Day One
A front-page report in Mint says Rentomojo's public offering was fully subscribed on the first day of bidding on Wednesday, as it seeks to become India's first listed furniture rental company. The 12-year-old company, in which venture firm Accel holds a 20.9% stake, received bids for 22.07 million shares compared with 21.77 million shares on offer. Non-institutional and retail investors bid for 1.48 times and 116 times the shares set aside for them, while the IPO opened with five other public offerings on Wednesday, a record for single day in India, after a sluggish start to 2026 amid the US Iran war. Rentomojo's public offering comprises a fresh issue of shares worth Rs 150 crore and an Rs 1,106 crore offer for sale by existing shareholders, including Accel and Edelweiss Financial Services.

India's first listed furniture rental company draws strong retail and institutional interest ahead of its September 17 listing. Rentomojo's public offering received bids for 22.07 million shares compared with 21.77 million shares on offer, with non-institutional and retail investors showing strong demand.

Key detail: Price band ₹384-404 per share, valuing the company at ₹24,266 crore at the upper end. Fresh issue of ₹150 crore plus ₹1,106 crore offer for sale by existing shareholders including Accel and Edelweiss Financial Services.

Source: Mint

Next step: Monitor listing performance on September 17.

4. Kalyan Jewellers Launches ATM Brand in Tamil Nadu
A front-page report in Financial Express says Kalyan Jewellers launched ATM (Akshaya Thanga Maligai) in Tamil Nadu in August with a flagship store in Chennai. The company plans to open at least four more outlets in the state within six months and aims to expand into more regional markets. Kalyan Jewellers has set aside Rs 330 crore for broader regional expansion this financial year.

Regional expansion into Tamil Nadu with a dedicated brand marks a strategic push into South India's jewellery market. Kalyan Jewellers launched ATM (Akshaya Thanga Maligai) in Tamil Nadu in August with a flagship store in Chennai.

Key detail: At least four more outlets planned within six months. Rs 330 crore allocated for broader regional expansion this financial year.

Source: Financial Express

Next step: Watch for store openings in Tamil Nadu and potential expansion into other southern states.

5. Slikk Pivots from Speed to Fashion Curation and Private Labels
A front-page report in Mint says Bengaluru-based fashion startup Slikk is pivoting its growth strategy from relying on sixty minute delivery speeds to focusing on private labels, tighter product curation, and expanded dark stores. This strategic shift comes as major retailers like Myntra and Reliance Retail normalize rapid fashion delivery, prompting co-founder and chief executive Akshay Gulati to prioritise personalised discovery over sheer speed to maintain a competitive edge.

As quick-commerce giants normalize rapid delivery, Slikk's shift to curation and private labels redefines the fashion startup playbook. Co-founder and CEO Akshay Gulati prioritises personalised discovery over sheer speed to maintain a competitive edge against Myntra and Reliance Retail.

Key detail: Strategic shift from sixty-minute delivery speeds to tighter product curation and expanded dark stores.

Source: Mint

Next step: Monitor how the pivot affects Slikk's market position in the competitive fashion retail landscape.

6. Nexus Select Trust Acquires Galaxy Infra for ₹1,600 Crore
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says that Nexus Select Trust will acquire a 100% stake in Galaxy Infra Creations Pvt Ltd for Rs 1,600 crore. The assets include a 5.16 lakh sq ft shopping mall and a 164-key Hyatt Regency Hotel in Guwahati, both currently under construction. The deal marks Nexus Select Trust entry into northeast India.

The acquisition marks Nexus Select Trust's entry into northeast India, a region with growing retail and real estate potential. The deal includes a 5.16 lakh sq ft shopping mall and a 164-key Hyatt Regency Hotel in Guwahati, both currently under construction.

Key detail: 100% stake in Galaxy Infra Creations Pvt Ltd for ₹1,600 crore.

Source: Free Press Journal

Next step: Track development progress on the Guwahati mall and hotel.

7. ONDC Shifts Strategy to Farmers and Local Retail via DigiHaat
A front-page report in Mint says the Open Network for Digital Commerce has shifted its strategy to prioritise aggregation of farmers' produce and promote Indian-made goods through DigiHaat and DigiDukaan. Following a leadership transition at the Bengaluru-based entity and raising Rs 4,430 crore from strategic investors including Zoho, Uber and Amul, the government-backed platform aims to resolve structural supply chain gaps using interoperability rather than operating as a traditional marketplace.

The government-backed platform's new strategy to aggregate farmers' produce and promote Indian-made goods could reshape rural retail supply chains. Following a leadership transition and ₹4,430 crore raised from strategic investors including Zoho, Uber, and Amul, ONDC prioritises interoperability over traditional marketplace models.

Key detail: Focus on DigiHaat and DigiDukaan to resolve structural supply chain gaps.

Source: Mint

Next step: Watch for farmer adoption rates and interoperability-driven supply chain improvements.

8. Onion Prices Surge 52.66% Amid Steep Food Inflation
A front-page report in Financial Express says food inflation is likely to rise further amid steep prices of key agricultural commodities such as onion, rice, sugar and mustard oil. Retail onion prices rose 52.66 per kilogram, up 90% from a year earlier, while prices in Delhi‑NCR crossed 60 per kilogram. The government is offloading onions at a subsidised rate of 35 rupees per kilogram to curb the rise.

Steep vegetable inflation pressures consumer budgets and could ripple through the broader retail food segment. Retail onion prices rose 52.66% per kilogram, up 90% year-on-year, with Delhi-NCR crossing ₹60 per kilogram.

Key detail: Government offloading onions at subsidised rate of ₹35 per kilogram to curb the rise. Food inflation likely to rise further amid steep prices of rice, sugar, and mustard oil.

Source: Financial Express

Next step: Monitor whether government intervention stabilises prices ahead of festive season.

9. India Laptop Sales Face 5% Drop as Memory Chip Costs Soar
A front-page report in Mint says India’s laptop market is projected to see overall sales decline by five percent in the July to September quarter due to soaring memory chip costs. Prices for personal computers have already increased by around fifty percent, driven by an artificial intelligence boom that has doubled the cost of RAM and solid-state drives. Retailers warn that these steep hikes will significantly suppress consumer demand ahead of India's critical festive shopping season.

Soaring memory chip costs driven by the AI boom threaten retail electronics demand during the critical festive shopping season. PC prices up approximately 50%, with RAM and SSD costs doubling.

Key detail: Retailers warn that steep hikes will significantly suppress consumer demand in the July-September quarter.

Source: Mint

Next step: Track whether retailers absorb costs or pass them to consumers ahead of festive sales.

10. Smartphone Prices Rise 2% in India as Brands Raise Costs
A front‑page report in Statesman says that smartphone prices in India have risen by two percent so far this year, while worldwide prices have jumped fifteen percent. A large share of the market is priced below twenty thousand rupees, and brands such as Realme and Oppo have raised their prices by up to five thousand rupees on some models.

Even modest price increases in the sub-₹20,000 segment could dampen retail smartphone sales during peak buying periods. Brands including Realme and Oppo raised prices by up to ₹5,000 on some models, while global prices jumped 15%.

Key detail: A large share of the Indian smartphone market is priced below ₹20,000, making price sensitivity a key factor.

Source: Statesman

Next step: Watch for seasonal discounting to offset price hikes during festive months.

11. RBI Adds Five Currency Pairs to Retail Forex Platform
A front-page report in Mint says the Reserve Bank of India will add five currency pairs to its retail foreign-exchange platform, seeking to give individuals easier access to a wider range of currencies. The FX Retail is now set to introduce five additional currency pairs, enabling the customers to meet their needs in euro, British pound, Swiss franc, the Canadian dollar and the Emirati dirham, RBI chief general manager Dimple Bhandari said at the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai on Wednesday.

Expanded currency access on the retail forex platform supports India's growing outbound travel and business travel demand. Five new pairs — euro, British pound, Swiss franc, Canadian dollar, and UAE dirham — added to FX Retail.

Key detail: RBI chief general manager Dimple Bhandari announced the expansion at the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai.

Source: Mint

Next step: Monitor adoption of new currency pairs across retail banking channels.

12. IGL Enforces CNG Safety Drive, Denies Refuelling Without Certificates
A front-page report in The Hindu says Indraprastha Gas Ltd will refuse to dispense compressed natural gas to vehicles lacking a valid hydro-test certificate. Under government regulations, every CNG cylinder must be hydrotested every three years at a Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation-approved centre. Indraprastha Gas Ltd is conducting a safety drive across all its stations to verify certificate validity before refuelling.

Safety enforcement at fuel stations affects retail transportation costs and consumer access to CNG as a fuel option. Indraprastha Gas Ltd will refuse to dispense compressed natural gas to vehicles lacking a valid hydro-test certificate.

Key detail: Every CNG cylinder must be hydrotested every three years at a Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation-approved centre. Safety drives conducted across all stations.

Source: The Hindu

Next step: Track compliance rates and impact on CNG station throughput.

13. RBI Deputy Governor Launches Multicurrency Forex Services on Bharat Connect
A front-page report in Times of India says RBI deputy governor Rohit Jain launched multicurrency forex services on Bharat Connect through a controlled user group, with plans to expand to more channels and banks after assessment. Integrated with Clearcorp's FX-Retail, the platform now supports the euro, pound, Canadian dollar, Swiss franc, and UAE dirham alongside the US dollar, allowing customers to buy foreign currency, make overseas remittances, and reload forex cards with live rates and transparent pricing. The service is available through channels including Mobikwik, BHIM, bob World, PNB, Federal Bank, SBI, and Axis Bank.

Multicurrency forex services on a payments platform signal deeper integration of banking and foreign exchange for retail consumers. RBI deputy governor Rohit Jain launched services through Bharat Connect via Clearcorp's FX-Retail.

Key detail: Platform supports euro, pound, Canadian dollar, Swiss franc, and UAE dirham alongside the US dollar. Available through Mobikwik, BHIM, bob World, PNB, Federal Bank, SBI, and Axis Bank.

Source: Times of India

Next step: Monitor channel expansion and customer adoption rates across integrated banking platforms.

14. NPCI Launches Agentic AI Platforms and India's First Sovereign Banking Model
A front-page report in Financial Express says the National Payments Corporation of India has launched two agentic AI platforms, AiNxt and Agentic Orchestration and Messaging, and unveiled Finance Model for India Banking, India's first sovereign compact model designed for retail banking use cases.

India's first sovereign compact model for retail banking marks a significant step in AI-driven financial infrastructure for the retail sector. NPCI launched AiNxt and Agentic Orchestration and Messaging platforms, plus Finance Model for India Banking (FiMI).

Key detail: FiMI Banking is India's first sovereign compact model designed for retail banking use cases.

Source: Financial Express

Next step: Watch for integration with retail banking partners and real-world use case deployment.

15. Yubi Group Launches Pye Lending Platform for Retail Borrowers
A front-page report in Financial Express says Yubi Group has launched Pye, a new lending platform aimed at retail borrowers, which connects applications to a network of lenders rather than a single one, matching borrower profiles to the best suited partner by need, loan type and timeline.

A network-based lending platform for retail borrowers could democratise access to credit across India's consumer market. Pye connects applications to a network of lenders, matching borrower profiles to the best partner by need, loan type, and timeline.

Key detail: Unlike single-lender models, Pye's network approach increases approval chances and optimises loan terms for retail borrowers.

Source: Financial Express

Next step: Monitor lender onboarding and borrower adoption rates across the network.

16. Bandhan Bank Enters Credit Card Market with Four Mastercard Variants
A front-page report in Mint says Bandhan Bank entered the credit card market with four Mastercard variants, prompting a 4.25 percent stock rise over two trading sessions. The move shifts toward unsecured lending while secured advances rose to 56.8 percent of the book, with management targeting 60 percent eventually. Bandhan aims to convert its 32 million customer base into around 10 million credit card users, though competition and underwriting standards remain challenges.

Bandhan Bank's entry into unsecured lending with four Mastercard variants signals a strategic shift in retail banking competition. The move prompted a 4.25% stock rise over two trading sessions.

Key detail: Secured advances at 56.8% of the book, targeting 60%. Bandhan aims to convert its 32 million customer base into around 10 million credit card users.

Source: Mint

Next step: Track credit card adoption rates and underwriting standards in the competitive retail banking landscape.

text:
Happy and Good Thursday!  I just learned the story behind “The Arkansas Traveler,” and it is more than just an old fiddle tune.

The legend says that sometime in the early 1840s, Sanford “Sandy” Faulkner and several other men became lost while traveling through rural Arkansas. Depending on which version you hear, they were either in the Boston Mountains or the woods of Yell County when they stopped at a small log cabin for directions.

The man living there was trying to play a tune on his fiddle but could only play its first half. When Faulkner picked up the fiddle and played the missing second half, the man’s whole attitude changed. He welcomed the travelers into his home and offered them food and a place to stay.

Nobody knows exactly how much of the story really happened. Faulkner turned it into a popular comedy routine, and similar versions appeared in other states around the same time. The tune was printed as sheet music in 1847 and later performed in vaudeville shows.

Arkansas artist Edward Payson Washbourne painted the famous cabin scene in 1856. More than a century later, in 1987, “The Arkansas Traveler” became our official state historical song. Have you heard that song?
