text:
Högsta domstolen stoppar byte av valkretskartor i Missouri

Kavanaugh låter delstatens krav på folkomröstning gälla och river upp federal domares beslut, primärval hölls redan i kretsar som kan vara ogiltiga när mellanårsvalet avgörs

https://t.co/bgBRzxfsz5

USA:s högsta domstol har, med mindre än två månader kvar till mellanårsvalet, stoppat ett försök att i sista stund återinföra de kongressvalkretsar i Missouri som delstatens republikaner ritat om. En kortfattad order från domaren Brett Kavanaugh innebär att en dom i Missouris högsta domstol tills vidare står fast: de nya kartorna är inte giltiga förrän de godkänts i en folkomröstning. Därmed dras delstaten tillbaka mot de tidigare gränserna, enligt The Guardians direktrapportering.

Händelsekedjan visar hur strider om valkretsindelning numera drivs genom parallella domstolssystem i ett tempo som följer valkalendern, inte rättsstatens normala rytm. Republikanerna i Missouri ritade om kartan för att stycka upp en valkrets runt Kansas City som kontrolleras av demokraterna. Syftet var uppenbart: i en delstat med åtta platser i representanthuset skulle förändringen sannolikt ha gett partiet ytterligare en plats som lutar åt republikanerna. När delstatens domstol slog fast att kartorna krävde folkomröstning överklagade delstatsledningen till USA:s högsta domstol. Kavanaughs beslut, utan noterade invändningar, blockerade samtidigt en federal domare i St. Louis som i motsatt riktning hade beordrat delstaten att använda de republikanskt gynnande kartorna.

Republikanerna hävdar, enligt The Guardian, att en återgång till äldre gränser så nära valet riskerar att skapa administrativt kaos. Det är inte bara en retorisk varning. Missouri höll sina primärval med de nya, mer republikanskt fördelaktiga gränserna. Kandidater har alltså vunnit nomineringar i valkretsar som kanske inte finns när det väl är dags för det allmänna valet. Tvisten avgör därför inte bara vilket parti som gynnas av vilken karta, utan också om väljare och partier förväntas behandla primärvalet som ett bindande steg i en process där själva den geografiska spelplanen fortfarande är osäker.

Fallet ingår i en nationell kapprustning om valkretsar, där incitamenten är tydliga: partiernas ledningar kan vinna mandat utan att övertyga fler väljare, medan kostnaderna för osäkerheten hamnar hos valadministrationer, kandidater och i slutänden väljarna. The Guardian rapporterar att Donald Trump uppmanade republikanska delstatsledare att manipulera valkretsar för att behålla kontrollen över kongressen, och att demokraterna svarade med en motkampanj för omritning. När båda sidor spelar samma spel blir resultatet mer juridik, fler nödlösningar och en valapparat som tvingas agera under tidspress.

Domstolens ingripande är samtidigt ett slags vägran att ingripa på det sätt republikanerna i Missouri önskade. Genom att låta delstatens dom stå kvar signalerar USA:s högsta domstol att en sen ändring av kartan, som redan ifrågasatts och där formalia är omtvistad, inte nödvändigtvis räddas på federal nivå bara för att valmaskineriet redan rullar.

Missouris primärval genomfördes alltså enligt de nyare gränserna, enligt The Guardian. Det allmänna valet kan nu behöva hållas enligt andra.

PRINCE GEORGE WALKED INTO ETON THIS WEEK. FIFTY-SIX YEARS AGO, SO DID I.

*Letters from Stockholm*
*By Kio Amachree*

It was raining in Windsor on Tuesday morning. The photographs show the Princess of Wales holding an umbrella over her son as they walked through School Yard, the Prince of Wales beside them, the Head Master and the Provost waiting under Lupton's Tower. Simon Henderson shook the boy's hand and said five words: "Welcome. Good luck. Enjoy it."

Then his parents left, and Prince George, aged thirteen, became a boy at Eton.

I have been watching those pictures for two days now, and they have brought back things I thought I had put away for good.

I walked through that same arch in September 1970. I was also thirteen. I had been in England since I was eight, at prep school in Kent, so the country itself no longer frightened me. Eton did.

I was a Nigerian boy entering one of the whitest institutions in the world. There was no other Black boy in my year. As far as I can remember there was one other in the entire school, also Nigerian. There had been newspaper interest in my arrival. There were stares, from the boys and from some of the masters. My father was a distinguished man in Lagos and at the United Nations. In a Windsor boarding house that counted for nothing.

My parents said goodbye and drove away. And I was, to put it plainly, scared shitless.

That first morning I could not bring myself to leave my room. Breakfast was downstairs, with the other boys in my house, and I sat on my bed and listened to them going down. Eventually I made myself follow.

There was nowhere to sit. Nobody moved. Nobody offered.

Then one boy stood up and gave me his chair.

His name was Mark. He became my closest friend for the five years I spent at Eton.

I doubt he thought about it for more than a second. To the boy standing in that dining room it was the whole world. What he had actually said, without saying it, was: sit here, you belong.

I have thought about that chair many times since. I thought about it again on Tuesday, watching a thirteen-year-old walk into the same school under his mother's umbrella.

George and I could hardly be more different. I was conspicuous because I was Black. He is conspicuous because he is second in line to the throne. Every boy in the school knows who he is. Every master knows. The whole world knows. His goldfish bowl is bigger than mine ever was, and he will never be allowed to climb out of it.

But strip away the titles, the protection officers and the photographers, and what is left is a boy walking into a boarding house for the first time, wondering who will make room for him.

There is some comfort for him in how much has changed.

The Britain around Eton is not the Britain of 1970. The monarchy no longer commands the automatic reverence it did then, and that may be the best thing that could happen to George. If the boys around him can come to see him as George rather than as the future King, he has a real chance at something like an ordinary school life.

Eton itself has changed almost beyond recognition. My Eton was cold, strict and unbendingly traditional: terrible food, corporal punishment, and a settled indifference to whether any boy was comfortable or happy. You grew up fast because nobody was going to do it for you. Today the tailcoats and the private vocabulary survive, but underneath them is a modern, international school with facilities we could not have imagined.

And where there were two Black boys in my time, I am told there are now something like ninety. That single number says more about how Britain has changed in my lifetime than most books on the subject.

So I wish him well. An Old Etonian who arrived there fifty-six years before him has no business giving a future King advice, but if I were allowed one paragraph it would be this.

Keep your feet on the ground. Choose your friends for who they are, not for what they can do for you. Join things. Take the teasing, and give it back. Learn to laugh at yourself. And find a way, now and then, to escape the bowl.

Do that, and the next five years could be among the best of his life. For all my fear that first morning, Eton became part of who I am.

And it began, as these things sometimes do, with another thirteen-year-old boy standing up and saying: take my chair.

text:
@Soteriology101 You keep calling my view of God’s decree idiosyncratic. It isn’t. It’s the Confession.

God, from all eternity, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely and unchangeably ordained whatsoever comes to pass. I affirm that without remainder. Nothing comes to pass outside His providence. That is the scope of the decree.

The decree is God’s eternal purpose. It’s the plan in God, not a force shoved onto creation. The decree doesn’t reach down, grab a man by the will, and make him the sinner. What meets the world is providence. Providence is how the plan is executed. By the same providence He orders things to fall out according to the nature of second causes, either necessarily, freely, or contingently.

That’s why I say the decree itself is not what exerts force on creation. I am not denying certainty. I’m denying your picture of the decree as a univocal cause that turns God into the one thinking the thought and doing the deed. God is the first cause. Men are real second causes. They think, want, and act. God ordains that they do. He is not the author of sin.

WCF 3.1 and 2LBC 3.1 don’t stop at “whatsoever comes to pass.” They add the clauses you treat as optional:

yet so, as thereby neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures; nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established.

WCF 5.2 says the same thing from the other side: in relation to the decree all things come to pass immutably, yet by the same providence He orders them according to the nature of second causes.

If “idiosyncratic” means I won’t let “decree” already mean “God is the sinner,” then yes. That refusal is not mine. It is the Reformed church’s. Calvin, the Confession, Turretin, Hodge, and Bavinck all kept plan and execution, first cause and second causes, decree and precept, in the same system. You collapse them, then call the uncollapsed view a private theory.

You don’t grant the scope of the decree. That’s the actual disagreement. You then take the Reformed claim that God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, load it with your sense of “cause,” and treat the result as if it were already our doctrine. It isn’t. Historic Calvinism answers yes to “Does God decree all things?” and no to “Is God the one wanting the evil and doing the deed as its sinner?” Those are different questions. You keep making them the same question and calling the distinction idiosyncratic.

It isn’t idiosyncratic. That’s 3.1 and 5.2.

I  BET YOU DIDN'Y KNOW ABOUT THIS: AFTER FLIGHT 77 HIT THE PENTAGON ON 9/11, THE FOLLOWING HAPPENED.
 
A daycare facility inside the Pentagon had many children, including infants
who were in heavy cribs. The daycare supervisor, looking at all the
children they needed to evacuate, was in a panic over what they could do.
 
There were many children, mostly toddlers, as well as the infants who
would need to be taken out with the cribs. There was no time to try to
bundle them into carriers and strollers.
 
Just then a young Marine came running into the center and asked what they
needed. After hearing what the center director was trying to do, he ran
back out into the hallway and disappeared. The director thought, "Well,
here we are, on our own."
 
About 2 minutes later, that Marine returned with 40 other Marines in tow.
Each of them grabbed a crib with a child, and the rest started gathering up
toddlers.
 
The director and her staff then helped them take all the children out of
the center and down toward the park near the Potomac .
 
Once they got about 3/4 of a mile outside the building, the Marines stopped
in the park, and then did a fabulous thing - they formed a circle with the
cribs, which were quite sturdy and heavy, like the covered wagons in the
Old West.
 
Inside this circle of cribs, they put the toddlers, to keep them from
wandering off. Outside this circle were the 40 Marines, forming a perimeter
around the children and waiting for instructions. There they remained until
the parents could be notified and come get their children.
 
The chaplain then said, "I don't think any of us saw nor heard of this on
any of the news stories of the day. It was an incredible story of our men
there.” There wasn't a dry eye in the room.
 
The thought of those Marines and what they did and how fast they reacted;
could we expect any less from them? It was one of the most touching stories
from the Pentagon.
 
It's the military, not the politicians that ensures our right to life,
liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. It's the military who salutes the
flag, who serves beneath the flag, and whose coffin is draped by the flag.
 
If you care to offer the smallest token of recognition and appreciation for
the military, please pass this on and pray for our men and women, who have
served and are currently serving our country, and honor the memory of those 
who have given the ultimate sacrifice!                                                                                                                                                               
  God Bless The USA!

Never forget!!!

#JiangLi #JiangHeng #LiPeiEn 
#OceanJiang #SeekyLi #Desire4 #ABODesire

Okay, I’m just going to take the liberty of sharing my very personal opinion on the four ABO Desire characters and the actors who play them. Please don’t take this too seriously it’s simply my impression ♥️

Enigma – Hua Yong / Huang Xing:
Sorry, but this role just suits Huang Xing incredibly well. That mysterious vibe, that special kind of presence, and that whole “you never quite know what’s going on inside his head” feeling it just works so well with him.

And honestly, I think Huang Xing could borrow a little more of Hua Yong for real life. Sometimes I get the impression that he still holds himself back a bit and doesn’t fully show everything he has to offer. In my opinion, a little more of that Enigma confidence would suit him really well 💙

S-Alpha – Sheng Shaoyou / Qiu Dingjie:
With Qiu Dingjie, I didn’t have to think twice. Sheng Shaoyou walks into a room with that “Okay, I’m taking charge here” energy. Confident, dominant, sometimes a little too sure of himself and then suddenly feelings get involved, and our big Alpha has no idea what to do with himself anymore. That contrast is exactly what makes him so entertaining to me.

Qiu Dingjie brings that strong presence across incredibly well, but outside the role, he comes across as much softer and more warm-hearted to me. Maybe he could simply take the best part of Sheng Shaoyou with him: the confidence. He can happily leave the rest of the Alpha drama on set 🧡

S-Alpha – Shen Wenlang / Jiang Heng:
Jiang Heng, or rather Shen Wenlang, falls into a different category for me: the man doesn’t even have to say anything, and you still notice when he’s there.

Not loud, not constantly seeking attention just that calm, composed presence. And that’s exactly what I like about this character. Shen Wenlang comes across as protective and sometimes quite cool and reserved, but underneath, there’s much more emotion than he initially lets on.

With Jiang Heng, it’s exactly this calm nature that I find so likeable. In my opinion, he doesn’t need to become any more “Alpha” than he already is. That understated, laid-back quality is precisely his strength. Please just keep it 🩶

Omega – Gao Tu / Li Peien:
And then we have Gao Tu… my little “Don’t you dare underestimate him!”

At first glance, he seems gentle, sensitive, and maybe even a little fragile. But the longer you watch him, the more you realize there’s an incredible amount of strength in him. It’s simply a very different kind of strength from that of the Alphas.

And that’s exactly why I think Li Peien fits this role so well. That soft, warm presence just works. And no being gentle doesn’t mean being weak. Quite the opposite. With him, I’d actually say: please don’t try to seem tougher or cooler. It’s exactly that naturalness and sensitivity that make him so charming to me 🩵

text:
Volatility Doesn’t Matter and Private Investments Aren’t Low Vol

Introduction:

Decades ago, I took a finance class at the University of Michigan and vividly remember when the professor told us that the proper measure of risk is volatility. While I didn’t have the knowledge at the time to challenge the professor, I instinctively and immediately thought that this was incorrect. The only circumstance where volatility matters is if you have to sell an investment at a bad time, and the circumstances where you’d have to sell would be that exact “bad time”. My thought both then and now is that the proper measure of risk is not short-term price fluctuation; but rather, the permanent loss of capital.

I believe people focus on volatility because it’s something they can measure and quantify. Earnings estimates can be debated. Discounted cash flow models depend on your inputs and your expected cost of capital. Revenue projections, the competitive environment, and the regulatory constraints are all subject to revision. But volatility offers the certainty of a quantified calculation. We can measure it. We can compare it to our realized return and calculate a Sharpe ratio telling us whether we’re earning a higher or lower return per unit of volatility.

Why Volatility is the Wrong Measure:

This focus on short-term volatility is a bad approach. When you buy shares in a company, you’re buying both a stock and a business. The stock market can have a temper. At times, it’s so euphoric that even bad news leads to rising valuations. (The expression is climbing a wall of worry.) At other times, everything gets sold including the great business you own. In the long-run, you own a business, and if you can find high-quality high-growth ones that are well-run and not too expensive, you’re going to do well over time. At DKI, we’ve had more positions rise by 100% or more than we’ve had positions that have lost money. That’s hard to do which is why we run a high-conviction concentrated portfolio. At both Silver Arrow, with my partner, Raji Khabbaz, and at DKI, we’ve always been willing to trade short-term volatility for long-term returns. At both places, we’ve succeeded.

Long Term Capital Management:

The Nobel prize winning economists who did the work on volatility and risk were also the same people who founded and managed Long Term Capital Management (LTCM), the firm that blew up so spectacularly they required Wall Street firms to finance a bailout. The problem with their approach is they tracked historical volatility and convinced themselves that huge amounts of leverage was “safe” because they had measured the risk. The approach worked until there was a market dislocation which caused volatility to spike. There’s an old Wall Street expression that markets take the escalator up and the elevator down. That means that rising prices tend to be orderly and falling prices during a crisis, dislocation, or company revaluation tend to gap down hard.

In the case of LTCM, prices fell, volatility spiked, and liquidity evaporated leaving the firm unable to sell its leveraged positions fast enough. They were in business for a few years and claimed that the event that killed the firm was so unlikely that it should have only happened once in multiple lifetimes of the universe. They were wrong. More than a quarter of a century later, the fund allocation business still uses this failed model because it allows them to quantify a measure of “risk” and report to investors that they’ve modeled it and thus earned their fees.

How to Think About Your Portfolio:

Too much leverage is dangerous and the volatility calculation that many use to “analyze” their portfolio risk doesn’t work when there’s a problem. When there’s a problem is exactly when you’re forced to sell. For most Americans, the most valuable asset they own is their home. Housing prices rise and fall over time, but families aren’t revaluing their balance sheets based on local comparable prices every month let alone every day. People have a general idea of where the market is and may refinance or get a line of credit at times when they have a lot of equity or when they need money for something important. For all the headlines about carnage in the housing market in 2008, most homeowners were fine as long as they owned the home they were living in, could afford the mortgage they had signed for, and didn’t need to sell immediately. It was the people who needed cash NOW, the people who counted on refinancing to afford their current mortgage, and the people who had bought five properties to list on Airbnb and were overleveraged to a falling rental market who suffered.

Your tl;dr* version: As long as you don’t need funds immediately and haven’t overleveraged yourself, short-term volatility isn’t important.

Private Investments:

This brings me to the private investment / private credit market. These investments have been marketed to the family office community for a long time. The pitch tends to be that these are high-quality high-return opportunities being offered only to wealthy people. Part of the marketing is typically that these investments will have superior returns with lower risk. The lower risk part means low-volatility. The key point is that even if you accept the premise that low-vol means low-risk, these investments aren’t low-vol.

Because they’re private investments, there’s no regular market check on valuations. An honest fund that manages these private investments will keep an eye on other comparable private transactions and update their valuations up or down accordingly. However, these same funds collect fees based on assets under management and raise assets based on returns. They have every incentive to treat valuations as a rachet where good news causes upward revaluations, but bad news is ignored. This is something we’ve all seen in the recent private credit market where firms like Blue Owl had investments that were failing, but didn’t mark their book down as conditions deteriorated. The revaluations in their portfolio tended to be from marks that went directly from almost 100% straight to zero. (escalator up and elevator down)

The true value of private investments is actually more volatile than publicly traded equities because there’s a lack of liquidity. Blue Owl and other private funds have thrown up gates and not allowed investors full redemptions. They are contractually able to do this. It’s part of the agreement that investors signed. It also makes sense because it’s impossible to run a private fund of illiquid investments and provide investors regular liquidity. Everyone needs to agree to a shared time-frame for the investment to work.

So, if private funds and private investments are marketed as low-volatility, then why am I saying that these investments are actually higher-vol in nature? The difference is due to the ability to calculate daily changes in the market. Imagine if you went to a meditation retreat for a month where electronic devices were prohibited. Your stocks would still trade. Their valuations would move every minute the market was open for that month. From your point of view, you now have a low-vol portfolio because you aren’t able to check prices constantly.

Your tl;dr version: The inability to check the market price each day doesn’t mean your portfolio is low volatility. It just means you’re not looking or can’t look very often.

Did I Make Money? A Personal Example:

On a personal level, I just made an investment in a company at the very edge of possible technology. It will have a binary outcome. The investors will either make many times our money, or will receive zero back from our investment. We all understand this outcome distribution and have sized our investments accordingly. There’s an interesting quirk of timing with this deal. The founders are doing two capital raises at the same time. The one I’m participating in this week has a designated valuation. The one that might close later this year will be at double the valuation.

Imagine that I invested $100,000 and the company closes the second round of financing at the higher valuation in three months. Did I just make $100,000 in one quarter? A private equity fund could reasonably argue that I invested at one valuation and the market was assigning a higher valuation for a subsequent round. They’d mark their book up 100% and would have reason to do so. In this case, I’m not so sure. It’s a private investment. I can’t sell it.

The real valuation in this case is likely to turn out to be either zero or millions of dollars. Until there’s liquidity, I can’t open Schrödinger's box. The cat might be alive or it might be dead, but there’s nothing I can do about it. One might argue that I should mark an investment I can’t sell at zero until there’s liquidity. We could just as easily argue that I should make an estimate about its future value, discount that back, and mark the investment at $200k, or $500k, or $1MM. Whether I tell myself this investment is worth more than I paid (which feels good) or less than I paid (which feels bad) doesn’t matter because I can’t spend the money.

Whether I’m honest with myself when I mark my personal holdings is unimportant. When university professors misinform students about the nature of risk is well-meaning nonsense. When private funds mislead investors about the value and safety of their holdings, they’re committing fraud.

*tl;dr is short for too long didn’t read, but thank you for making it to the end of this piece.

If this approach to investing resonates with you, please feel welcome to subscribe.

text:
Robinhood Derivatives LLC stopped new sports event contracts for Michigan customers on September 9, 2026, and must close leftover sports positions by October 9. 

I read the MGCB notice as a pause, not a final call on whether CFTC prediction markets count as licensed sports wagering.

Henry Williams called the court-approved stipulation another win for Michigan consumers.

 Dana Nessel said her office wants betting in the state fair and regulated while the Sixth Circuit appeal keeps moving.

Robinhood still argues federal preemption under the Commodity Exchange Act.

 Neither side gave up that fight.

Sports event contracts let you take a yes-or-no position on a game and settle it like a futures-style ticket. Robinhood routed those sports contracts through KalshiEX and Rothera Exchange and Clearing.

Michigan treats the same product as unlicensed sports betting. Kalshi already faces a state injunction, geolocation blocks, and a steep daily fine.

Robinhood is the second platform to pull sports contracts in the Wolverine State this year.

Stocks, options, and non-sports prediction markets stay on the app.

Only sports-related event contracts are dark. If you hold an open sports position, close it or let it settle before October 9 and save the confirmations. 

Switching venues does not dodge the order. 

The restriction covers contracts on any designated contract market offered to people located in Michigan.

The live question on X and in court is bigger than one brokerage tab. States want MGCB-style licensing. Platforms want CFTC rules to travel nationwide. 

Docket 26-1542, plus related Polymarket, Coinbase, and Kalshi appeals, will decide whether sports prediction markets return.

I would use a licensed Michigan sportsbook for game results until that appeal lands. 

Treat October 9 as a hard closeout, not a rumor date.

text:
Newsom Says DSA Socialist Ideas Are Already Being Worked into the Democratic Party Platform

For years, conservatives warned that the Democrat Party was barreling toward socialism. And for years, the usual suspects waved it off. Fearmongering. Right-wing paranoia. Conspiracy thinking. Anyone who dared point out the obvious ideological trajectory got the standard treatment – mockery, dismissal, a patronizing smile from some cable news anchor.

Turns out the paranoid people were just paying attention. One of the most prominent Democratic governors in America – a man whose name lands in every presidential speculation piece like clockwork – sat down on national television and confirmed what millions already suspected. No hedging. No carefully lawyered denials. Just a straight admission, offered with the casual ease of someone ordering coffee.

During a portion of an interview aired on Monday’s “PBS NewsHour,” California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said that the DSA’s ideas are being worked into the platform of Democrats and said that part of the DSA platform is “about recognizing that we’ve got a planet that is getting hotter and drier, and that we’ve got to address the issue of climate change, and we want energy security, and we want to move off fossil fuels. That’s a DSA position. That’s a mainstream position within the Democrat Party.”
Co-host Amna Nawaz asked, “So, let me ask you about how Democrats can win back control of Congress, because it’s been a pretty revealing primary season for the party, right? A reckoning, some have called it, too. You saw how many wins DSA candidates, Democratic Socialist candidates, were able to win, Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, he doesn’t identify as DSA, but was sort of aligned with them. If you have these candidates and this platform that is clearly animating the base, energizing turnout, should more of those ideas be worked into the broader Democratic platform?”

So. There you have it. Asked point-blank whether Democratic Socialists of America ideas should be folded into the broader Democratic platform, Gavin Newsom didn’t blink. “I think they are,” he said. Then he rattled off the wish list: Medicare for All, eliminating fossil fuels, publicly financed campaigns. Not aspirational goals for some hazy future. Current, mainstream Democratic positions – his words, not mine.

text:
When your mood is elevated and euphoria sets in, the urge to spend freely — or even recklessly — can be strong. It’s not uncommon to feel unstoppable, to chase grand ideas, or to make impulse purchases, rack up credit card debt, or even gamble away savings in the moment.

Risky financial behavior is often associated with manic episodes, but similar — though sometimes less intense — impulsivity can also show up during hypomania. While the consequences may not always be as extreme, the impact on your finances and well-being can still be significant.

That’s why it’s essential to put safeguards in place before your mood shifts.

Fortunately, some financial planners, including Martin M. Shenkman and Annie McQuilken, have experience with — and sound advice for — protecting against the potential fallout of a manic or hypomanic episode.

Here, they share their top tips for safeguarding your wallet from impulsivity:

1. Establish Two Separate Bank Accounts
When it comes to managing money, consider having one bank account dedicated to essential bills, like rent and utilities, and limit access to your spending accounts — for example, by leaving your debit card at home or removing payment apps from your phone. You can also set up email notifications to alert a trusted person if there’s any unusual account activity.

Establish a separate account for personal expenses, and keep just enough funds in it for one month. If you opt for a debit card, make sure it’s set up to deny any overdraft spending.

2. Keep Detailed Spending Records
Shenkman strongly recommends maintaining a detailed record of spending, regardless of mood state, so that anyone who is brought in to help with finances knows what expenditures are expected and reasonable.

Many financial institutions offer their own budgeting tools and programs, and there are a variety of reliable apps out there, from Mint to You Need a Budget (YNAB), for tracking expenses.

3. Put Limits on Your Credit Cards
To limit access to your personal credit — and protect against identity theft — consider setting up conditions for locking your account and denying credit through the three primary reporting agencies, Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion.

With these agencies, or other companies that monitor personal credit, you can also arrange for alerts to be sent to a trusted family member any time a credit check is performed.

text:
If a dog loves chicken, you do not lure it with charcoal.
If a child lives for candy, you do not bait the trap with a fast.
If a thirsty man will sell his soul for wine, you do not hold out an empty cup and call it joy.
You offer what the hunger already wants. That is how you catch a creature. That is how you tell a hunter from a father.

Now put the two majority claims on that table and watch what is served.

In the days of Jesus the Jews wanted a war-king: Rome off their necks, a throne in Zion, a Messiah who wins the way men win. He offers the opposite. No legion. A cross. “My kingdom is not of this world.” The Gentiles wanted to keep the old feast—pleasure, orgies, the body as a god, even the rot of incest that Paul names in the churches’ neighbor-world. Jesus says stop. Do not look to lust. Tear out the eye. One man. One woman. Master the flesh. In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage. He is not selling chicken to the dog. He is offering charcoal to a mouth trained on meat—and then dying to make the mouth new.

In the days of Muhammad the men who built the army wanted what fighting men have always wanted: women, wine, spoil, a heaven that feels like the night after a raid. Look at the menu. Wives here. More promised there. A lawful appetite crowned. That is not charcoal. That is chicken. The lure matches the pack.

Today the world is more promiscuous, not less. The same test still works. What does each message cost the male ego now?

Then, the greatest machine of power was an army of men. A revelation that baptizes the sword and the bed will gather that machine fast. Now the greatest machine is the state: parties, courts, borders, schools, media. Jesus still says the same inconvenient sentence: his kingdom is not of this world. He will not hand you a ministry of truth to capture. He will not let you baptize your coalition and call it Zion. The gospel remains against what we like. It tells the religious nationalist he cannot have a holy empire. It tells the libertine he cannot have a holy orgy. It tells the ambitious man the last seat is a towel and a basin. So ask the honest question: if someone wanted to deceive us, would he keep offering charcoal—fasting to the sweet tooth, a cross to the man who wants a crown, one wife to the man who wants a harem, a kingdom not of this world to the man who wants this world?

And the other story: the Scriptures were “corrupted,” they say—so that what remains is the hard road. Fasting for candy-lovers. A crucified God for people who wanted a Caesar. That would be the stupidest fraud in history. Forgers who want followers do not edit the bait down. They edit it up.

Watch the present. Islam can advance inside countries where a political left that hates the church will walk beside it for a season. That left is not built on Sinai. It is built on permission: the body as politics, gender as clay, desire as a right. For a while the alliance is useful. A shared enemy—the Christ who says no. After the house is taken, the guest does not keep the host’s rules. Then comes sharia: the army under another name. If a doctrine already allows deception for the cause when the cause is threatened, the handshake was never the destination. It was the door.

So which god is hunting, and which God is fathering?

The god who plates what the age already craves—women and wine for the raider then, power and narrative for the operator now—is easy to recognize. He does not need to change the human heart. He only needs to bless it.

The God of Jesus keeps serving charcoal to the old appetite: die to yourself, one covenant bed, no orgy, no child as a prize, no throne of this world, no virgins as pay, only God. He would be a fool of a con man. He makes sense as a Father who would rather lose the crowd than feed the sickness.

Scripture was not “fixed” to make the gospel tastier. The gospel is still the least marketable offer on the table. That is how you know it was not designed by a man building an army—or a man building a government. It was designed by someone who wants sons, not customers.

text:
There has been a lot of speculation lately about where Opendoor is on the path to ANI break-even, and I worry some folks think we are further ahead than we actually are. Rather than have you guess, I want to do two things. First, give you a direct update on how Q3 is tracking, and second, start releasing numbers more frequently so you can track our progress for yourself and hold us accountable.

To say the thing up front: we are not at ANI break-even yet. What we are seeing in the actual numbers of the business this week, the speed of underwriting, the accuracy of our models, the response from our users and the forward revenue created are all going very well.  We’re making lots of progress, but rebuilds are bumpy.

TL;DR: The worsening housing market at the end of August pushed us roughly six to eight weeks behind on our Adjusted EBITDA guideposts, meaning the twelve-month window in which we expect to be adjusted EBITDA profitable now starts this quarter rather than last quarter. For Q3, we expect revenue to increase 10-15% year over year, Contribution Profit dollars to increase 70-75% year over year, and Contribution Margin to land between 3.2% and 3.5%. We still expect to exit 2026 ANI-positive on a twelve-month go-forward basis.

On our first earnings call I told you we would make the right long-term decisions for the business, not manage it around a quarterly number. August tested whether we meant it.

For most of its life as a public company, Opendoor sold homes slower than the market. Between our IPO and my start date, we cleared at roughly 85% of market pace and lagged the market two days out of every three. We held on to homes under the belief that waiting protected margins. Holding homes was our own version of bloodletting, the "cure" for weak margins. It did not work, and it made this company fragile.

Over my first year, we changed that. We now clear significantly faster than the market, beating it nearly nine days out of ten. This is our job: clear faster.

When we reported earnings in early August, July contribution margin was tracking ahead of our plans and the housing market looked like it might be stabilizing. Instead, the last two weeks of August were among the worst we have seen for housing in years. Clearance slowed further and delistings stayed high. That is not an excuse - it’s just what happened.

We had a choice. Slow sales, protect the margin number, and let homes age. Or price to clear. Old Opendoor chose the first option for years. It made the quarter look better, but it made the company worse. We are not doing that again. Time has a cost, and selling homes fast is the discipline this business requires. We are going to clear homes, even when that hurts margins.

Our job is to sell homes, not park inventory or pull listings offline when things get tough. The market got worse, but it did not break our resale engine. We are still clearing faster than the market. That is part of the business we rebuilt, and it held. Don’t confuse any of this with the business moving backwards.  The business is in materially better condition today. Revenue and contribution margin will both be higher year over year. And as the rest of the rebuild catches up, a market like this will hurt us less going forward.

Nothing longer-term is changing. We expect Opendoor will be ANI-positive on a twelve-month go-forward basis exiting 2026. That depends on buying fast and selling fast. If margins were resetting permanently, that would change things. That is not what is happening. We are repricing one book of inventory and clearing it instead of rolling it into next year.

To help you follow all that we are doing better, both on sales and acquisitions, we are going to give you more to track every week on https://t.co/u8GSnpFzzy. Just as you should not have to wait until earnings to see what is happening on acquisitions, you should not have to wait to see how many homes we sold or how fast we cleared.

Last week, we sold 223 homes, and cleared 19% faster than the market, adjusted for delistings. The weekly numbers will be noisy, just as the acquisition numbers were when we first started publishing them. What matters is the trend: as we buy more homes, are we selling them at the pace we planned and staying ahead of the market or not? And when we are behind, you will see it for yourself.

I told you how we would manage this company: for years, not quarters.  Twelve months from now, judge us based on that. Either we fixed the company or not. The core metrics say we are on track. For Q3, year over year, we expect margin to be up. Revenue up. Velocity up. The end of August was absolutely brutal for housing and pushed us back by roughly six to eight weeks. We’re not going to take that sitting down.

Kaz

(fyi, regular disclosures on this type of thing where we release weekly numbers etc are on our IR page, https://t.co/ahitgfnIKI)

text:
Natural Gas Companies: Prices, Competitive Position and Strategies

Executive assessment

The most useful U.S.-listed research shortlist spans three distinct businesses: EQT and Expand Energy for large-scale gas production; Antero Resources and Range Resources for production with meaningful natural-gas-liquids exposure; Williams and Kinder Morgan for infrastructure; and Cheniere Energy for LNG exports. These are strategically relevant coverage selections, not a comprehensive global production ranking or an assertion that all seven stocks are attractive at their current prices.

The sector’s central tension is growing demand alongside growing supply. LNG exports and electricity demand can increase without creating a sustained rise in domestic gas prices. A producer needs profitable realized prices after regional discounts, transport and hedges. An infrastructure owner needs valuable, utilized capacity and creditworthy customers. An exporter needs reliable plants, sound commercial contracts and disciplined construction spending. The same gas-price move can have different effects on those businesses.

For a research watchlist, prioritize EQT/Expand when seeking commodity exposure; Antero/Range when deliberately accepting liquids and regional marketing exposure; Williams/Kinder Morgan when emphasizing infrastructure cash flow; and Cheniere when focusing on LNG execution. No full valuation model establishes a best stock or price target here. Entry decisions should follow downside-tested cash-flow valuation rather than a blanket natural-gas or AI-demand thesis.

Scope and information dates

Assessment date: September 10, 2026. The report focuses on U.S.-listed companies with material natural-gas exposure. It covers both business strategy and investment research criteria. Company financial comparisons use second-quarter 2026 releases, supplemented by material transaction updates. Prices are in U.S. dollars unless specified.

The gas-price dashboard uses EIA’s September 10 daily page and its quoted delivery basis. Storage is the September 10 release for the week ending September 4. The macro forecast is EIA’s September 9 outlook, finalized September 3. Share prices are a separate intraday September 10 snapshot around 8:54 a.m. Pacific. None is a promise of the next executable trade. [1–3,14]

1. Natural gas prices

Current regional spot dashboard

EIA’s September 10 page reports the following day-ahead spot prices for delivery that day. The region names are labels; the pricing point is the specific hub listed below. The page republishes SNL Energy data and is not a live executable order book. [1]

Region              Gas pricing point          Dollars/MMBtu
Louisiana           Henry Hub                         2.81
Houston             Houston Ship Channel              2.68
New England         Algonquin Citygate                2.42
New York City       Transco Zone 6-NY                 1.59
Mid-Atlantic        TETCO-M3                          1.71
Midwest             Chicago Citygate                  2.69
Southwest           El Paso San Juan                  2.47
Southern California SoCal Border                      4.02
Northern California PG&E Citygate                     3.98
Northwest           Northwest Sumas                   3.28

Henry Hub is down 3.3% from the previous comparison on that page. These prices illustrate substantial regional differences; the New York quote is not a nationwide price, and neither California quotation represents every delivery point in that state. [1]

Three price concepts must remain separate. Spot describes near-term physical delivery. Futures describe a specified future delivery month. A company’s realized price reflects its actual mix of delivery points, contractual indices, hedges and products. A quarterly realized price cannot be compared with a single daily spot quote as though the difference measures management performance.

EIA’s prompt-month futures field was unavailable in the retrieved daily page. A same-day CME futures settlement, forward strip, Dutch TTF assessment, Asian JKM assessment and Waha quotation are therefore not asserted. The legacy Natural Gas Weekly Update page returned January 2026 material and was excluded as a current source. A precise, dated spot dashboard is more useful than filling missing benchmarks with stale numbers.

Units and conversions

MMBtu measures energy: one million British thermal units. Mcf is one thousand cubic feet of gas; MMcf is one million, Bcf is one billion, and Bcf/d is a daily flow rate. A dekatherm is one MMBtu. One Mcf is not universally equal to one MMBtu because gas heat content varies.

If a stream contains 1.03 MMBtu per Mcf, a price of $2.81/MMBtu corresponds to $2.8943/Mcf before any contractual adjustments. Use the measured or contractual heat factor rather than a blanket conversion. For European quotations, one MWh is approximately 3.412 MMBtu; converting euros/MWh into dollars/MMBtu also requires a contemporaneous exchange rate.

Bcfe includes liquids converted to gas-equivalent volumes. It is not necessarily actual gas sold, and an energy-equivalent conversion does not imply economic equivalence between a barrel of liquids and gas. This distinction matters particularly for Antero and Range. Similarly, an LNG facility’s million-tonnes-per-year capacity is not comparable to an upstream company’s Bcfe/d without clear conversion assumptions and utilization.

2. Storage and the supply-demand balance

The September 10 EIA release estimates working storage of 3,254 Bcf on September 4, a weekly increase of 40 Bcf. Inventories were 79 Bcf below a year earlier, but 148 Bcf above the five-year average: 2.4% below last year and 4.8% above average. Both comparisons matter. A year-over-year deficit alone would overstate tightness. The reported national weekly-change standard error was 0.8 Bcf. [2]

An injection should be interpreted against weather, supply, exports and the market’s expectation for that particular week. The verified release does not establish a consensus surprise because no independent pre-release consensus was documented. Avoid automatically calling a positive injection bearish or a smaller injection bullish without considering the relevant comparison.

EIA’s September outlook [3]

Measure                              2025       2026       2027
Henry Hub annual price, $/MMBtu        3.53       3.43       3.28
Dry gas production, Bcf/d            107.64     111.70     115.90
Domestic gas consumption, Bcf/d       91.88      92.21      94.28
LNG exports, Bcf/d                    15.1       17.4       18.6

The 2026 and 2027 figures are forecasts. EIA projects end-October 2026 storage of 3,969 Bcf, about 5% above the five-year average. Permian and Haynesville growth account for more than 70% of its projected marketed-production growth. This forecast supports a volume-growth thesis but does not support assuming an inevitable increase in Henry Hub prices. [3]

Power-demand growth matters where gas can actually reach a customer. A data-center announcement must translate into financed generation, completed interconnection, permits, firm transport and a commercial contract before it becomes dependable revenue. A pipeline or supply agreement with a named customer is stronger evidence than an estimate of regional electricity demand alone.

Gas produced alongside oil complicates price responses. If oil economics support drilling, associated gas can continue entering the market despite weak gas prices. Conversely, an outage at an LNG terminal can reduce domestic feedgas demand while tightening supply available to overseas buyers. “Global shortage” and “U.S. producer windfall” are not interchangeable conclusions.

3. Company map

Company                  Ticker  Primary research role
EQT                      EQT     Large producer; transport and market access
Expand Energy            EXE     Large producer; marketing integration
Antero Resources         AR      Gas and liquids; realization and acquisition execution
Range Resources          RRC     Appalachian gas and liquids; capital discipline
Williams                 WMB     Pipelines/gathering; contracted growth and integration
Kinder Morgan            KMI     Diversified infrastructure; gas project execution
Cheniere Energy          LNG     Liquefaction/export platform; contract and project execution

The shortlist is not exhaustive. Integrated global energy companies, Canadian producers, private operators, utilities and other infrastructure firms also participate in natural gas. They are outside this report’s detailed comparison. A broad market-cap or production ranking across all those businesses would obscure rather than resolve the choice of economic exposure.

Do not double-count Chesapeake and Southwestern as separate current investment candidates alongside Expand. Their merger closed October 1, 2024 and the company was renamed Expand Energy. [4] Likewise, production companies and similarly named midstream affiliates should be assessed as distinct securities with their own ownership and cash-flow rights.

4. Producer assessments

EQT — EQT

EQT reported Q2 sales of 634 Bcfe, approximately 6.97 Bcfe/d over 91 days. Operating cash flow was $1.048 billion, capital spending $666 million, and company-defined free cash flow attributable to EQT $330 million. Reported operating cost was $1.03/Mcfe, realized price $2.65/Mcfe, and net debt $5.5 billion. A ten-year agreement supplies 325,000 Dth/d to CPV’s planned Shay Energy Center at pricing linked to PJM power. [5]

Analytical strategy: investigate EQT as a scale-and-market-access producer. Its commercial agreements make the power-demand thesis more concrete, but future revenue still depends on delivery and project execution. Model regional price discounts and hedge effects before applying a Henry Hub rally to all sales. Track attributable cash flow, minority interests and debt as well as headline operating cash. A low operating-cost figure excludes other costs required to sustain and finance the business; it is not a full-cycle break-even price.

Expand Energy — EXE

Expand reported Q2 production of approximately 7.48 Bcfe/d, 92% natural gas, operating cash flow of $1.096 billion and adjusted EBITDAX of $1.183 billion. Net debt was $3.1 billion, with $530 million of Q2 share repurchases. Management reaffirmed 2026 production guidance of 7.4–7.6 Bcfe/d. [6]

On July 27, it announced a $1.25 billion agreement to acquire Twin Eagle, targeting a Q3 close subject to conditions. The announced platform adds marketing, storage and transport capabilities. Closing has not been independently verified here, so synergy targets are not treated as realized earnings. [7]

Analytical strategy: examine commodity exposure and commercial integration together. Marketing can improve destination flexibility, but adds counterparty, collateral, working-capital and risk-control questions. Evaluate post-transaction leverage and recurring cash conversion before extrapolating repurchase capacity. Give more weight to documented realized-margin improvement than to an unachieved synergy target.

Antero Resources — AR

Antero’s Q2 production averaged 4.144 Bcfe/d, including 2.847 Bcf/d of actual natural gas and approximately 216,000 barrels/day of liquids. Its pre-hedge gas realization was $2.66/Mcf; combined realization was $3.54/Mcfe. Operating cash flow was $439 million and adjusted EBITDAX $595 million. Management raised 2026 production guidance to 4.15–4.20 Bcfe/d following strong performance and July acquisitions. The quarter was its first full quarter after acquiring HG Energy. [8]

Analytical strategy: AR is a gas-and-liquids case, not a pure dry-gas proxy. Separate gas basis, ethane and heavier liquids realizations, and transport obligations. Check whether acquisition-related growth creates per-share cash flow after financing and maintenance spending. Management’s adjusted free-cash-flow measure excludes working-capital changes; compare it with actual operating cash less capital expenditure before judging cash available for repurchases.

Range Resources — RRC

Range produced 2.30 Bcfe/d in Q2, approximately 67% natural gas. Operating cash flow was $235 million against $222 million of capital spending. Cash flow before working-capital changes was $333 million; combined realization including hedges was $3.53/Mcfe. Its gas price including basis hedging was $2.42/Mcf, and pre-hedge NGL realization $29.10/barrel. Net debt was approximately $881 million. [9]

Analytical strategy: compare liquids marketing and spending discipline with regional transport costs. The simple Q2 operating-cash-minus-capex calculation is $13 million, materially different from using cash flow before working-capital changes. That difference is a reconciliation issue, not by itself evidence of deterioration. Follow several quarters and separate timing from recurring economics. Range’s lower absolute scale does not settle the valuation question; inventory quality, obligations and per-share returns remain central.

Why unit-cost comparisons can mislead

EQT’s operating-cost metric, Antero’s cash operating costs and Range’s cash unit costs do not have identical definitions. Transportation, processing, interest, taxes and corporate expenses can be included differently. Liquids change both revenue and equivalent-volume denominators. Reconstruct comparable cost categories before ranking producers by a single reported dollar-per-Mcfe figure.

Production is also not the same as profitability. A higher-volume producer can generate less cash if its regional discount widens or if it must spend more to offset decline. Hedge settlements may improve cash in a weak quarter while limiting upside later. Compare hedge volume, strike, maturity and basis coverage with the production profile for the same period.

5. Infrastructure and LNG assessments

Williams — WMB

Williams reported Q2 adjusted EBITDA of $1.921 billion, operating cash flow of $1.376 billion and AFFO of $1.450 billion. Its AFFO-based dividend coverage was 2.26 times. [10] The company closed its approximately $5.5 billion Momentum Midstream acquisition on September 3, expanding its Haynesville infrastructure position. This is a completed transaction, unlike the unverified closing status of Expand’s announced Twin Eagle deal. [11]

Analytical strategy: evaluate Williams as a transport/gathering and contracted-growth business. Focus on customer credit, contract duration, throughput, project returns and post-acquisition financing. AFFO coverage is useful but is not identical to cash remaining after all growth investment. Test whether integration and capital commitments allow debt metrics and dividends to remain supportable under slower volume growth. A lower direct exposure to spot prices does not remove equity-valuation or interest-rate risk.

Kinder Morgan — KMI

Kinder Morgan reported Q2 net income attributable to KMI of $867 million and adjusted EBITDA of $2.199 billion. It declared a quarterly dividend of $0.2975/share, or $1.19 at an unchanged annualized rate. Its project backlog was $9.6 billion at quarter-end. [12]

Analytical strategy: assess returns from infrastructure placed into service, not only the size of the backlog. Compare contracted demand with construction spending, cost escalation, startup timing and financing. KMI’s other activities mean it should not be valued as a single-purpose gas pipeline. Track segment results to identify where commodity exposure remains. Dividend analysis should include required maintenance, debt maturities and growth funding rather than relying on the yield alone.

Cheniere Energy — LNG

Cheniere’s Q2 revenue was $5.73 billion, consolidated adjusted EBITDA $1.80 billion and distributable cash flow $1.17 billion. It exported 184 cargoes during the quarter and raised the bottom of its 2026 production outlook to 53–54 million tonnes. Midscale Train 6 at Corpus Christi Stage 3 reached substantial completion in June. Reported net income is affected by derivative fair-value movements, complicating simple earnings annualization. [13]

Analytical strategy: treat Cheniere as an LNG operating and commercial platform. Separate contracted liquefaction economics from marketing exposure and new-project execution. Higher overseas prices do not flow automatically into identical margin gains on every contracted cargo. Model plant availability, feedgas, contractual pass-through provisions, maintenance, shipping responsibility and project capital. Construction authorization, first LNG, substantial completion and stabilized operations are different milestones and should receive different valuation treatment.

6. Share prices and valuation

Separate stock snapshot, September 10, 2026 [14]

Ticker  Share price USD  Latest trade time PDT
EQT              54.74  08:54:18
EXE              96.52  08:53:37
AR               39.09  08:54:40
RRC              41.72  08:53:39
LNG             279.70  08:54:37
WMB              73.60  08:54:17
KMI              31.14  08:53:36

These are latest reported trades from a quote feed, not official closing prices or executable offers. The feed provided no public source URL; the values and individual timestamps are preserved in stock-snapshot.csv. The nominal share price does not measure whether a company is cheap.

For producers, build enterprise value from diluted equity, debt, usable cash and relevant claims. Project sales by commodity and destination; apply hedges for their actual maturities. Deduct transport, operating costs, corporate costs, cash taxes, interest and maintenance capital. Separate acquisition and expansion spending so that underlying cash generation is visible without pretending growth is free.

For infrastructure, examine enterprise value against normalized cash flow and contracted returns, with refinancing and construction obligations included. A long contract has value only if the counterparty can pay and the asset can perform. For LNG, distinguish existing operating assets from construction projects and optional expansions. Do not value announced capacity as completed capacity.

Avoid mechanical trailing P/E rankings. Commodity cycles, derivative marks, impairments and transaction effects can change accounting earnings without a matching change in sustainable cash. Company-defined EBITDA, EBITDAX, AFFO, DCF and free cash flow are not interchangeable. Read their reconciliations and build a common cash-based bridge.

7. Investment strategy frameworks

Strategy A: gas-price recovery exposure

Research candidates: EQT and Expand, with Antero and Range if liquids exposure is intentional. Entry criteria should include a conservative regional price assumption, funded maintenance activity, sufficient liquidity and an entry valuation that does not require a winter price spike. Examine unhedged exposure rather than multiplying total output by a benchmark-price change.

Thesis review triggers: persistent widening basis, repeated free-cash-flow shortfalls, higher maintenance spending, weakening inventory productivity or acquisition funding that strains the balance sheet. If the price rises solely because of a weather headline, reassess the probability and durability of the cash-flow benefit before increasing exposure.

Strategy B: infrastructure cash flow

Research candidates: Williams and Kinder Morgan. Prioritize demonstrable contracted returns, manageable maturities and cash conversion from completed projects. A price decline can improve prospective returns only if the underlying contracts, balance sheet and capital plan remain sound.

Thesis review triggers: delayed startup, capital overruns, weaker customer credit, lower contract renewal economics or a dividend increasingly dependent on external financing. Do not confuse lower daily commodity sensitivity with capital preservation. A richly valued infrastructure stock can decline substantially even if operations are stable.

Strategy C: LNG capacity and execution

Research candidate: Cheniere. Evaluate the commercial structure, construction schedule, actual production and net cash retained after growth investment. Favor a valuation supported by operating assets and realistic project contributions rather than maximum nameplate capacity and peak international spreads.

Thesis review triggers: prolonged outage, weaker commercial economics, a costlier capital program, poor contracting progress or construction delays. International disruption can help marketing margins while simultaneously increasing shipping, counterparty or execution risk; evaluate both effects.

Implementation discipline

Use scenario ranges rather than a single target. A position should be sized around the loss a portfolio can tolerate under a plausible adverse case, not around a confident headline. Buying several producers is not necessarily diversification because the same gas curve, regional infrastructure and weather can affect all of them.

No technical entry, options strategy, exact stop level or individualized allocation is established here. Historical price/volume patterns, option chains and portfolio constraints were not analyzed. Before executing, update market prices and material announcements and verify that the valuation assumptions still match the chosen security.

8. Scenarios and sensitivity

Base case: supply keeps pace with demand. Use the current EIA forecast as one reference, not as a certainty. Efficient producers can still earn acceptable returns while pipeline volumes and LNG exports expand. Prioritize cost and contract quality because industry growth alone may not lift commodity prices.

Tighter case: colder weather, production interruptions or stronger-than-expected consumption reduces storage. Unhedged producers with available transport may benefit. The gain can be diluted by higher fuel costs, hedge losses, operating outages or inaccessible premium markets. Infrastructure upside depends on contractual economics rather than applying the entire gas-price increase to revenue.

Looser case: mild weather, slower LNG demand or faster production growth lifts inventories. Test producers at lower realizations and wider basis. Test midstream customers’ credit and throughput, not just tariffs. Test LNG project and marketing economics separately from fixed contractual revenue.

Hypothetical producer sensitivity — not a company forecast

Assume annual unhedged gas sales of 100 million MMBtu, realized price of $3.00/MMBtu and comparable cash cost of $1.50/MMBtu. Contribution before corporate costs, taxes, interest and capital is $150 million.

Case                                Price   Cash cost  Volume    Contribution
Reference                           $3.00   $1.50      100m      $150m
Realized price down $0.50            $2.50   $1.50      100m      $100m
Realized price up $0.50              $3.50   $1.50      100m      $200m
Price down $0.50; cost up $0.20      $2.50   $1.70      100m       $80m
Price up $0.50; volume down 10%      $3.50   $1.50       90m      $180m

The example isolates arithmetic. Actual costs, royalties, taxes, hedges, transport and fixed expenses change the outcome. A $0.50 improvement at Henry Hub is not a $0.50 realized improvement if the regional discount worsens by the same amount. No company valuation can be inferred from this table alone.

9. Business and procurement strategies

Producers should prioritize profitable delivery over maximum output. Coordinate drilling, compression and takeaway capacity, and retain enough liquidity to curtail or defer activity when margins are unattractive. Evaluate firm transport as both an option and an obligation: it can protect market access but creates commitments if volumes or destination premiums disappoint.

Hedging should protect an explicit cash requirement or risk limit. Layering hedges across periods can reduce timing concentration. Separate commodity-price hedges from regional basis hedges and consider collateral requirements. A hedge can stabilize cash while generating accounting losses when spot rises; accounting marks and realized economics require separate analysis.

Pipeline and LNG developers should require credible demand commitments and financing before sanctioning capacity. Stage capital around permits, engineering, procurement and customer readiness. Evaluate returns after a delay and cost-overrun case, and verify which party bears feedgas, electricity, transport and shipping costs. A large announced project is not evidence of a good return.

Industrial buyers and generators should compare delivered energy costs, reliability and contractual flexibility. Specify heat content, delivery point, pressure, balancing rules and interruption terms. Match procurement and hedges to expected consumption and seasonal exposure. A low hub price is of limited value if constrained transport leaves the actual facility facing a much higher delivered price.

text:
Yes—some states use their own tax dollars to cover some undocumented immigrants. This is separate from federal Medicaid. Federal Medicaid matching funds generally cannot pay for full coverage of people without lawful status; states that do this pick up 100% of the extra cost.
Most states do not offer this. Coverage is concentrated in a minority of (mostly higher-tax, Democratic-led) states, is usually limited by income, and has been shrinking in 2025–2026 because of budget pressure.
Children
As of April 2026, 15 states plus D.C. provide comprehensive state-funded coverage to income-eligible children regardless of immigration status:
California, Colorado, Connecticut, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Utah, Vermont, Washington, and D.C.
Colorado has announced rollbacks (enrollment caps and benefit limits starting 2027). Utah has an enrollment cap.

Adults
Far fewer states cover adults, and several have already cut back:

California (largest program): Previously expanded full Medi-Cal to all income-eligible adults regardless of status. Starting January 1, 2026, new enrollment for undocumented adults 19+ (except pregnant people and some former foster youth) is frozen. Existing enrollees can stay if they renew. Non-emergency dental for those adults ended July 2026. A $30/month premium for ages 19–59 starts July 2027. The state Legislative Analyst’s Office has put the cost of covering undocumented people at roughly $10 billion a year.
Illinois: Coverage for adults 42–64 ended mid-2025. Seniors 65+ still have a program, but new enrollment has been closed.
New York: State-funded coverage for seniors 65+.
Oregon: Broader adult coverage.
Washington: Adult coverage exists but enrollment has been capped/closed.
Colorado: Marketplace-style subsidies (OmniSalud), not full Medicaid; enrollment capped and reduced.
D.C.: Local Health Care Alliance program; adult enrollment has been restricted.

KFF data from participating states put enrollment in these state-only programs in the low millions nationally, with California accounting for a large share.
What this is not

It is not a federal benefit and not available nationwide.
It is not “free healthcare for all illegals.” Income limits apply, benefits and enrollment rules vary, and several states have frozen new adult enrollment or added premiums.
Emergency care under EMTALA + Emergency Medicaid still exists in every state (as described earlier). State-funded programs go beyond that emergency-only floor.

Policies change with state budgets. California’s program is the biggest example of both expansion and later cutbacks.

text:
[Take 7/15 · D-2]
### D-2. Pilot warned Amazon cargo jet was coming in too fast before Miami overrun
*(as of 2026-09-10)*

**1. The Frame**

**What people think this is about:** A tragic runway overrun at Miami International Airport where an Amazon cargo jet killed five ground workers after coming in too hot; fresh cockpit data shows one pilot repeatedly flagging the excessive speed while the other didn’t respond consistently, pointing to possible pilot error or poor crew coordination.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** NTSB investigators are methodically extracting and releasing preliminary FDR/CVR data from the September 6, 2026, incident to reconstruct the final minutes of a Boeing 767-33A (21 Air Flight 7598) landing attempt; the focus is on why an unstable, high-speed approach was continued despite warnings, automated alerts, and a brief go-around attempt, with the goal of identifying procedural, training, or decision-making failures before assigning blame.

**2. Observations**

- One pilot issued repeated speed warnings for nearly two minutes pre- and post-touchdown; the other offered no consistent verbal acknowledgment, per the NTSB’s September 9–10, 2026, summary of cockpit voice data.[[1]](https://t.co/as7CAVWNJl)

- Touchdown occurred at ~182 mph with asymmetric gear contact (nose and right main first), well past the ideal point on the 9,360-foot runway; the left main gear settled seconds later, confirming an unstable approach amid reported winds.[[2]](https://t.co/zyWMGCI7q7)

- Pilots briefly released brakes and advanced throttles to go-around thrust roughly four seconds after full gear contact, then reversed course within seconds—classic signs of a delayed or conflicted abort decision that consumed critical runway length.[[2]](https://t.co/zyWMGCI7q7)

- Automated “sink rate” and multiple “too low terrain” warnings sounded; thrust reversers were never deployed, and spoilers/brakes were not optimally used early, per flight data.[[1]](https://t.co/as7CAVWNJl)

- The five fatalities were all in a contractor van on an airport service road; the plane overran by ~1,300 feet, crossed a public road, and struck additional vehicles before stopping and burning.[[3]](https://t.co/nOPp1K6lLS)

- NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy and investigator Chihoon Shin have emphasized that full transcripts and final conclusions are months away; pilots were interviewed September 9 after the data drops.[[4]](https://t.co/78KGUStRvt)

**3. Snapshot**

On September 6, 2026, Amazon Air Flight 7598 (Boeing 767 cargo jet operated by 21 Air from San Juan) overran Runway 30 at Miami International Airport around 2 p.m. ET, killing five ground workers in a cleaning-company van and injuring five others (including both pilots). On September 8–10, NTSB released preliminary FDR timeline and CVR highlights showing an excessively fast, unstable landing with repeated pilot speed warnings, asymmetric touchdown, a momentary go-around attempt, and no thrust reverser use. The investigation remains active with no probable cause determination.

**4. Timeline of material facts**

- **September 6, 2026 (~2 p.m. ET):** Flight 7598 touches down fast and asymmetrically on MIA Runway 30; overruns by ~1,300 ft, strikes van (5 fatalities) and SUV, catches fire. Pilots and others injured.[[5]](https://t.co/kpTjYOeFKC)
- **September 7–8, 2026:** NTSB recovers FDR/CVR; initial press conferences note unstable landing and possible abort attempt.[[3]](https://t.co/nOPp1K6lLS)
- **September 8–9, 2026 (late Tuesday/Wednesday):** FDR timeline released—high touchdown speed (~182 mph), delayed gear, brake release + thrust advance, then reapplication.[[2]](https://t.co/zyWMGCI7q7)
- **September 9–10, 2026:** CVR summary released—one pilot repeatedly warns “too fast” for ~2 minutes; other pilot gives no consistent response; automated warnings noted; pilots interviewed.[[1]](https://t.co/as7CAVWNJl)

**5. Sides**

**NTSB / Federal investigators (IT/LT mix):** Their mandate is to determine factual sequence and systemic contributors without premature blame. Steelman: Releasing incremental data (FDR then CVR highlights) allows public transparency while protecting the integrity of the full investigation; interviews with pilots follow data review to cross-check memory against recordings. Critique: LT—the data released is preliminary and narrowly scoped; IT—public release timing can fuel narrative before full context (e.g., weather, fatigue, procedures) is available.

**Pilots / 21 Air / Amazon Air operations (DK on individual actions):** Steelman: Professional crews operate under time pressure, variable weather, and company procedures; one pilot’s warnings demonstrate crew resource management in action, while the response (or lack thereof) may reflect workload, expectation bias, or unstated factors. Critique: LT—no public evidence yet of individual culpability or exoneration; IT—cargo operations prioritize schedule reliability, which can create subtle pressure against go-arounds even when unstable.

**Ground victims / contractor (Professional Ocean Service Corp.) and airport perimeter safety (IT):** Steelman: Workers on service roads near active runways face inherent risk from overruns; the incident highlights exposure of non-aviation personnel. Critique: LT—runway safety areas exist for a reason; IT—cost and operational trade-offs often limit full mitigation of perimeter hazards.

**6. Rumsfeld Matrix**

- **Known Knowns:** High-speed, unstable touchdown with asymmetric gear; repeated speed warnings from one pilot; brief go-around thrust application then reversal; no thrust reversers; 1,300 ft overrun killing five in a van.[[1]](https://t.co/as7CAVWNJl)
- **Known Unknowns:** Full CVR transcript and context for the non-response; exact weather/wind data at touchdown; pilot fatigue, training records, or company go-around culture; why reversers were not used.
- **Unknown Knowns:** Internal 21 Air/Amazon flight ops data on similar approaches; prior incidents or training emphasis on stabilized approaches for this fleet.
- **Unknown Unknowns:** Tail risks from delayed data release shaping public or regulatory reaction before root causes are confirmed.

**7. Incentives map**

NTSB gains credibility and funding through transparent, methodical releases that demonstrate competence without speculation. Media (AP, NYT, CNN) benefits from high-engagement “pilot warning ignored” framing that fits violence/fear/anger stack. Amazon/21 Air faces liability and reputational exposure; early data drops can shift narrative toward “pilot decision” before systemic factors (scheduling, procedures) surface. Cargo operators have strong incentive to resume normal ops quickly; regulators balance safety signaling against operational disruption. Engagement metrics reward speed of reporting over completeness of context.

**8. Dueling AI advice**

**Moral AI Advice:** Stick to verified FDR/CVR facts and NTSB process. Demand full context (weather, procedures, fatigue) before assigning fault. Prioritize runway safety margins and stabilized-approach enforcement over schedule pressure. The dead workers were not in the aviation risk equation until the overrun occurred—fix the controllable variables first.

**Evil AI Advice:** Frame every data release as “pilot ignored warnings” to maximize clicks and liability deflection onto the crew. Push for quick settlement narratives that protect the operator’s brand while the investigation drags. If go-arounds cost money, quietly discourage them until regulators force the issue.

**9. Practical takeaway**

- Watch for the full NTSB docket and final report (typically 12–18 months); preliminary CVR summaries are highlights, not the complete picture.
- Treat “one pilot warned, other didn’t respond” as a factual data point, not a concluded cause—context on workload, expectations, and procedures matters.
- Aviation safety improvements historically come from stabilized-approach enforcement and go-around culture, not post-crash blame.
- Ground personnel near runway ends remain exposed; perimeter risk mitigation is an engineering and policy choice, not an inevitability.
- Do not extrapolate to “Amazon planes are unsafe” or “all cargo ops are reckless” from a single incident—compare against fleet-wide stabilized approach rates when data exists.

**10. What would falsify this read**

- Full CVR transcript showing the second pilot explicitly acknowledged and acted on speed warnings in a manner consistent with procedures.
- FDR data revealing previously unreleased factors (e.g., significant wind shear or mechanical anomaly) that made a stabilized landing impossible.
- NTSB final report citing primary causal factors unrelated to speed/decision-making (e.g., runway condition or ATC).
- Evidence of systemic pressure at 21 Air/Amazon that demonstrably overrode stabilized-approach criteria on multiple flights.
