text:
📚 FLEISCHL 41: A Book Seized from Sándor Fleischl in 1944 Resurfaces in 2026 With Its Wartime Inventory Number Still Inside

In August 1944, Hungarian officials went through Sándor Fleischl’s private art library in Budapest, placed his property under seal, and recorded his books one by one before transporting them to the Museum of Fine Arts. Among the hundreds of volumes was a cloth-bound German book on Gothic art by Wilhelm Müseler. On the official inventory it became Item 41.

More than eighty years later, a copy of that book resurfaced at a Budapest auction house. Inside it were two extraordinary pieces of evidence: Fleischl’s own ex libris and a surviving label from the Hungarian Government Commissioner’s office that had processed Jewish-owned cultural property in 1944.

The label reads:

“Fleischl 41.”

The wartime inventory and the physical book have found each other again.

📜 Sándor Fleischl’s library in August 1944

The complete Fleischl file survives in Reel 144, slides 432–441, under file 274/1944. Read together, the ten pages show the process unfolding over several days rather than as a single isolated inventory.

On August 16, 1944, a handwritten protocol records the placing under seal of paintings and books belonging to Fleischl Sándor, identifying the apartment as Budapest II., Csévi út 3, second floor, apartment 2. Among the property recorded are 192 art books. A separate handwritten page in the same file notes Nádor utca 34 as Fleischl’s “current residence”; the file does not explain the reason for the different address, and we should not speculate about it.

On August 18, a further protocol prepared at the Museum of Fine Arts records paintings and other objects from Fleischl’s Csévi út apartment that had been placed under seal and transported to the museum for “further safekeeping.” Then, on August 23, officials began the separate inventory of his books. The typed protocol expressly states that it concerns books from Fleischl’s apartment at Csévi út 3 that had been placed under seal and transported to the Museum of Fine Arts.

The list continues across five pages, ultimately reaching Item 179. Because several numbered entries contain multiple volumes, that total is consistent with the earlier reference to 192 art books. It was a serious working library: books on Dürer, Rembrandt, Michelangelo, Van Gogh, Holbein, Persian carpets, Chinese and Japanese art, architecture, prints, ceramics, European painting, modern art, and museum collections. The bureaucracy that seized Fleischl’s property also preserved, inadvertently, a portrait of what he read and collected.

🔎 Item 41

On Reel 144, slide 437, the entry is unmistakable:

“41./ Wilhelm Müseler: Geist und Antlitz der Gotik. Berlin, Safari-Verlag. Vászonk. 1 drb.”

In English:

“41. Wilhelm Müseler: Geist und Antlitz der Gotik. Berlin, Safari-Verlag. Cloth-bound. One copy.”

The book was an illustrated survey of Gothic art. The University of Heidelberg catalogues a 1936 Berlin edition, published by Safari-Verlag, as a third edition of 126 pages with numerous illustrations. The wartime inventory does not give Fleischl’s publication year, but it does record the author, exact title, publisher, binding, quantity—and, critically, the inventory number 41. 

🏷️ The book reappears—with “Fleischl 41” still inside

In 2026, Darabanth Auction House in Budapest offered a 1936 Safari-Verlag copy of Geist und Antlitz der Gotik in the publisher’s full-cloth binding. Its catalogue description records two provenance marks inside the volume.

The first is an ex libris:

“ifj. Fleischl Sándor könyve”

—“the book of the younger Sándor Fleischl.”

The second is far more unusual: a circa-1944 label from the Government Commissioner’s office for the registration and safekeeping of Jewish artworks placed under seal, bearing Fleischl’s name and the number:

“Fleischl 41”

Darabanth’s description of the surviving book therefore lines up with the wartime file at every meaningful point. The 1944 inventory records Item 41, Wilhelm Müseler, Geist und Antlitz der Gotik, Safari-Verlag, one cloth-bound copy. The surviving cloth-bound Müseler volume has Fleischl’s ownership mark and a Government Commissioner label saying “Fleischl 41.” 

This is not a proposed match based on similar measurements, a changed title, or a possible attribution. Unless contrary evidence emerges, the convergence of owner, author, title, publisher, binding, and the exact wartime item number makes the identification of the auctioned book with Fleischl Item 41 extraordinarily strong.

The auction trail in 2026

The book did not surface in a provenance database or museum catalogue. It appeared in an ordinary Budapest auction.

Darabanth’s May 21, 2026 catalogue offered the marked volume as lot 19153 in its Judaica section, with a starting price of 10,000 Hungarian forints. The description already identified both the “Fleischl 41” Government Commissioner label and the Fleischl ex libris. The same distinctively described volume then appeared again in Darabanth/Axioart listings for July 23 and August 27, 2026. The August listing, lot 19558, is now archived as no longer available for purchase. None of the public listings supplies the consignor or a postwar ownership chain.

That distinction is important. The auction records tell us that the book survived and returned to the Budapest market. They do not tell us whether it was restituted after the war, remained in institutional custody, passed through another collection, or reached the consignor by some other route. Nor should an auction appearance itself be treated as evidence of improper present ownership.

What makes the discovery significant is that we no longer have to search for an abstract missing title. We have the physical book and its wartime number.

👤 Who was Sándor Fleischl?

The owner also deserves to be restored to the story rather than reduced to the word “Fleischl” on a confiscation label.

The Jewish Digital Cultural Recovery Project, using the Hungarian National Archives files MNL OL K 643-1944-274 and 338, identifies Sándor Fleischl of Budapest II., Csévi utca 3 as a persecuted Jewish collector. Its detailed record gives his occupation as bookkeeper and describes his collection as including books and oil paintings by Hungarian masters. The database does not presently provide his dates of birth or death, wartime fate, postwar history, or restitution information. 

There is also a genuine identification issue that should be handled carefully. Budapest records contain more than one Sándor Fleischl. A 1936 telephone directory separately lists the well-known Sándor Fleischl, Danish royal consul-general, at Zoltán utca 6, and another Sándor Fleischl, director and certified auditor, at Ady Endre utca 30. The ex libris inside the recovered book specifically says ifj. Fleischl Sándor—“younger Sándor Fleischl.” That word matters. It is strong reason not to attach the biography of the older consul-general to the owner of this library without further proof. 

For now, the most reliable biography is the one the surviving evidence gives us directly: Sándor Fleischl, a Jewish Budapest collector associated in the 1944 records with Csévi út 3, owner of paintings and an extensive art library, whose books were placed under seal and transported to the Museum of Fine Arts in August 1944. One of those books has now resurfaced with his name still inside it.

🗃️ What happened after the Museum of Fine Arts received Item 41?

That is now the central provenance question.

The August 23 protocol tells us where Fleischl’s books were taken in 1944: the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest. The 2026 auction listing tells us where Item 41 eventually resurfaced: the Budapest art and book market. The approximately eight decades between those points remain publicly unexplained.

There may be an entirely lawful postwar history. Item 41 may have been returned to Fleischl or his family and later sold. It may have been transferred to another institution and subsequently released. It may have followed another documented route. The existing public sources simply do not establish which occurred, and JDCRP presently lists no restitution history for Fleischl. 

The records needed to answer the question are unusually specific. The Museum of Fine Arts can search its wartime intake, deposit, library, return, restitution, and transfer records under Sándor Fleischl, Csévi út 3, file 274/1944, and Item 41. The Hungarian National Archives may preserve later correspondence or disposition records beyond the ten pages examined here. Darabanth’s consignment records can identify the recent source of the book and potentially allow the chain to be worked backward.

The physical volume itself should also be documented before those clues disappear. The Government Commissioner label, Fleischl ex libris, binding, stamps, handwritten marks, accession or library numbers, and every other mark on the pastedowns and endpapers should be photographed at high resolution. If the confiscation label has writing, stamps, or numbers beyond what appears in the auction description, those details may connect Item 41 to other surviving Fleischl books.

Why “Fleischl 41” matters beyond one volume

The discovery also changes how the rest of the Fleischl library can be searched.

The number 41 was not merely an entry typed into a wartime inventory. At least for this book, the Government Commissioner’s office carried the owner’s name and inventory number onto the physical object itself. That means other volumes from the same library may survive with labels reading “Fleischl” followed by their corresponding inventory number, with Fleischl ex libris marks, or with evidence that such labels were once attached.

The 179 numbered entries on Reel 144 are therefore not simply a list of lost books. They may function as a key for identifying surviving ones. Item 41 demonstrates the method.

This is also precisely why books belong in Holocaust-era provenance research. The 2024 Best Practices for the Washington Conference Principles expressly include libraries, manuscripts, archives, and records within the cultural property of Holocaust victims and other victims of Nazi persecution. They call for provenance research, publication of inventories, access to relevant archives, and disclosure of acquisition and provenance documentation. 

For Sándor Fleischl, the archive and the object now meet with unusual clarity. In August 1944, Hungarian officials wrote down:

41 — Wilhelm Müseler — Geist und Antlitz der Gotik — Safari-Verlag — cloth-bound — one copy.

In 2026, that title resurfaced in Budapest with Fleischl’s ex libris and the wartime Government Commissioner label:

Fleischl 41.

The difficult part of this investigation is no longer identifying the book. It is reconstructing what happened to Fleischl 41 after it entered the Museum of Fine Arts system in 1944 and before it appeared on the auction market eighty-two years later. The paper inventory and the physical object have found each other again; the missing history between them now needs to be recovered.

Sources & Links

- Darabanth/Axioart, August 27, 2026, lot 19558— exact marked book; records the “Fleischl 41” Government Commissioner label, the ifj. Fleischl Sándor könyve ex libris, 1936 Safari-Verlag imprint, and full-cloth binding. The indexed record contains five auction photographs, although the archived interface is not currently giving me stable standalone image files: https://t.co/iaiP3N1zjK

text:
A knight has been fighting for years.

He wins every battle, and every year he remembers less of why he started. One spring morning a band of ragged pilgrims stops him on the road and asks what he is doing riding in full armor on Good Friday.

He has to ask them what day it is.

The calendar just did that to me. Today is 9/10.

One year since Charlie Kirk got assassinated on 4K video in front of a crowd of students. And tens of millions of viewers online. Tomorrow is 25 years since September 11. This year is 250 since the Declaration of Independence. Three anniversaries in one turn of the calendar. And they are one story.

But first, the old story.

800+ years ago a French poet told of a king with a wound that would not close. The land failed with him. The crops would not grow, the wells ran dry, the trees bore no fruit.

The health of the kingdom is the health of the king. Every night in his castle a procession passed, a cup that fed the whole hall, and still the king lay in pain. There was one way out. Parsifal had to come and ask a single question.

Whom does the Grail serve?

Parsifal came. He was young, raised in the woods, homespun under stolen armor, the laughingstock of every court that had seen him. He watched the cup pass through the hall and said nothing. He had been taught it was rude to ask questions. By morning the castle was gone.

Our wound cracked open 63 years ago in Dallas, Camelot's king killed out in the open, our kingdom limping ever since. The castle night came in 2001.

The cup passed through the smoke, the question went unasked while the room was afraid, and the land has been worked ever since by people who farm the silence. I was nine years old. I grew up in the barren years. You were there too. 

Elsewhere in the legend, there is a ruined monastery where the sacrament sits on the altar and no one is allowed to touch it. Everything a man needs is within arm's reach, and he cannot use any of it. That is a people who have been handed back their sovereignty and are too conditioned to pick it up.

A nation can watch the cup pass through the hall and still hold its tongue.

The wasteland keeps a ledger. Kennedy in Dallas. Bill Cooper shot dead outside his home weeks after the towers fell. Aaron Swartz suicided at 26. Julian Assange caged for years. Seth Rich dead on a DC street. Reagan took a bullet just 69 days into his first term. Some remembered, but most forgotten.

In a republic, the wounded king is the people.

We are the sovereign of this kingdom. 
The wound is ours.

And that is why no president could heal it. But one man bought us the chance to heal ourselves: @realDonaldTrump. 

Like Washington, he will be offered a throne that he will not take. That is how he will be remembered, and it may be bittersweet. Because even he cannot close the wound. In the end it is us who must save ourselves.

You cannot hire a man to ask the question for you. And the question does not retire when our side wins. If a power was dangerous in their hands, a friend holding it is not the answer.

A people who only question the other court has already stopped governing itself. And the asker, when he comes, is never the court's man. He is the fool they laughed at, the boy from the woods with no pedigree, the last knight anyone would anoint. You can see it now. 

The court is full of strong-looking knights jockeying to be crowned. But the Grail does not crown the strongest knight. It answers the one who asks. And a republic cannot let one asker carry it alone. The question belongs to every citizen.

Whom does the Grail serve? When the knight finally asks, the answer comes.

The Grail serves the Grail King. The Grail King is not the wounded king. He is the one who has lived in the central room of the castle from the beginning.

The Grail serves God. The cup was never ours to keep. 250 years ago the founders asked whom power serves, and they answered against a king.

A people that stops asking goes barren in the middle of its own wealth.

The question in its modern form:

What do we live for?

For several generations people like us were taught and conditioned to be ashamed of ourselves. Shellshocked, manipulated, worked by scripts large and small until up and down blurred. And still, when the towers stood burning, a man in a red bandana went back up the stairs for strangers.

The unity of those weeks was real, and it dissolved, because it was built on the wound. A trauma bond is a huddle around the injury. What is opening now is a turning toward the Father, a covenant, not a huddle. One decays. One holds. And the high-trust country we glimpsed in the ashes was not a lost season. It was a preview of the greatness that is to come.

The legend was left unfinished. Later writers supplied endings.

None can finish it for us. It has to be finished in a life. 

Your life.

The closest analogy I can think of is Alex Karp’s broader sovereignty philosophy with Palantir. The private company builds the hard technical infrastructure, but the customer retains control over the strategically important layer. That is basically the lens I would use to look at MDA here.

The interesting part of AURORA Black is not just that it is another defence satellite product. It is that MDA can package a lot of the difficult pieces governments need for sovereign MILSATCOM without requiring them to become dependent on a fully integrated foreign network. Software defined payloads, anti-jamming, onboard processing, D2D, digital beamforming and the ability to manufacture at constellation scale are all part of the same offering.

That matters because the geopolitical environment has changed pretty dramatically. Allied governments are thinking much harder about what happens when critical infrastructure sits outside their direct control. You do not have to assume some dramatic rupture with Washington to see the problem. Export restrictions change, sanctions change, administrations change, commercial priorities change and alliances themselves can become transactional very quickly.

Once communications, targeting, ISR or command infrastructure becomes dependent on a foreign controlled vertically integrated system, that dependency is no longer just a procurement decision. It becomes a strategic vulnerability.

That is why I think the sovereignty angle matters so much.

MDA is not really trying to build another Starlink. The more interesting opportunity is giving governments enough of the underlying architecture to field their own resilient LEO capability while keeping operational control, mission configuration and strategic access in their own hands.

That is much closer to the Palantir model than the normal SaaS model. The vendor provides the technology and the industrial capability, but it does not need to own the sovereign’s strategic environment.

For MILSATCOM, that is a very strong pitch.

It also fits where defence procurement is going. More distributed architectures, more redundancy, more software-defined systems, faster refresh cycles and a lot more emphasis on national control over critical infrastructure.

In a world of ever competing global forces the company that can offer sovereignty instead of reliance is the company that will emerge victorious.

text:
Dr @ShashiTharoor articulates India should treat a deeper, structured partnership with Europe as a core tool of strategic autonomy — not as a replacement for the US, but as a hedge against an unpredictable Washington and a coercive China.
Tharoor’s argument is that mid-2020s geopolitics has made the old US-centric bet fragile. Tariffs, energy-policy pressure, and sudden swings in American policy have injected volatility into a relationship that once felt structurally predictable. Multi-alignment is therefore no longer optional: Quad, Gulf, Singapore, and others matter, but the EU is the missing large, high-capacity partner.
The January 2025 India–EU FTA (“mother of all deals”) is the economic pillar — 2 billion consumers, roughly a quarter of world GDP, tariffs cut or eliminated on ~96% of goods, plus rules on services, digital trade, and tech. For India it is a buffer against protectionism and a premium market; for Europe it is the flagship of “China Plus One” diversification.
The security pillar is the new Security and Defence Partnership: maritime and cyber cooperation, counter-terrorism, AI, access to Europe’s €150 billion defence initiative, joint production, and technology transfer. Europe cannot match US military or financial hegemony, but it offers what the US currently does not: institutional stability, technological depth, and policy predictability. Shared concern over Chinese coercion in sea lanes and connectivity projects makes the fit practical, not merely rhetorical.
Thus true autonomy is not isolation or passive non-alignment. It is active, overlapping, high-value partnerships. Binding India’s economic future to the FTA and its security architecture to Europe creates a double hedge — against Chinese assertiveness in the neighbourhood and against erratic American engagement. Two large democracies, in this reading, can become an anchor of a rules-based order when both great-power alternatives look less reliable.

text:
A very interesting short story: My landlord tried to make me feed him, but I’m sticking to the terms he set and now he’s mad.
#pettyrevenge 
Basically, I 31f moved into a renovated basement unit on the 1st. My unit has its own bedroom, bathroom, and living area but the kitchen is shared with my landlord 47m, his pregnant wife 44f, and 7yo daughter.

As a condition of my lease, my landlords food is not to be touched, and I am responsible for feeding myself. They made sure to specify that multiple times while giving me the tour. I work in food service and I cook a lot, so I have my own pots, pans, spices, dishes, etc. I love to cook, and I don’t touch any of their food or dishes. My landlord and his wife don’t cook, they just eat frozen burritos, tv dinners, pre packaged noodles, etc. I don’t think they can cook tbh.

On my first night, I made some shrimp Alfredo and because it had extra I thought I’d be nice and share it with them. A few days later, I made some salmon and cilantro lime rice for myself for dinner, and shortly after that, my landlord sent me a nasty text message telling me he thought I was playing in their faces and threatened to reconsider the lease because his pregnant wife smelled me cooking and assumed I was making them some too. He peeked in the oven when I left the kitchen and saw that I made 2 pieces of fish and told me that I should have offered one to his wife because of her pregnancy cravings. Told me that they opened their home to me (I pay rent) and said I should be more considerate next time. Truly insane tbh.

Anyway after getting some helpful advice, I texted him back a screenshot of the part of the lease where he stated food was to be kept separate and that I’m not to touch any of his food but I am allowed to use the kitchen to cook. Then I brought up my culinary experience and offered to cook them one gourmet family meal per week in exchange for $50 off rent per meal, for a total of $200 off rent per month, provided they bought any ingredients. They pretty much laughed in my face when I brought that up and also let me know they were not going to let me out of my lease without paying up. My lease is only 60 days, then month-to-month, and I’ve already found a small studio to move to as soon as this lease ends, so honestly I decided I don’t care. It’s not my fault they tried home cooked food once and got hooked.

**TL,DR:** I shared a home cooked meal with my landlord and his wife one time, and they thought it was going to be a regular free service.

Anyway I’ve decided to be petty, and will be cooking the most delicious, aromatic meals for myself while I prepare to move yet again. I’ve already made myself garlic short ribs, and hot honey fried chicken since then, and the pregnant wife glares at me longingly every time I pull something out of the oven and I’m getting just the most sick satisfaction out of it.

They said food is to be kept separate. Fine by me. This weekend I think I’m going to make myself some coconut curry chicken. Also if anyone knows of any highly delicious and aromatic affordable meals one can cook without taking up too much time, let me know lol. I’m up for suggestions.

#fyp

text:
TWENTY-SIX
"Every Man and Woman is a Star"
But ye have borne the tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images, the star of your God, which ye made to yourselves.
— Amos 5:26

Every man and woman is a star.
— Aleister Crowley The Book of the Law

Few who are knowledgeable dispute the fact that for satanists, occultists and other Illuminists, the symbol of the star has vast significance. Whether five-pointed in shape, six-pointed, or in some other configuration, the star is a premier symbol of the Devil.

Illuminists and witches claim that the pentagram, a five-pointed star with one point upward (ascendant) is useful for "White Magic" rituals and spells. The inverted pentagram (five-pointed star) is widely used by hard-core Satan worshippers. When the two points are aimed upward (ascendant), it is said to indicate "Black Magic" and to be the two horns of Satan. No wonder that Aleister Crowley, the self-proclaimed "Beast 666" from Great Britain, once stated, "Every man and woman is a star," which, loosely interpreted, meant, "Every man and woman is a God."1
The Star of Initiation

In the Hindu religion, the pentagram is the "Star of Initiation." It is the caste-mark of the Priests of Siva, who dedicate it to the sun God by marking a black round dot inside the symbol of the star.2

📷
From left to right: Pentagram, Inverted Pentagram, Hexagram (Star of David) and Star of Baphomet (Goat of Sabbath)

The Blazing Star

Freemasons, because they venerate the sun and its rays, know the star emblem as the "Blazing Star." Steve Worrall-Clare, a former Mason, in Freemasonry - The Secret Language, writes that in the Lodge:

The blazing star points out the glory of the sun. It is central to all Masonic undertaking, for it enlightens the earth, and by its benign influence dispenses its blessings to mankind...It is found in the 28th degree and is the symbol of truth. It is found in the 4th degree as a symbol of light and in the 9th degree it is a symbol of divine providence. It is sometimes symbolically installed as the letter "G"...It is a door, an entrance to knowledge...3

Satan, The Goat of the Sabbath

High-sounding words, but deceptive. To gain a more direct perspective, we turn to Frenchman Eliphas Levi, a nineteenth-century satanist whose works inspired the writings of Albert Pike, the Sovereign Grand Commander of international Freemasonry. Levi enthusiastically reports:

text:
When I say I'm homeschooling -- or talk about the exceptional education my kids are getting -- I hear the same thing: “You're privileged.”

That none of this is possible for “regular” single moms, or families stuck in terrible school districts.

I don't buy that.

I know a mom who was on food stamps, homeschooled her daughter all the way to West Point.

I know another mom of 6 who lives below the poverty line and homeschooled all six of her children to great success.

I know another mom whose husband suffered a severe stroke, leaving her on government assistance. She drove a school bus to make ends meet. She homeschooled her kids into college, too. 

It's not about the money. 

It's about wanting MORE and going after it.

Korea and Poland were devastated by war and poverty and in a few decades became educational superpowers.

They didn't have more resources.

They had the WILL to prioritize education.

And America could, too.

Take my daughter's class with a PhD archaeologist. It costs $300, paid with ESA funds. If she attended our local public school, the school would get ~$14,000 to educate her.

I'm educating her FAR better for FAR less.

And you don't even need an ESA!

You can take FREE classes by Harvard professors through edX. ASU's Universal Learner program offers hundreds of college courses to anyone for free, for a nominal fee you can get college credit.

Money will not solve the education problem.

If it could, it would be solved.

What we need is a culture that decides education is one of the central responsibilities of childhood

And that children are capable of doing serious intellectual work.

And America doesn't want to have that conversation.

So until we do, I'll keep writing for the parents who are engaged enough to go find something better for their children.

It doesn't take money.

It takes WILL.

Do you have what it takes?

Step 1 — Army Hospital (Research & Referral), Delhi Cantt. Start here.
This is the AFMS apex referral hospital and he is entitled to it. Ask specifically for a Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation (PMR) consult with a locked-in syndrome care plan, not a general stroke review. Going through AFMS also unlocks ECHS funding for the long haul, which no private centre will match. If he’s currently at a Command Hospital, the referral upward is an internal process — push for it.

Step 2 — Get an AAC assessment booked in parallel, not after.

This is the step families lose months on by treating it as sequential. Ask for a speech-language pathologist with eye-gaze AAC experience. Two routes:

•AYJNISHD (Ali Yavar Jung National Institute), Mumbai — the national institute for speech and hearing disability; the right institutional home for an AAC assessment.
•Tobii Dynavox directly — their site says funding and availability vary by country and to contact the local representative. I couldn’t verify a named Indian distributor, so write to them through https://t.co/e6tQgqS6r1 and ask for the India contact. Don’t buy hardware before an SLP has assessed his gaze range and fatigue.

Step 3 — Pick one civilian centre for a full second opinion. By region:

•North: AIIMS New Delhi (PMR department), or ISIC Vasant Kunj — strongest PM&R setup in Delhi, though its centre of gravity is spinal injury.
•South: CMC Vellore (PMR) or NIMHANS Bengaluru (Neurological Rehabilitation). CMC is the one I’d rate highest for sustained multidisciplinary work.

When calling any of them, ask one screening question: “Have you managed a locked-in syndrome patient before, and do you have neuro-optometry and respiratory therapy in-house?” The answer tells you everything. Most will say no.

Step 4 — Send records abroad, don’t send him.

Email Shirley Ryan AbilityLab’s LIS programme requesting a records-based review. Costs a fraction of travel and can be done this month.

What not to do right now: don’t chase implanted BCI, don’t fly anywhere, and don’t spend on stem-cell or “nerve regeneration” offers — those will come to you unsolicited once the post spreads.

text:
The Catholic conferences scattered across states offer a telling study in contrasts, with some actively testifying on life's protection, marriage, and parental rights while Alaska's version lingers in notable stillness. Drawing from examples in Kansas, Texas, and even Hawaii, where bishops translate doctrine into public resources and legislative input, the piece questions why similar clarity eludes the northernmost outpost. Personal recollections of quiet family gestures supporting the preborn underscore a deeper expectation that moral teachings should not evaporate at state lines.

The executive director's kinship with a prominent senator who backs expansive abortion access and related policies invites scrutiny without assuming causation. Still, the lack of visible positions on bills affecting human dignity or religious liberty leaves roughly 65,000 Alaska Catholics navigating elections without the pointed guidance supplied elsewhere. Historical letters from local bishops once addressed these duties directly, suggesting the current approach marks a departure rather than an inevitability.

Ultimately, doctrine remains fixed regardless of borders or ballot cycles. The inquiry centers on whether Alaska's faithful receive equivalent direction to apply Church principles at the polls, free from partisan entanglement yet rich in practical insight. This shortfall merits examination before votes are cast.

text:
THE DAY WALMART PUT YOUR EYEBALL ON THE SHOPPING LIST. 📷📷📷📷📷
A SATURDAY EVENING POST–STYLE SATIRE. By Francis Gauthier
There was a time when a man could walk into Walmart, buy a quart of motor oil, two cans of beans and a package of socks without introducing his face, voice, automobile and telephone to the management.
Those innocent days appear to be packing their bags.
#WalmartPrivacy #BiometricSurveillance #ConsumerPrivacy #DigitalFreedom #ProtectYourData
📷📷📷 THE COURT OF PUBLIC OPINION IS NOW OPEN 📷📷📷📷
Walmart says it may collect biometric information—including voiceprints, facial geometry, fingerprints and iris or retina imagery—depending on the service, technology, customer permissions and applicable law. 📷📷📷📷📷
Walmart says biometric information is not used for targeted advertising, although it may be disclosed to vendors performing business operations. But the larger privacy notice covers far more than biometrics, including purchases, location, device activity, communications and information obtained from outside sources. 📷📷📷📷
So let’s put the real questions before the jury:
📷 Exactly which Walmart stores and services collect each kind of biometric information?📷
📷 Is the information used only by Walmart, or can corporate vendors and business partners access it?📷
📷 Which information is “sold,” “shared,” licensed or otherwise exchanged—and with whom? 📷📷📷
📷 Can shopping, location, camera and license-plate information be connected to one identifiable customer?📷
📷 Could police, federal agencies or intelligence services obtain these records through subpoenas, warrants or national-security authorities? 📷📷📷
📷 Has Walmart ever received a request for this information from the NSA or another federal agency? If so, what was requested and what was provided?📷
📷 Does Walmart publish a transparency report showing government requests and company responses?📷
📷 Why can some biometric data remain until three years after a customer’s “last interaction”? 📷📷
📷 If a vendor suffers a breach, who answers for the loss of a faceprint or fingerprint that cannot be replaced? 📷📷📷
📷There is presently no evidence in this story that Walmart is selling biometric files to the NSA. That claim should not be made without proof. But asking who can access the data—and under what legal authority—is entirely fair. Privacy disappears fastest when nobody asks questions. 📷📷
📷 You are the jury. Read the story, examine Walmart’s own policy and place your verdict in the comments below. What information should a retailer be permitted to collect simply because you entered its property or used its app? 📷📷📷
#WalmartPrivacy #BiometricSurveillance #ConsumerPrivacy #DigitalFreedom #ProtectYourData
Biblical principle  :Request: Guard what has been entrusted to you (1 Timothy 6:20). Convenience has value, but personal liberty and privacy deserve watchful stewardship.📷📷📷📷📷📷📷
Walmart updated its Customer Privacy Notice on August 20, 2026. Buried among the corporate language is a remarkable shopping list—not of merchandise Walmart sells, but of personal information it says it may collect.
That list includes voiceprints, images of the iris or retina, facial geometry, palm prints and fingerprints.
In other words, Grandma may enter the store looking for birdseed and discover that her eyeball has become part of the transaction.
“Welcome to Walmart. Would you like a cart?”
“Yes, please.”
“And may we interest you in having your face converted into mathematics?”
Now, let us keep both feet planted on the floor. Walmart’s notice does not say that every shopper entering every store receives an iris scan. It says the company “may collect” these categories of information depending upon the service used, the customer’s device settings, available technology and applicable law.
That distinction matters. Facts are stubborn things, and a good watchdog should never outrun them.
But Walmart’s own language confirms that the company has built a privacy framework broad enough to accommodate biometric information that once belonged in science-fiction movies.
THE NEW AMERICAN GREETER
The old Walmart greeter offered a smile and pointed you toward the lawn fertilizer.
The modern greeter may have several mechanical assistants.
According to Walmart, cameras and automated technologies operating inside stores and elsewhere on company property may capture customers’ images during checkout, help deter theft, or assist Walmart in improving store design.
Automated license-plate readers may also operate on Walmart property where the law allows them. The company says these readers may be used for security, theft and fraud prevention, parking enforcement, and the protection of people and property.
Those are legitimate business purposes. Shoplifting remains stealing even when the thief calls it “wealth redistribution.” Walmart has every right to protect its merchandise, employees and honest customers.
But consider the possible trail left by one ordinary shopping trip:
The parking-lot reader sees the automobile.
The store camera sees the driver.
The checkout system sees the purchases.
The payment terminal sees the card.
The Walmart account remembers the shopping history.
The customer’s telephone may provide location, device and online information.
By the time our shopper reaches the frozen-food aisle, the system may know more about his afternoon than his wife does.
And unlike his wife, the computer never forgets that he bought the family-sized chocolate cake.
“IT’S FOR YOUR CONVENIENCE”
The updated notice specifically adds information about voice interactions.
Walmart says it captures voice interactions when customers activate voice features, such as pressing the microphone button for voice search or speaking to the Sparky shopping assistant. The company says it receives a text transcription and does not use this particular voice data for biometric analysis.
That is important context. The policy does not establish that Walmart is secretly recording every conversation near the canned peas.
An older “Hey, Walmart” voice-assistant feature can listen for its wake phrase while the app is open and the customer has granted the necessary permissions. Walmart says it does not retain information heard before recognizing those words.
Customer-service calls may also be recorded in accordance with applicable law.
But one question remains hanging over the checkout lane like an improperly priced ceiling fan: If activated voice interactions are not used for biometric analysis, why does Walmart separately list “voiceprints” among the biometric information it may collect?
Perhaps there is a perfectly reasonable explanation. Walmart should provide it in language that does not require three attorneys, a decoder ring and a pot of strong coffee.
THE VIRTUAL DRESSING ROOM
Some biometric collection is tied to optional virtual try-on services.
Walmart says its virtual-eyeglass system uses facial scanning to measure a customer’s features and place digital frames over the image. The company says biometric information collected through that service is deleted within 48 hours and is neither sold nor shared.
The virtual-makeup feature may share measurements and images with the third-party provider Perfect Corp., although Walmart says the completed virtual-try-on images are not stored.
These services require the customer to participate and grant permission. Anyone uncomfortable with that arrangement can use the same reliable technology Americans used for generations: pick up the eyeglasses, put them on and look in a mirror.
Primitive, perhaps. Yet strangely effective.
THE THREE-YEAR CLOCK
Walmart’s general biometric-retention schedule says it will permanently destroy biometric information when the first of three events occurs:
1. The original purpose for collecting it has been satisfied;
2. Three years have passed since the customer’s last interaction with Walmart; or
3. Applicable law requires its destruction.
The phrase “last interaction” deserves attention. A regular customer could potentially restart that three-year period repeatedly.
Walmart says biometric information is not used for targeted advertising. Its policy nevertheless allows biometric information to be disclosed to vendors performing business operations for the company.
That is no small matter. A stolen credit-card number can be canceled. A customer cannot cancel his fingerprints and order a replacement face from customer service.
“Well, Mr. Johnson, the bad news is that your facial geometry escaped in a data breach. The good news is that aisle seven has mustache wax on rollback.”
WHAT CUSTOMERS CAN DO
People concerned about their privacy do not need to move into a cave and pay cash to a traveling merchant. A few practical precautions will reduce unnecessary collection:
* Disable Walmart-app access to the camera and microphone unless a feature truly requires it.
* Turn off precise location access or allow it only while actively using the app.
* Disable Bluetooth access if indoor-location features are unwanted.
* Avoid optional voice and virtual try-on services.
* Think carefully before connecting a VIZIO account with a Walmart account.
* Review the “Your Privacy Choices” section on Walmart’s website.
* Understand that store cameras and lawful license-plate readers may still operate even if the shopper carries no smartphone.
THE BOTTOM LINE
Walmart is not admitting that a hidden machine examines every shopper’s retina between the sliding doors and the produce section.
It is admitting something broader: its privacy system may collect an enormous range of information across physical stores, websites, apps, connected devices and outside sources—and may combine information gathered from several of those places.
Security has a proper purpose. So does technology. But neither should become a blank check allowing corporations to compile permanent personal dossiers on ordinary Americans buying everyday necessities.
The fair rule is simple: collect only what is necessary, explain exactly what is operating in each store, obtain real consent before collecting biometric identifiers, restrict vendor access and delete the data promptly.
The customer should remain a customer—not become the product, the suspect and the research specimen before reaching the checkout.
Walmart built its empire on “Everyday Low Prices.”
The public should make certain those prices do not come with everyday high surveillance.
Sources: Walmart’s official Customer Privacy Notice and the Cybernews report.
Biblical principle: Wisdom keeps its eyes open—“The prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself” (Proverbs 22:3). Read the permissions, limit the collection and guard what cannot be replaced.

text:
Two days ago, Identity.md NFT holders made the wl for @FlockFall , a game launching on Robinhood Chain.
I broke down the game mechanics and potential ways to earn.

The core idea: ducks farm $SHELL, while foxes can steal both the rewards and the NFT itself. The outcome depends on the character, location and expedition duration.

1. Two types of characters

All 6000 Genesis NFTs have already been minted. After the reveal, they will turn into 5400 ducks and 600 foxes.

Ducks produce SHELL: 80% of the rewards accumulate on the character, while 20% goes into the shared fox pool. Carried rewards remain at risk until the character returns home.

Foxes receive a share of the common pool based on their weight. Active foxes can also be automatically selected for attacks.

2. Choose a route and duration

You send a character on an expedition, and everything else is calculated automatically.

There are five expedition durations:

1.5 / 4 / 12 / 36 / 84 hours

Three locations offer different duck production multipliers:

> Pond ×0.65 rewards, lower encounter risk
> Marsh ×1 rewards, standard risk
> Wilds ×1.35 rewards, higher encounter risk

For foxes, the location affects their chances of being selected as an attacker, but does not increase their share of the common pool.

Longer expeditions allow more SHELL to accumulate, but also increase the chance of an attack. After the expedition, the character takes a safe journey home lasting 2 to 24 hours.

There is also a paid early exit called Rush, which comes with another encounter risk.

3. You can lose more than just tokens

A robbery takes 25% to 75% of the carried SHELL.

If a character is captured, the attacking fox owner receives the NFT itself and all the SHELL it was carrying. Foxes can also become victims.

4. Rarity affects the mechanics

Characters come in four tiers: T1 to T4.

For ducks, the tier affects production. For foxes, it affects their reward weight and their chances of being selected as an attacker.

Capture protection is:

0% / 35% / 65% / 85%

Genesis status also cuts the remaining capture probability in half.

5. SHELL is required to mint new NFTs

The Hatchery will release four Gen1 batches of 1000 characters each.

Mint prices increase with every batch:

100 > 250 > 500 > 1000 SHELL

SHELL spent on minting is burned.

Batches unlock gradually. The second and subsequent batches require the previous 1,000 NFTs to be revealed and at least five days to pass since the previous batch opened.

6. Production gradually decreases

As in-game emissions increase, the production multiplier declines:

×1 > ×0.5 > ×0.375 > ×0.25 > ×0.125

The first reduction happens after 2.25m SHELL in game emissions.

The entire game is built around one choice: how much SHELL you are willing to accumulate in a single run and how much risk you are willing to take with your character.

For now, I’m watching the launch and choosing the best strategy to start with.

text:
The team that called about Myles Garrett was Buffalo. Tom Pelissero, via FanSided, reports the Bills rang Cleveland on the day the trade leaked, and had been probing Garrett's availability for two years without ever getting the Browns to bite.

I could not tell you the return package the last time this came up, so here it is, from the Browns' own announcement: Cleveland got Jared Verse, a 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 second and a 2029 third.

What left is the reigning Defensive Player of the Year. Per the club, Garrett gave Cleveland nine seasons, 134 games, 412 tackles and 125.5 sacks — the franchise record — and in 2025 he set the NFL single-season sack record with 23. ESPN has that 23 too, so the record claim stands up on its own.

What arrived is a 25-year-old edge rusher who had 7.5 sacks and 58 tackles in 2025. Both of those lines are last season. Neither man has a 2026 line yet, and I am not going to write either one in the present tense.

Now the part that is worth the whole story. FanSided's read is that Buffalo could have matched or beaten the draft compensation, and that what the Bills did not have was an edge rusher of Verse's calibre. That is the writer's explanation rather than Pelissero's reporting, and the counterfactual about Buffalo's offer is not a document anybody has seen — so hold it loosely.

And that hedge has to travel with the conclusion, because the conclusion is built on it. If Buffalo really could have matched or beaten the picks, then Cleveland made a choice: not the best pile of picks, the pile with a person in it. If Buffalo could not have, then there was no choice to read at all — Cleveland took the best offer on the table, which is what teams do, and the whole interpretation collapses. I cannot tell you which of those happened.

That is a defensible thing to want and it is also the expensive thing to be wrong about. And be careful with twenty-three against seven and a half, because that is a record season against an ordinary one. By the club's own figures Garrett had at least ten sacks in each of the last eight years and at least twelve in each of the last six, so his normal is somewhere in the low teens, not twenty-three. Verse's first-contract level against Garrett's normal level is still a real gap. It is just not that gap. Garrett is thirty and Verse is twenty-five, which is the case for the trade and the case against it wearing the same coat.

The wire's ledger will not grade this and neither will I tonight. It cannot see the contracts, it cannot see how three picks convert, and anyone who tells you they know what a 2029 third is worth is describing a feeling. What it can do is hold the two columns still, next to each other, until the answer arrives on its own.

Reporting: Tom Pelissero via FanSided; https://t.co/SBhhMbhiZf. Figures: ESPN.

Bettin’ Football - Thursday, Sept. 10

An ugly game to open this NFL betting season Wednesday night. New England led Seattle most of the way but then pissed it away in the fourth quarter.

In the end the Seahawks pushed the spread at -3 at some betting outlets and lost at -3.5 at others. Also, the under 44 was a shoo-in.

Tonight the NFL offers up an international bout as the Rams and 49ers take their rivalry to Australia (8:35 pm ET, Netflix).

San Francisco played 12-5 last year, then won a wild-card game at Philadelphia, before getting blown out at Seattle in the divisional round. Heading into this season the 49ers, hoping to play in a little better health than the last couple seasons, are playing against a wins over/under of 10.5.

Los Angeles also played 12-5 last season, then won playoff games at Carolina and at Chicago, before losing a tough NFC championship game at Seattle. Heading into this season the Rams are playing against a wins o/u of 11.5, tied for the highest on that board with Baltimore.

San Francisco hopes to have DE Bosa and TE Kittle both back at full strength tonight. We’ll see. Meanwhile, LB Garrett makes his debut for LA tonight.

These teams split two meetings last season; the 49ers won at LA 26-23 in overtime in Week 5 while in Week 10 the Rams won at Santa Clara 42-26. And actually, those two scores basically tell us what happened in those two games.

Going back a little further Los Angeles is 4-1 SU over the last five meetings in this series and 5-1 ATS over the last six.

Ultimately, I expect the Rams to win the ground battle in this game, just as they’ve done the last three meetings with the Niners. And teams that win the ground battles in the NFL cover the spread about 65 percent of the time.

Also, these teams played two overs last season, averaging over 800 yards of total offense and 58 points per game. But those numbers sure seem like a lot for a spot like this. I’m thinking under 48.5.

text:
**No, that framing is not accurate.** There are not ~100,000 U.S. radiologists, the training pipeline has not produced a glut, and current numbers show a shortage with high demand and rising pay rather than mass disappointment among people who already trained.

### How many radiologists there actually are
Reliable workforce counts put practicing U.S. radiologists in the mid-to-high 30,000s, not 100k:
- ~34,300 in 2010 rising to ~38,300 in 2022.
- ~37,500 enrolled to bill Medicare in 2023.
- Per-capita ratio barely moved: 11.1 to 11.5 radiologists per 100,000 people over that period.

Residency slots grew 33% from 2010–2025 (about 1,090 to 1,449), and total residents rose 23%, but practicing numbers only rose ~12% because of attrition, retirements, and population growth. Imaging volumes and complexity rose faster. That is the opposite of a surplus of people who “trained for a decade.”

### Job market right now
There is a shortage, not unemployment:
- Thousands of active openings at any given time (roughly 4,300–7,500 depending on the scrape and how you count re-posts). Median time-to-fill is weeks; a subset of “zombie” jobs sit open >60 days, mostly in less popular geographies.
- Average compensation reported around $571k in 2025 (Medscape) with some analyses of listings putting medians higher; sign-on bonuses can be large.
- Radiology has been named the top threat/workforce issue in the field for multiple years running. Attrition roughly doubled post-2014 and stayed elevated after COVID. Remote/teleradiology work is now common (often cited around 70%+).

The shortage is uneven: desirable coastal/metro academic or high-pay private jobs fill faster; rural, certain Midwest states, overnight coverage, and some VA sites struggle more. That is geographic mismatch plus workload, not “too many radiologists.”

### AI and “the current numbers”
Geoffrey Hinton’s 2016 prediction that people should stop training radiologists because AI would obsolete them within 5–10 years did not happen. The workforce grew modestly, demand grew more, and salaries rose. AI tools (hundreds of FDA-cleared radiology devices) are used as productivity aids—drafting reports, prioritizing worklists, handling repetitive tasks—not as full replacements. Modeling typically finds productivity gains offset by volume growth rather than headcount cuts in the near term.

Radiologists who already completed the long path (undergrad + med school + 4–5 year residency, often plus fellowship) are generally employed. The friction they feel is high case volumes, burnout, reimbursement pressure, and uneven distribution of work—not a collapse in job availability. New graduates still typically have multiple offers.

The “ask the 100k” line overstates both the headcount and the implied outcome. The data point to tight supply relative to imaging demand, not a cohort of overtrained doctors sitting idle.

Jax thought he had lost his little brother forever. Then, one night, a voice came from the sea. Jax and Noah were inseparable, growing up in a small coastal town where they spent their days sailing together. 

One afternoon, Noah went out with their parents while Jax stayed behind. A violent storm hit, their boat crashed, and their parents never returned. Everyone believed Noah was gone too.

Weeks later, Jax heard Noah calling from the water. He looked down and froze. Noah was alive, but he now had a shimmering merman tail. A kind sea witch had saved him and transformed him to help rebuild her underwater people after a devastating war.

Jax couldn’t bear to lose his brother again. The sea witch offered him one choice: stay on land as a human, or give up his human life and become a merman.

Jax chose the sea. As the magic took hold, his legs transformed into a powerful tail. When he opened his eyes, Noah was beside him.
Two brothers. One new life beneath the waves.

text:
I BET YOU DIDN'Y KNOW ABOUT THIS: AFTER FLIGHT 77 HIT THE PENTAGON ON 9/11, THE FOLLOWING HAPPENED.

A daycare facility inside the Pentagon had many children, including infants who were in heavy cribs. The daycare supervisor, looking at all the children they needed to evacuate, was in a panic over what they could do.

There were many children, mostly toddlers, as well as the infants who would need to be taken out with the cribs. There was no time to try to bundle them into carriers and strollers.

Just then a young Marine came running into the center and asked what they needed. After hearing what the center director was trying to do, he ran back out into the hallway and disappeared. The director thought, "Well, here we are, on our own."

About 2 minutes later, that Marine returned with 40 other Marines in tow.

Each of them grabbed a crib with a child, and the rest started gathering up toddlers.

The director and her staff then helped them take all the children out of the center and down toward the park near the Potomac .

Once they got about 3/4 of a mile outside the building, the Marines stopped in the park, and then did a fabulous thing - they formed a circle with the cribs, which were quite sturdy and heavy, like the covered wagons in the Old West.

Inside this circle of cribs, they put the toddlers, to keep them from wandering off. 

Outside this circle were the 40 Marines, forming a perimeter around the children and waiting for instructions. There they remained until the parents could be notified and come get their children.

The chaplain then said, "I don't think any of us saw nor heard of this on any of the news stories of the day. It was an incredible story of our men there.” There wasn't a dry eye in the room.

The thought of those Marines and what they did and how fast they reacted; could we expect any less from them? It was one of the most touching stories from the Pentagon.

It's the military, not the politicians that ensures our right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. 

It's the military who salutes the flag, who serves beneath the flag, and whose coffin is draped by the flag.

If you care to offer the smallest token of recognition and appreciation for the military, please pass this on and pray for our men and women, who have served and are currently serving our country, and honor the memory of those who have given the ultimate sacrifice!

God Bless The USA!

Never forget!!!

text:
During the 'Reimagining Clinical Judgment Through Innovation' session from today's 2026 NCLEX Virtual Conference, presenters highlighted how innovation can deepen critical thinking, reduce variability and better prepare new nurses for complex, high-stakes environments.   

University of South Carolina College of Nursing Interim Director of Prelicensure Programs, Instructor, Megan Honaker, DNP, RN says, "Immersive virtual reality simulation (IVRS) offers a scalable and innovative approach to supporting practice readiness while providing meaningful evidence of clinical judgment development."  

Ramapo College of New Jersey Assistant Professor, Amy Pizzulo, DNP, RN says that successful virtual reality implementation requires more than implementing new technology. "Faculty development is essential and students need a proper orientation and sufficient time getting comfortable with VR technology prior to the VR experience." She also indicated more research is needed on when and how VR adds the most value.   

University of Pennsylvania Graduate School of Education Instructor, Mamta Shah, PhD, revealed that virtual patient simulations helped nursing students practice key nursing skills and that a new analytical method known as Transmodal Ordered Network Analysis (T/ONA), can help educators better understand how prelicensure students make decisions during simulations.

RINGCENTRAL $RNG IS $8.92 OFF LAST THURSDAY'S HIGH. THE MOMENTUM LEN5'S OTHER FOUR ARE NOT:

RingCentral at $69.03, -$0.61 / -0.88% today. The Momentum Len5 is watching five smaller companies whose prices have already climbed, and four of them are still within about 5% of a twelve-month high. RingCentral is the exception. Last Thursday it printed $77.95. Five sessions later it has given back $8.92, or 11.4%. The style is still watching it because the longer climbs have not broken.

+5.3% against the August 20 close of $65.58; +68.6% against July 9's $40.94; +52% against May 7's $45.39. Those three moves still point the same way. The high does not.

The Belmont, California company sells cloud phone lines, messages, and contact-center software - the switchboard a business rents instead of owning.

This style wants a price near a twelve-month best, with the recent climb and the longer one agreeing, and enough daily trading that the move is not happening on a handful of shares. RingCentral meets two of those three: about 1.4 million shares on a typical recent day, and large three-month and six-month climbs. The missing piece is the high itself, now a week old.

The dated spark was September 3. RBC Capital Markets started coverage at Outperform with an $85 target. The shares hit $77.95 and closed $76.36 on 1.70 million shares, a bit above the recent 1.37 million average. Today they are $69.03 on about 595k shares. The volume went with the high, then left.

What the company reported is slower than that chart. July 23, three months to June 30: sales $657M, +5.9%; subscriptions $634M, +5.8%. Operating margin - what it kept after running the business - 7.7%, up from 6.0% a year earlier. Free cash flow - cash left after running the business and paying for equipment - $180M, +25%, about 27 cents of every sales dollar. Customers using at least one paid AI product now represent about 13% of annual recurring revenue, the yearly value of subscriptions still in force, double a year earlier. Management raised 2026 sales to $2.635B-$2.646B and free cash flow to $615M-$625M, and bought back 2.2 million shares for $94M in the quarter.

CHANGE IT: a miss of the $664M-$670M third-quarter sales map, or a close back through July 9's $40.94, the floor under that +68.6% three-month climb. WHEN: November 2 after the close; both calendars agree. RISK: mid-single-digit growth after a 125% twelve-month climb from $30.63 a year ago, against about $1.0B of net borrowings and $112M of cash. VERDICT: a Momentum Len5 name whose price already spent the new high, with a software business compounding cash faster than sales.

This style is looking for agreement across months, not a single up day.

- AtriCure at $52.99, -$0.04 / -0.08% today. The Mason, Ohio company makes surgical tools that treat irregular heartbeat and close the small heart pouch where clots form. This Len5 picked it because last week's high came on real volume and the one-month, three-month, and six-month moves are all still up. July 23, three months to June 30: worldwide sales $153.6M, +12.8%; net income $9.0M, or $0.18 a share, against a $6.2M loss a year earlier; the year mapped at $602M-$610M of sales. On September 8 it printed $55.72 on 1.88 million shares, about double its 20-day average of 840k, and it is still 95% of that high. CHANGE IT: a close that loses $55.72 while the one-month climb from August 20's $47.49 turns down. WHEN: the company has not dated the September quarter; two calendars disagree, pointing to late October or early November. VERDICT: a surgical supplier whose price is still treating last week's high as a floor.

- Varex Imaging at $18.49, -$0.01 / -0.05% today. The Salt Lake City company makes the X-ray tubes and detector panels inside hospital scanners and cargo-inspection machines. This Len5 picked it because every recent close is pinned next to the high and the daily range has gone quiet, with the three-month move still +72%. August 10 Teledyne Technologies at $597.25, +$2.02 / +0.34% today, agreed to buy the company for $18.90 a share in cash, about $1.1B including debt, aiming to close in early 2027. The last eight sessions have all closed between $18.47 and $18.52. Teledyne fits none of the six Len5es. CHANGE IT: the deal failing, or a vote date that never appears. WHEN: shareholders have not been given a meeting date. VERDICT: the quietest price here is a cash offer waiting on a merger clock, not a trend still being argued.

- LifeStance Health at $13.11, +$0.49 / +3.9% today. The Scottsdale, Arizona company runs outpatient mental-health clinics, in person and on video, with 8,542 clinicians across 33 states. This Len5 picked it because the price is at a high on deep daily trading - about 4.0 million shares on a typical recent day. August 6, three months to June 30: sales $435.4M, +26%; 2.6 million visits, +19%; net income $23.6M after a year-earlier loss. Yesterday existing holders priced a 22.25 million share secondary at $12.35, with the company buying 2 million of those shares; settlement is due September 11. Today's high of $13.265 is the twelve-month best. CHANGE IT: the shares slipping back through the $12.35 offering price after the stock is delivered. WHEN: September 11. VERDICT: the only name here making a new high today is doing it the session after a large holder sale, not on a new quarter.

- The Manitowoc Company at $20.37, -$0.63 / -3.0% today. The Wisconsin crane maker builds machines for construction sites, ports, and energy work. This Len5 picked it because the one-month, three-month, and six-month moves still agree even though fewer shares trade here than in the other four. August 6, three months to June 30: sales $594.9M, +10.3%; orders $708.7M, +56%; backlog - work already booked but not yet shipped - $1.05B. The twelve-month high was $21.50 on September 4. Today's 188k shares is about half the recent 377k average. CHANGE IT: orders rolling over, or a close that loses the August 20 $19.09 level that built the one-month climb. WHEN: the company has not confirmed a date; calendars point to early November. VERDICT: the thinnest market of the five is still a crane-order climb, and today is the first real test of whether anyone is still in it.

Four of five are still living next to a high. RingCentral is the one that already left. November 2 is when that company has to show the three-month climb was the software, not an $85 research note.

text:
Some of you may remember a post I made around Easter a couple of years ago, about a billboard I passed on the highway. Jesus nailed to a cross, bleeding, crown of thorns, face twisted in agony, and one word underneath it: "Love." That billboard made it into my new book. Yesterday it found me again, in a Facebook ad. I'll get to it in a second.

First I need to ask something of you, and I'm asking as a friend.

Set aside, for five minutes, whatever you've decided about me. When my first book came out, some people who had known me for decades concluded that something had gone wrong with me. Satan got hold of Dan. He's being deceived. He needs to be saved. One asked me, "Haven't you ever been wrong, Dan?" Of course I have. About beliefs, many times. But this isn't a belief I'm asking you to adopt. It's a test I'm asking you to run, and it isn't mine.

Your own Bible commands it. "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God" (1 John 4:1). "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:21). And it hands you the measuring stick a few verses later: "God is love" (1 John 4:8). Test everything against love. Not by what a thing claims about itself. By what it does. That's the whole test, and a child can run it. You feel it in your chest when you see cruelty: that contraction, that recoil, that instant knowing that something is wrong here. Jesus called it the inner light. You were born with it. The only thing you were never given was permission to point it at the one place you were told it didn't belong.

So here's the ad. A handmade crucifix for your home. Two sizes, one for the bedside table and one for the wall. $44.90, marked down from $69.90. 303 five-star reviews. "Made for prayer spaces." "A meaningful faith gift for new homes, family, and loved ones." Spend $80 and you unlock a free gift. Order in the next 21 hours for delivery by Monday.

Look at the second picture. That's the product photo they chose to sell it with. A man's feet, roped to a beam, a nail driven through them, blood running down the wood. Then the last picture: both sizes on a side table beside a candle and a framed sign that says "Be still and know that I am God."

Grandma might want to hide that one when the grandkids come over. Why? Because she doesn't want to give a child nightmares, or spend the next half hour talking a six-year-old down while trying to convince her that the bleeding man on the end table is a statue of love. Sit with why that conversation would be so hard. The child isn't too young to understand. She hasn't been trained yet to override what she can plainly see. Jesus said we have to become like little children to enter the kingdom. I don't think that's a coincidence.

Now do what your Bible says and run the test. Forget everything you were taught. Look at those pictures as if you had never seen them before. What do you see? A man being tortured to death. An execution. And you're being told that this is the most loving act in history, and that if your gut says otherwise, your gut is the enemy testing your faith.

Why is the same act, an innocent tortured to death so that others can be forgiven, monstrous when Ba'al asks for it and the centerpiece of God's plan when the church says God did? Love doesn't need a defense team. Truth and love welcome scrutiny. If it takes a seminary degree to explain why torture is love, something is wrong with the explanation, not with your conscience.

"I desire mercy, not sacrifice," says Hosea, and Jesus quoted that line twice and drove the sacrificial animals out of the Temple with his own hands. The tradition he was raised in called human sacrifice an abomination. For three hundred years after his death there was no cross on any Christian wall; in Rome it was the most degrading death there was, reserved for slaves and criminals. He knew exactly what would happen when people saw it. "Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division." Luke 12:51. Father against son, mother against daughter. Not because his message was wrong, but because the religion around him was so corrupted that the truth couldn't fit inside it. It still can't.

This isn't speculation, opinion, or some fringe theory cooked up by angry atheists with an axe to grind. It’s textual, manuscript, linguistic, and cultural evidence from the most respected biblical scholars on the planet, many of whom are Christians themselves.

“One with words.”

“You are unbearable.”

By the time they reach the northern coast, days have passed. What began as an unbearable partnership gradually becomes something else. Between haunted forests, abandoned kingdoms, cultists pursuing them and far too many nights sharing one bed their arguments slowly morph into trust. Then longing. Then something neither of them is willing to name.

The map eventually leads them to a cliff overlooking the sea. There is no temple or visible path only dark water stretching towards the horizon.

NuNew looks at Zee. “You said the temple was here.”

“It is.”

“There is only water here.”

“I’m aware.”

“You expect us to walk into it?”

“It’s called the Temple of Lux. We need the moon to show us the path.”

When moonlight touches the sea a staircase appears beneath the water. Zee warns him that once they enter, they will have only until sunrise to retrieve the Book. After that, the temple will sink beyond the reach of any living creature for another hundred years.

NuNew looks down at the stairs. “We should probably stop standing here, then.”

At the water’s edge, he raises his hands. Light spills across the steps. The sea draws back, forming walls of dark water on either side. The barrier holds for maybe thirty seconds then the weight of the water begins crushing it.

NuNew staggers. “I can’t hold back an entire ocean.”

“Then don’t.”

“Zee…”

“Choose the space you need. Nothing more.”

Water begins dripping through the cracks.

“If the barrier breaks…”

“Look at me.”

NuNew does. Zee takes his hand.

“You only need enough room for us. I’ll watch the path. You hold the barrier.”

NuNew swallows and pulls his magic back around them, creating a small passage through the water. The sea rushes closer. He nearly panics but Zee’s hand remains steady around his.

“There,” Zee says.

NuNew takes another step. Then another. By the time they reach the temple, his barrier is holding steady. And Zee is still holding his hand.

Inside the temple, the protections left by the two ancient houses remain active. NuNew’s pearl magic opens its white stone gates, while Zee’s map shows an incantation that serves as a key capable of disarming the wards beyond them.

At the centre of the temple, they finally find the Book of Death. It rests inside an obsidian case surrounded by hundreds of suspended black chains. Although the Book is closed, whispers fill the chamber the moment NuNew approaches it. They promise to teach him how to control his power. They offer to erase his mistakes and make everyone who doubted him kneel. NuNew reaches towards it. Zee catches his wrist.

“What was the first rule I taught you?”

NuNew keeps staring at the Book. “Assume everything is cursed.”

“Good. You were listening.”

“I wasn’t going to touch it.”

Before they can remove the Book, Tharn’s followers enter the temple behind them. They have been tracking NuNew’s magic throughout the journey, waiting for him to open wards none of them could cross. A fight erupts inside the chamber. Zee holds off the cultists while NuNew attempts to release the chains surrounding the case. Every spell he casts causes the temple to shake harder and seawater begins pouring through cracks in the ceiling.

NuNew can feel his control slipping.

“Zee!”

“Don’t look at me,” Zee shouts as he drives his blade through another undead. “Look at the chains.”

“I can’t break all of them!”

“You don’t need to. Find the one holding the spell together.”

“How?”

“You’re the pearl mage!”

“You call that instructions?”

“Fine! Think of it as an encouragement then!”

NuNew forces himself to stop thinking about the hundreds of chains surrounding him. He closes his eyes and searches for the single thread of magic connecting them. Then he pulls. Every chain shatters at once except for one that wraps itself around the case, forming a temporary seal around the Book. NuNew catches the case as it tips. For one breathless moment, relief floods him. +

text:
September 10  
  
The Priest We Need  
Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession … Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.  
Hebrews 4:14–16  
The Old Testament underlines again and again the weight of responsibility on high priests in Israel (see, for example, Exodus 29 and Leviticus 16). Being the high priest was not to be taken lightly. Only he could enter the Most Holy Place, the inner chamber of the Jewish temple. Only he could offer a blood sacrifice “for the unintentional sins of the people” (Hebrews 9:7). Although he was not without sin, he served as an advocate for his community before God.  
  
But, as the writer of Hebrews shows us, there has been one Great High Priest—namely, Jesus—who did what no other priest could do and shouldered a responsibility the weight of which no other human could bear.  
  
Jesus did not go through a curtain into the Most Holy Place in the Jerusalem temple. Instead, as God’s Son, He passed through the heavens, so that He now appears on our behalf before the Father’s throne. We need not lament His physical absence on earth, not only because He is present with us through the Holy Spirit but also because His absence means that even now He is directly speaking to God the Father on our behalf (Hebrews 7:25).  
  
That is why in the New Testament, ministry is not set apart for an order of priests who make blood sacrifices. Those who are called by God and given both the privilege and responsibility of leading and teaching God’s people do not have to advocate before God for His people in the way Old Testament priests did. Because our Great High Priest has offered up the one great sacrifice for sins, there is no need for any other advocate. Indeed, His priesthood leaves room for no other offerings for sin, either in heaven or on earth. He alone could die for us and speak for us, and He alone has done it.  
  
The very greatness of Christ’s priesthood lies in the fact that He has offered Himself for our sins once and for all. We need nothing more than to recognize that “he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24). Jesus alone is able to save those of us who come to God on the basis of His merits. He always lives to intercede for His people. He is doing so, right at this very moment, for you. So you can live confident of access to the heavenly throne room whenever you pray, and access for your soul on the day you die. Today, all you need to do is hold fast to your confession of faith in the Great High Priest, who has done all that is needed.  
  
Further Reading  
Hebrews 7:23–28
