#Formula1 #Italy: #Kalshi Market Scan

Report date: September 10, 2026
Market snapshot: approximately 12:27 p.m. PDT / 19:27 UTC
Race: Italian Grand Prix, Monza, September 6, 2026

DECISION: NO NEW ITALY TRADE

The Italian Grand Prix is already complete. Kalshi's Italian race-winner and podium markets are finalized. This is a post-race settlement review, not a live race prediction. The official result and the verified Kalshi outcomes agree: Kimi Antonelli won; George Russell and Max Verstappen completed the podium. [1–3]

The next-race watchlist below concerns Spain on September 13, not Italy. It is included for continuity and does not replace the requested Monza review. No trade has been placed.

OFFICIAL MONZA RESULT

Position  Driver              Team           Time / gap
1         Kimi Antonelli      Mercedes       1:51:15.281
2         George Russell      Mercedes       +3.857 seconds
3         Max Verstappen      Red Bull       +14.718 seconds
4         Lando Norris        McLaren        +19.056 seconds
5         Oscar Piastri       McLaren        +19.253 seconds
6         Lewis Hamilton      Ferrari        +24.655 seconds

The race ran 53 laps. Charles Leclerc was classified as a non-finisher. [1]

FIA's race account describes Antonelli recovering from 19th on the grid to win at home. This is evidence of a successful comeback in one race, not proof that starting position never matters or that the same driver is underpriced in the next event. [4]

KALSHI SETTLEMENT AUDIT

Race-winner event: KXF1RACE-ITAGP26
Podium event: KXF1RACEPODIUM-ITAGP26

The public API returned 22 Italian winner contracts and 22 Italian podium contracts in the inspected series. All 44 showed status 'finalized'. Winner contracts require the named driver to finish exactly first in the main race originally scheduled for September 6. Podium contracts require a top-three finish in that race. [2,3]

Selected contracts; monetary values are per YES contract

Driver       Winner result   YES settlement   Podium result   YES settlement
Antonelli    Yes             $1.00            Yes             $1.00
Russell      No              $0.00            Yes             $1.00
Verstappen   No              $0.00            Yes             $1.00
Norris       No              $0.00            No              $0.00
Piastri      No              $0.00            No              $0.00
Hamilton     No              $0.00            No              $0.00
Leclerc      No              $0.00            No              $0.00

Antonelli's winner contract, KXF1RACE-ITAGP26-ANT, closed September 6 at 19:08:43 UTC and settled at 19:14:45 UTC. Its YES settlement value is $1.00. Its stored last trade is $0.99, while the returned best bid/ask fields show $0.00/$1.00 with zero quoted size. Those fields do not establish an executable trade today. [2]

A remaining latest-expiration field dated September 20 does not override finalized status and the recorded September 6 settlement. Confusing expiration metadata with current trading availability would produce an incorrect scan.

These settlements are gross contract payouts, not net profits. A winning YES bought for 60 cents earns 40 cents before fees; a losing YES loses its acquisition cost. Actual account results depend on fills, quantities and charges. No personal account history was accessed.

WHAT CAN BE LEARNED FROM MONZA

First, separate predictions from outcomes. A settled YES is not a retrospective 100% pre-race probability. The archived last price may come from late in the race, after decisive information arrived. Without time-stamped pre-race trades or order books, it cannot substantiate a claim that a driver was a bargain before the start.

Second, distinguish winner and podium exposure. A driver can lose the race while still satisfy a top-three contract, as Russell and Verstappen did. Buying correlated contracts does not create independent bets; several positions may depend on the same car reliability, strategy or incident.

Third, evaluate process rather than one result. A sensible review asks what information was available before entry, what probability was estimated, and whether the price offered adequate compensation for uncertainty. A spectacular comeback alone cannot validate a repeatable betting strategy.

NEXT-RACE WATCHLIST — SPAIN, NOT ITALY

Formula 1 identifies the next weekend as the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, September 11–13. The Kalshi contracts below explicitly reference the main race originally scheduled for September 13, 2026. They were active at the snapshot. [2,5]

Event identifier: KXF1RACE-SPAGP26
Selected YES quotes in cents; snapshot only, before fees

Driver         Bid    Ask    Ask-price break-even before fees
Antonelli       35     36                  36%
Norris          24     25                  25%
Russell         15     16                  16%
Hamilton        11     12                  12%
Verstappen       8      9                   9%
Leclerc          7      8                   8%
Piastri          4      5                   5%

These asks are purchase costs, not independently estimated win probabilities. Their sum is 111 cents even before adding other drivers, so buying this selected group at the displayed asks does not create an arbitrage. A seven-driver subset also does not cover every possible winner.

The snapshot showed only 14.04 contracts at Piastri's best ask, compared with thousands for several others. Quoted depth can vanish or change. A small top-of-book spread does not guarantee that a larger order can execute at the same price. This report has not inspected deeper order-book levels. [2]

RESEARCH STRATEGY FOR A FUTURE LIVE RACE

Wait for relevant practice, qualifying, grid penalties, weather and reliability information, then estimate probabilities using the conditions of that specific event. Avoid carrying a Monza conclusion mechanically into Madrid. This report does not include a calibrated Spain model or a current weather analysis, so it makes no positive-edge pick.

For a $1 binary YES contract purchased at price p, expected profit per contract before charges is q − p, where q is the independently estimated probability of the specified outcome. After expected fees and execution costs c, the expression is q − p − c. A higher win probability is not enough; the difference must exceed costs and uncertainty.

Illustration only: if a driver costs 36 cents and the independent estimate is 40%, gross expected value is four cents per contract. If total costs are two cents, the estimated edge becomes two cents. If the probability estimate is wrong by five percentage points, that apparent edge disappears. The 40% estimate and two-cent cost here are hypothetical, not claims about Antonelli or Kalshi's applicable fee schedule.

Use limit prices and a predefined maximum amount at risk. Check the live order ticket for the applicable fees and contract terms. Do not use an old last trade as a guaranteed fill. Avoid treating a low-priced longshot as cheap merely because its dollar cost is small.

WATCH / PASS SUMMARY

Italy winner and podium: finalized; no new entry.
Italy qualifying and fastest lap: no event-level contracts verified in this scan; no settlement claim made for those categories.
Spain winner: active quotes located; watchlist only, with no modeled edge established.
Recommended research action: refresh Spain prices after new weekend evidence, then compare against an independently justified probability.

What is the Flesh Market and who owns it? https://t.co/rdRQ1I0ytL 
The Left Behind Series (1)

Investigating who owns Scotland over the years has revealed many fascinating aspects of geography, law, history and politics. This blog is the first in a series that investigates bits of land that have been “left behind”.

Undertaking the regular monthly updates for the https://t.co/BeBGb6tRMR website last month, I was reminded of one such instance. I had meant to write a blog about it some years ago.

In the hills of Galloway, there is a place marked on the Ordnance Survey map as Flesh Market. It is one of two locations in Kirkcudbrightshire. The other is at the northern end of Cairnsmore of Fleet (see map below)

Flesh Market to north of Cairnsmore of Fleet @Crown copyright and database rights 2026

In 2004, Grobdale of Girthon, a 2300 hectare hill farm, was put up for sale by the owner, William Graham. On the sale plan, the western boundary runs in an almost straight line and suggests that the Flesh Market forms part of the farm for sale.

Extract from 2004 Sale Plan of Grobdale of Girthon

In late August 2004, however, an update was provided to prospective purchasers along with the notification of a closing date. The update noted the following;

We are advised, about 40 years ago, the march fence was straightened between lands owned by the Forestry Commission and Grobdale of Girthon and the position of this fence is shown on the sale plan forming part of the sales particulars. The true position however is that the area hatched black on the attached plan forms part of the Grobdale title whereas the area shown cross hatched black lies outside the Grobdale title.

Update provided by selling agent 31 August 2004.

The Flesh Market forms the part not owned by Grobdale. The update correctly makes no claims as to who does own it but merely points out that it does not form part of the land being offered for sale. 

The land to the west is owned by Scottish Ministers as part of the vast 8700 hectare Laurieston Forest. The land immediately adjoining Grobdale was acquired by the Secretary of State for Scotland in March 1965 from Elizabeth Murray Usher, the owner of the historic Cally Estate. The plan accompanying the deed quite clearly excluded the Flesh Market (see below) and appears to be the source of the selling agents’ original belief that Grobdale must own the Flesh Market.

Deed plan accompanying the 1965 sale to the Secretary of State for Scotland

Grobdale of Girthon, meanwhile, had also been owned by Murray Usher and was sold by her in June 1945.

Minute from Search Sheet 6 (Kirkcudbright) of the sale of Grobdale of Girthon

The plan for that sale also clearly excluded the Flesh Market

Deed Plan accompanying the 1945 sale of Grobdale of Girthon

Thus we have the situation illustrated below where Grobdale of Girthon (in blue together with hatched area) is registered in the Land Register and the Lauriston Forest to the west (in red) is also on the Land Register but the Flesh Market sits isolated in between them owned by neither Scottish Ministers nor the current owner of Grobdale of Girthon.

Scottish Ministers land (red) and Grobdale of Girthon (blue including hatched area)

So who owns the Flesh Market?

The obvious answer is the successor to Elizabeth Murray Usher who (presumably) owned it at the time of the 1946 and 1965 sales but somehow omitted to convey it in either sale.

The Cally Estate today is much diminished and her descendants put it up for sale in 2025 (see map below – the Flesh Market is located just above the arrow ). It was re-marketed by Strutt and Parker earlier this year. In the brochures you can read some historical background to the Murray Usher family ownership. [1]

Sale plan from 2025 sales brochure

A community buyout of the estate has been proposed.

The remainder of the Cally Estate consisted of various properties in Gatehouse of Fleet. These are now owned by the Murray Usher Foundation.

Whether the Flesh Market is still owned by the Murray Usher family or the Foundation is not clear and can only be resolved by deeper historical research – but it seems very likely. 

Meanwhile this “left behind” bit of land has clearly been forgotten about. 

Future blogs in this series will reveal what can happen as a consequence.

WHAT IS THE FLESH MARKET?

The best known Flesh Market in Scotland is probably the historical one located in Edinburgh – the location of the Burgh’s meat market.

Map showing historic Edinburgh Flesh Market

But this is plainly not an explanation for these two rural locations in isolated places in the hills and away from any centres of population.

In a paper published on the Gatehouse Folk website, there is a discussion (page 4 of the pdf) of the origins of the name. The northern location may have been a site where deer were driven off the cliff-edge to their death, a common practice many centuries ago. But this would not appear to be a satisfactory explanation for the Flesh Market at Grobdale. The paper suggests that it may have been a droving stance.

However, the land here is exceptionally boggy and would appear to be unsuitable for such use. Some years ago someone (I cannot remember who) suggested to me that cattle had been known to get stuck in this bog and may have been slaughtered in situ thus giving rise to the place name.

If anyone has any information or insights, please do comment.

NOTES

[1] The 2025 brochure can be downloaded here (7Mb pdf) and the 2026 brochure here (7Mb pdf)

The post What is the Flesh Market and who owns it? first appeared on Land Matters.

September 10, 2026: The useful frontier.

Today's AI progress looks less like a single model leap and more like a buildout of usable intelligence across machines, clinics, networks, media, and power systems. The frontier is getting practical: AI is learning from demonstrations, moving through validated infrastructure, and showing up where scale, reliability, and cost actually matter.

Robotics had the clearest signal. [Skild AI](https://t.co/ZzfjGCOqDs) launched S1, a robot foundation model designed to learn previously unseen, long-horizon tasks from a single video demonstration without retraining, and NVIDIA says Skild reached a $100 million annual revenue run rate 10 months after its first commercial deployment. In tests on new multistep tasks, [S1](https://t.co/ZzfjGCOqDs) succeeded about 66% of the time at each step, versus 9% for a similar AI system, and Skild estimates one short video can substitute for roughly 380 hands-on training examples that could otherwise take 50 to 100 hours to collect. In plain English: factory robots are starting to learn from watching, not just from being laboriously reprogrammed.

That matters because physical AI is moving into messy real environments, not just controlled demos. [Skild, NVIDIA, and Foxconn](https://t.co/ZzfjGCOqDs) are deploying the Skild Brain on dual-arm manipulators for high-precision assembly of NVIDIA Blackwell systems, including a workflow that installs a busbar and limit block, fastens 16 screws, and adapts to disturbances. In construction, [Monumental](https://t.co/GAcM7V5BkM) is learning the same lesson from bricklaying robots: 92% of contractors have difficulty filling roles, the U.S. is short 4.5 million homes, and the company found that only about 10% of its technology is specific to bricklaying while the other 90% is general capability for operating robots on job sites. The useful breakthrough is not a humanoid pose; it is getting robots to handle materials, edge cases, weather, subcontractor dependencies, and the surprising black brick that was not in the training set.

Autonomy is also becoming an infrastructure problem. [NVIDIA](https://t.co/PZfP3ZYARc) says the global robotaxi market is projected to reach $400 billion by 2035, with more than 6 million commercial vehicles in operation, and describes robotaxi deployment as a three-computer stack: model training, simulation and validation, and in-vehicle computing. Its platform work points to why this is hard: robotaxi systems need fleet data for training, simulated rare events for validation, and redundant in-car sensing and compute for real-time driving. [NVIDIA](https://t.co/PZfP3ZYARc) also says adding reasoning data improved one autonomous-driving trajectory-prediction metric by 43%, reducing minimum average displacement error from 2.08 to 1.18. The headline is not just "cars drive themselves"; it is that commercial autonomy requires a full industrial stack from cloud to car.

Medicine offered a quieter version of the same shift from tool to system. [Nature Medicine](https://t.co/LDlva4wIsC) published lessons from real-world implementation of an AI-agent eye clinic in China, emphasizing that the move from AI-assisted tools to AI-native care requires workflow integration, clinician engagement, and measurable clinical value. In cancer research, [Medical Xpress](https://t.co/hc7hJSU8jO) reported that AI-designed proteins outperformed existing CAR T designs against BCMA tumors in mice, while noting that only about 4% of U.S. patients with advanced or metastatic cancer are currently candidates for CAR T therapy and closer to 3% will actually benefit. The promise here is not magic diagnosis or instant cures; it is a larger design space for therapies and care models that can be tested against real clinical value.

The compute layer is opening up too. [d-Matrix](https://t.co/5efhd5hAFa) will use NVIDIA NVLink Fusion to connect its next-generation Raptor XPUs into NVIDIA's rack-scale AI infrastructure, with sixth-generation NVLink offering 3 TB/s per XPU of all-to-all bandwidth, 3x lower XPU-to-XPU latency than off-the-shelf Ethernet, and 10x higher packet rates. The practical meaning is that specialized inference chips can plug into a mature rack, networking, power, cooling, software, and supply-chain platform instead of requiring every silicon company to rebuild the whole data-center stack. That same capacity story shows up in financing and geography: [Zankore](https://t.co/cwrfhBYf6j) secured a $3.1 billion senior term loan facility for an AI cloud buildout that starts at 100MW and scales toward 1GW, while [Loft Orbital, Marlan Space, and Mistral](https://t.co/HjDUNNe9nv) signed a $1 billion deal to launch a 50-satellite compute constellation.

The demand side is becoming measurable. [Pocket FM](https://t.co/xwG9OE8hpB) doubled its revenue run rate to $500 million as AI powers 93% of its audio content, uses AI to produce 99% of new content, and says production has become about 80 times cheaper. Meanwhile, the power system is adapting around AI and manufacturing load: [Utility Dive](https://t.co/TPlsquF8T2) reports that data centers and manufacturing expansion will drive U.S. electricity use 2% higher this year and next, while solar generation is expected to grow 21% this year and 18% in 2027; [Google and PG&E](https://t.co/3SfAcH1so3) are testing a privately funded virtual power plant through the SHARE program that could expand to commercial, industrial, and utility-scale resources. AI's next constraint is not imagination. It is execution: watts, racks, workflows, validation, and repeatable deployment.

The future arrives first as a system that works.

This AI Briefing is generated by using AI to review and synthesize multiple reports on AI infrastructure, bottlenecks, capital spending, and measurable business adoption into a single summary.

AI can make mistakes. For informational purposes only. Not financial advice.

text:
I had to go back to the actual timeline to make sure I hadn't goofed on the SEC enforcing it's bylaws and the application of Brentwood. I see the pushback -- e.g., punishing the coach for criticizing the refs -- but still see a First Amendment problem. It's a nun pro tunc First Amendment problem.   

Brentwood II turned on a rule that existed before the offending speech/conduct. TSSAA had a clear recruiting standard, the coach's letters violated it, and the school had adopted the rule itself.   

Look for the equivalent here. The pre-existing professionalism rule prohibits rostering a professional. LSU rostered no one. The August 26 SEC memorandum condemns recruiting as detrimental conduct but attaches penalties only to an institution that "includes an athlete on its roster." That trigger was never pulled, and the memo issued two days after Kiffin's first press conference on the matter. There's no SEC bylaw restricting a coach's criticism of conference policy.   

So what remains is a coach who said he felt for these pro players, said on GameDay the same and that he chose not to roster them because the risk was too high, and offered an obnoxious quip to ESPN at the halftime of the Clemson game. But the SEC proposes to punish Kiffin or even expel LSU, and it tells a federal court at ¶ 92 that his "statements and position" confirm the failure, while conceding at ¶¶ 81 and 94 that it will proceed whether LSU complies or not.   

Bottom line: strip out the speech and there is nothing left to punish.  

Now, again, even though nobody saw this coming, I think Kiffin and LSU didn't need to go here. The idea of an actual pro returning to college to compete has always been an anathema even though college athletes are, for all practical purposes today, pro athletes. All the AG's and governors spouting off in this dispute would do everyone a favor and butt out. 

Also, I think it is more than fair to say or even assume that the SEC and Sankey knows a lot more than anyone on this forum does, including yours truly. But going on the face of the complaint and the timeline of all of this, I still contend that a First Amendment problem is lurking, and that no one has really considered it.

text:
The Guardian: Trump’s $5,000 Midterm Pledge Decried as ‘Bribery’ as a Congressman Calls Him ‘the Biggest Liar’

The Guardian framed Donald Trump’s promise of $5,000 for every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans keep Congress in November as a bid to buy votes, not a fiscal plan. Speaking at an unprecedented Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Trump said that if Republicans win, voters win with them — and that the check would be called the “Trump dividend.” The newspaper placed the line against a national debt that crossed $40 trillion in August and against a trail of earlier payment pledges that never reached mailboxes.

A trillion-dollar bill on a $40 trillion debt

The arithmetic landed harder than the slogan. Ten-year Treasury yields are near 5 percent. Interest on the debt now exceeds what Washington spends on defense or Medicare. Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimated the one-year cost at about $1.2 trillion — more than all three rounds of Covid relief checks combined, and with no recession to justify the surge. The likely result, he argued, would be a spike in the deficit and then in inflation. His sharper warning was political: if the gambit works, every future candidate will learn that a trillion-dollar promise can win an election, and repeating that lesson across cycles is a path to insolvency.

Even Republicans sounded uneasy. Texas Representative Chip Roy asked how the party would pay for a back-of-the-envelope figure well over $1 trillion. Economist Peter Schiff said calling the checks “dividends” implied a surplus when the same policies have produced massive deficits, and that bond investors were already dumping Treasuries on the announcement alone. The Bipartisan Policy Center’s tariff tracker showed about $210 billion collected by early September 2026. At that pace, nearly five years of tariff revenue would be needed to cover a $5,000 payment — and only if every dollar survived legal challenges from retailers.

Promises that never arrived in the mail

Democrats treated the offer as the latest unpaid IOU. The DNC recalled DOGE “efficiency” checks and $2,000 tariff rebates that remained slogans without transfers. California Governor Gavin Newsom called the money a vote-buying payout after policies had already made households poorer. Representative Robert Garcia went further, calling Trump “the biggest liar ever to serve in government” and arguing that the $5,000 dividend is another in a series of promised payments that never materialize. Vice President JD Vance later tried to narrow the idea toward means-testing. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno, by contrast, said he would draft a bill to pass the “Trump Dividend” right after November 3.

Between The Guardian’s language of bribery and the congressional charge of serial lying sits a larger question: is the American economy being run as a national budget, or as a campaign whose checks are written against public debt? The pledge is contingent on the midterms. The cost is contingent on how much more Washington can borrow before the bond market sets the price. Until then the check is a political instrument more than a fiscal one — and The Guardian’s verdict is the frame through which the story entered the global debate.

text:
Bill Gates stood inside Tesla's Austin Gigafactory and called a 500-mile electric semi impossible.

The trucks were parked 40 feet away.

Pepsi had been running them since 2022. Real routes. Real freight. Rated for 82,000 pounds.

Musk offered him the keys. Drive one. Or send an engineer you trust and let him drive it.

Gates said no.

Not "show me." Not "let me check the spec." Just: it won't work.

Musk stopped arguing and started counting.

A long-haul electric truck can only fail 2 ways on paper. Either the pack stores too little energy per kilogram, or the truck burns too much energy per mile. Wh/kg or Wh/mile. That's the entire disagreement.

So he asked which one. Which number is wrong, and what do you think the right one is?

Gates didn't know the first number.

He didn't know the second one either.

He had flown to Austin, walked past working trucks, and issued a verdict on a machine whose 2 governing figures he had never once looked up.

50 years of building software. The largest tech company on earth. A net worth with 11 digits in it.

And zero measurements behind the word "impossible."

Musk didn't win that room with a better opinion. He won it with a question that costs nothing to ask.

Which number do you think is wrong?

He had the verdict. He just didn't have the numbers.

📊 So, did I make a mistake going this heavy into quantum?

Maybe.

A 35% exposure to one emerging technology is objectively aggressive.

If quantum sentiment collapses, these stocks aren't going to politely take turns falling.

They will probably fall together.

But that's the risk I've consciously chosen for this portfolio.

What matters more to me now is improving how I choose where to add capital inside that risk.

My current ranking based on fundamentals:

🥇 $IONQ — 8/10
🥈 $QBTS — 7.5/10
🥉 $RGTI — 7/10
🎲 $QUBT — 7/10

Interestingly, the companies aren't necessarily in the same order if we're talking about where I'd invest new money today.
Because a great company can still be an expensive stock.
And a weaker company can sometimes offer a better asymmetric opportunity.

That's probably the biggest lesson I'm taking from this year's performance.

Don't just ask whether quantum computing will be huge.

I think it will.

Ask whether the company you're buying today can capture enough of that future to justify the price you're paying for it now.

That's a much harder question.

And probably the one I should have been asking more often.

Let me offer a refined perspective based on wisdom and experience. First, and I am sorry to say this, the developer in question is not truly experienced in life enough to look through the lens of history and predict anything. He never LIVED through every technology jump in the last 45 years. ALL of them were filled with doomers.

I'm Gen X, we remember it all from Mtv fears of destroying youth, to...wait for it....the GLOBAL DOOM of the year 2000 when computers will go into a fault and launch the nukes, while sending us into the dark ages. (Never happened) We were also told, cel phones would give us all brain damage and kill us by 2000, nope. And told that the internet was a fad. Nope. Then we were told that the iPhone was a device we CAN NEVER use at work or we will be fired. Wow.

My father, a boomer, lived through hiding in shelters during drills for atomic bombs that never fell on America. It was never even a real threat and even now, nukes...nope. We Gen X were fed the nuke nonsense also. And it was in all our movies from War Games to Terminator. But I hate to tell you all, the tech to wipe us out like Terminator, came out like 25 years ago. And guess what, nothing happened.

My grandfather was told that the great depression would "wipe out humanity," and that America will never recover. His father was told that electricity would kill us all and that cars, airplanes and women voting would wipe out humans. Nope. Nope and....BIG NOPE!

In another 10 years, when all this AI negative nonsense is no more, because Ai is in everything from the fridge to your car, office, computer, tv home security and all in between, everyone will go crazy about robots saying "humans should walk their own dogs." And I bet someone will quit a company that builds robots and say, "I was on the inside of robot development, they are dangerous and will kill you and your children."

Then flying taxis will emerge. Then nano bots that can make us live 200 years or more. Then space travel will scale. Then aliens who we meet with, and on and on. There will always be doomers. They will always seek air time and media for attention and to prove a thesis that never becomes more than a foot note in laughable history.

This guy is young, not his fault, but in his lifetime we will extend life beyond imagination, travel the stars, fly around in drone like taxis, have robot companions, be driven everywhere by the driverless car, and I can't even imagine what else.

The doomer will say each moment is death inbound.

The optimist will embrace, grow & evolve.

I have a child, he's four. And three more over the age of 18. All of them will see the world change beyond your or my imagination.

We must learn to adapt, grow, and evolve.
